title: IL-26 · Data Analyst Certification & Senior Mastery Bootcamp
tagline: From zero to certified senior: math, SQL, stats, certs, portfolio — calibrated to the Palantir & BNY Mellon hiring bar.
blurb: IL-26 is a 96-hour independent practice course for data analysts, sequenced strictly from zero: a math-foundations track (arithmetic through calculus concepts), then SQL and Python, statistics and A/B testing, advanced analytics engineering, seven certification-exam tracks with a domain-by-domain crosswalk, employer hiring-bar tracks modeled on the publicly described senior bars at Palantir and BNY Mellon, and a complete portfolio-and-interview system. All exposition is original practice material aligned to publicly described exam topic maps and hiring bars; it confers no certificate, claims no affiliation with any vendor or employer, and is not endorsed by Palantir or BNY Mellon.
honestyNote: This is an independent preparation and practice course aligned to publicly described exam topic maps and hiring bars; it is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Google, Microsoft, Tableau, CompTIA, IBM, AWS, Databricks, Palantir, or BNY Mellon, confers no certificate, and grants no credential. Company and certification names appear only as topic references. All exposition is original practice material, and the assessments are for self-study only.
objectives: Master the math foundations data analysts actually use — arithmetic, algebra, functions, logarithms, summation, sets and logic, descriptive statistics, probability, linear algebra, and calculus concepts — with worked examples and drills, each module marked with the downstream modules it unlocks.
Write senior-level SQL fluently: window functions, recursive CTEs, query optimization, and execution-plan reading on realistic schemas.
Apply statistics correctly in analysis work: distributions, confidence intervals, regression, hypothesis testing, and A/B test design with sample-size reasoning.
Design dimensional models and reliable ETL/ELT pipelines with dbt-style transformations, orchestration concepts, and data-quality checks.

Map the exam domains, formats, and study plans of seven data-analytics certifications (Google, PL-300, Tableau, CompTIA Data+, IBM, AWS, Databricks) via the Certification Crosswalk and build a personal certification roadmap.

Meet the senior hiring bar at Palantir-style and BNY Mellon-style organizations: interview-grade SQL under pressure, probability brainteasers, product-sense cases, ontology thinking, the banking data domain (trades, P&L, VaR concepts, reconciliation), financial reporting controls, and production analyst ownership.
Build decision-grade dashboards and analyses in BI tools and Python, communicating findings to stakeholders with clarity and influence.
Ship an undeniable 7-project portfolio — GitHub repos, dashboards, and a capstone — and perform in senior analyst interview loops (SQL live-coding, cases, take-homes).

arc.title: Math Foundations (Part 0)
arc.body: Modules M26-M34 build mathematics from zero: arithmetic and algebra, functions and graphing, exponents and logarithms, summation notation, set theory and logic, descriptive statistics from first principles, probability foundations including Bayes' theorem, linear algebra essentials taught visually, and calculus concepts for analysts. Every module carries worked examples, practice drills with solutions, and an explicit 'you need this for' pointer to the downstream modules it unlocks. Nothing later in the course assumes math you have not seen here.

arc.title: Technical Core
arc.body: Modules M08-M18 and M25 in strict sequence: advanced SQL, then Python for analytics, then statistics and probability, then hypothesis and A/B testing, then data modeling, pipelines, cloud platforms, BI and visualization mastery, Excel/Sheets power skills, governance and ethics, stakeholder communication, and R essentials. Each module lists its math prerequisites; the path never asks for a technique whose foundation was skipped.

arc.title: Certification Tracks
arc.body: Modules M01-M07 map the seven certification landscapes: Google Data Analytics, Microsoft PL-300, Tableau Certified Data Analyst, CompTIA Data+, IBM Data Analyst, AWS data analytics, and Databricks Certified Data Analyst. For each: exam domains, question formats, scoring, study plan, and a domain-by-domain crosswalk to the IL-26 modules that teach it. You leave with a sequenced certification roadmap, not just a list.

arc.title: Employer Hiring-Bar Tracks
arc.body: Modules M35-M40 calibrate everything to the senior hiring bar at two target employers, modeled strictly on their publicly described bars with no affiliation claimed. Palantir track: advanced SQL under interview pressure, Python/probability/product-sense, ontology and pipeline thinking. BNY Mellon track: the banking data domain (trades, positions, P&L attribution, VaR conceptually, reconciliation) and financial reporting controls (BCBS 239 principles, CCAR-style concepts, audit-trail BI). Plus a day-in-the-life module on production analyst ownership.

arc.title: Portfolio, Interviews & Launch
arc.body: Modules M19-M24 convert skill into proof: the 7-project portfolio architecture, GitHub portfolio engineering, dashboard portfolios hiring managers respect, a full capstone blueprint from ingest to write-up, senior interview-loop preparation (live SQL, cases, take-homes, behavioral), and a 90-day certification and job-readiness roadmap with weekly milestones.

modules.title: Arithmetic & Algebra Refresher
modules.summary: Rebuild fluency in order of operations, linear equations, ratios, and percentages from zero. You need this for -> percent-change KPIs, unit-rate comparisons, and algebra-driven derived metrics in every downstream module.
objectives: Apply PEMDAS order of operations to multi-step expressions by hand, without a calculator.
Solve one-variable linear equations by isolating the unknown on one side.
Compute ratios, proportions, percent change, and percentage-point differences correctly.
Translate plain-English data questions (discounts, growth, margins) into correct arithmetic.

notes.title: Order of operations (PEMDAS)
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** sanity-checking every computed metric by hand: if you cannot evaluate (120 + 30 * 4) / 2 correctly, you cannot trust a KPI you did not double-check.
- Parentheses first, then Exponents, then Multiplication/Division (left to right), then Addition/Subtraction (left to right).
- Multiplication and division are equals: 20 / 5 * 2 = 4 * 2 = 8, NOT 20 / 10 = 2. Go left to right.
- A fraction bar is a hidden parenthesis: (8 + 4) / (2 + 4) means compute top and bottom separately first.
- WORKED EXAMPLE:
```
2 + 3 * 4^2
= 2 + 3 * 16     (exponents first: 4^2 = 16)
= 2 + 48         (multiplication next: 3 * 16 = 48)
= 50             (addition last)
```
- Compare with (2 + 3) * 4^2 = 5 * 16 = 80: parentheses change everything.

notes.title: Solving linear equations
notes.body:
- A linear equation has the unknown to the first power only: 3x - 7 = 20. Goal: isolate x.
- Do the SAME operation to both sides, undoing in reverse order of operations: undo +/-, then undo *//.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (sales planning): revenue = 40x + 2000, where x = units sold. Target revenue 14000.
```
40x + 2000 = 14000
40x = 14000 - 2000      (subtract 2000 from both sides)
40x = 12000
x = 12000 / 40          (divide both sides by 40)
x = 300                  (300 units hits the target)
```
- Always plug back in: 40(300) + 2000 = 12000 + 2000 = 14000. Checks out.
- If the unknown appears on both sides (2x + 5 = x + 12), move all x-terms to one side first: x = 7.

notes.title: Ratios and proportions
notes.body:
- A ratio compares two quantities: Region A sold 45000 with 300 reps, so 45000/300 = 150 per rep. Ratios only make sense in the same units.
- A proportion says two ratios are equal: 3/4 = x/20. Cross-multiply: 3 * 20 = 4 * x, so 60 = 4x, x = 15.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (per-rep comparison): Region A: 45000/300 = 150 per rep. Region B: 60000/500 = 120 per rep. Region A wins per-rep even though B's total is bigger - never compare raw totals across different-sized groups.
- Unit rates are just ratios with denominator 1: dollars per click, tickets per agent-hour, defects per thousand units.
- Scaling a recipe scales by proportion: if 2 analysts finish 10 reports in a week, x analysts finish 25 reports: 2/10 = x/25, x = 5.

notes.title: Percent change vs percentage points
notes.body:
- Percent means 'per hundred': 40% of 250 = 0.40 * 250 = 100.
- Percent change = (new - old) / old. Always divide by the OLD value, never the new one.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: sales 120K -> 150K. Change = 150 - 120 = 30. Percent change = 30/120 = 0.25 = 25% increase.
- Percentage POINTS are the raw difference of two percentages: conversion 20% -> 25% is a 5 percentage point lift, which is a 25% relative increase (5/20 = 0.25). Saying 'up 5%' here is wrong and misleading.
- The classic trap: a metric 'up 50%' then 'down 50%' does NOT return to start. 100 -> 150 -> 75. Percentages compound asymmetrically.
- Margins are percentages too: (revenue - cost) / revenue = (80K - 60K) / 80K = 25% margin.

cards.front: What is the PEMDAS order?
cards.back: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right). 2 + 3 * 4 = 14, not 20.

cards.front: How do you solve 3x - 7 = 20?
cards.back: Add 7 to both sides (3x = 27), then divide by 3: x = 9. Plug back to check: 3(9) - 7 = 20.

cards.front: Formula for percent change?
cards.back: (new - old) / old, times 100 for %. Always divide by the OLD value. 120 -> 150 is (30/120) = 25%.

cards.front: What is the difference between percent and percentage points?
cards.back: Percent is relative: (25-20)/20 = 25% increase. Percentage points is raw difference: 25% - 20% = 5 percentage points.

cards.front: Solve the proportion 3/4 = x/20.
cards.back: Cross-multiply: 3 * 20 = 4x, so 60 = 4x, x = 15.

cards.front: Why compare per-rep sales instead of raw totals?
cards.back: Raw totals reward bigger teams. 45000/300 = 150 per rep beats 60000/500 = 120 per rep. Rates normalize for group size.

cards.front: 100 is up 50%, then down 50%. Final value?
cards.back: 75. Up 50%: 100 -> 150. Down 50%: 150 -> 75. Percent moves compound asymmetrically.

cards.front: Formula for profit margin?
cards.back: (revenue - cost) / revenue. (80K - 60K) / 80K = 25% margin.

quiz.q: What is 2 + 3 * 4^2?
quiz.explain: Exponents first: 4^2 = 16. Multiplication: 3 * 16 = 48. Addition: 2 + 48 = 50. (Module 26)

quiz.q: Solve 3x - 7 = 20.
quiz.explain: Add 7: 3x = 27. Divide by 3: x = 9. Check: 3(9) - 7 = 20. (Module 26)

quiz.q: Sales rise from $120K to $150K. What is the percent change?
quiz.explain: (150 - 120) / 120 = 30 / 120 = 0.25 = 25% increase. Divide by the old value. (Module 26)

quiz.q: Conversion rate moves from 20% to 25%. How many percentage points is that?
quiz.explain: Raw difference: 25 - 20 = 5 percentage points. (A 25% relative increase is a different statement.) (Module 26)

quiz.q: Solve 3/4 = x/20.
quiz.explain: Cross-multiply: 3 * 20 = 4x, so 60 = 4x and x = 15. (Module 26)
The fraction bar groups like parentheses: top = 12, bottom = 6, 12/6 = 2. (Module 26)

quiz.q: What is 40% of 250?
Revenue is $80K and cost is $60K. What is the margin?

modules.title: Functions & Graphing
modules.summary: Learn what a function is, domain and range, the linear/quadratic/exponential shapes behind real charts, and slope as a rate of change. You need this for -> reading any chart as a function, interpreting trend slopes, and modeling relationships in downstream modules.
objectives: Define a function as a rule giving each input exactly one output; distinguish functions from non-functions.
State the domain (allowed inputs) and range (possible outputs) for common function types.
Sketch and recognize linear, quadratic, and exponential shapes in charts.
Interpret slope as a rate of change in business terms (revenue per day, cost per unit).

notes.title: What a function is
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** every formula you will ever write: revenue = price * units is a function of units. Knowing which value is the input and which is the output stops circular-reasoning mistakes.
- A function is a rule: every input x produces EXACTLY one output y. We write y = f(x), read 'f of x'.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: f(x) = 3x + 50 (total cost: $3 per unit plus $50 fixed).
```
f(10) = 3(10) + 50 = 30 + 50 = 80
f(0)  = 3(0) + 50 = 50   (zero units still costs the $50 fixed fee)
```
- y = +/- sqrt(x) is NOT a function of x: input 9 gives outputs 3 AND -3. One input, two outputs breaks the rule.
- Think of a function as a machine: same input always gives the same output, every time.

notes.title: Domain and range
notes.body:
- Domain = all inputs the function is allowed to take. Range = all outputs it can produce.
- For p(x) = 40x + 2000 (revenue from x units), the domain is x >= 0 (negative units are nonsense) and the range is values >= 2000.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: g(x) = 1 / (x - 4). Division by zero is forbidden, so x - 4 = 0 is banned: domain = all real numbers EXCEPT x = 4. Its range is all real numbers except 0.
- For f(x) = sqrt(x), domain is x >= 0 (no real square root of a negative), range is y >= 0.
- In data work: the domain of a 'price' column is prices >= 0, and a range check (min/max) catches bad data like negative prices.

notes.title: The three shapes that run data work
notes.body:
- LINEAR: y = mx + b. A straight line. Constant rate: +$125 of revenue every day, forever. Steepness = slope m.
- QUADRATIC: y = ax^2 + bx + c. A U-shape (or upside-down U). Example: profit vs ad spend rises then falls past the saturation point.
- EXPONENTIAL: y = a * b^x. Doubling (or halving) each step. Viral signups, compounding, radioactive decay.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: points (1,2), (2,4), (3,8), (4,16). Each step DOUBLES: this is exponential, y = 2^x, not linear (linear would add a constant) and not quadratic.
- Chart reading: a straight line on a regular chart = linear; a straight line on a log-y chart = exponential (see M28).

notes.title: Slope as rate of change
notes.body:
- Slope = rise / run = (change in y) / (change in x). It is the rate: how many units of output per unit of input.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: cumulative tickets resolved: 240 by day 2, 840 by day 6.
```
slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
      = (840 - 240) / (6 - 2)
      = 600 / 4
      = 150 tickets per day
```
- Positive slope = increasing, negative = decreasing, zero = flat. A steeper slope = a faster rate.
- In revenue = 125 * day + 2000, the slope 125 is '$125 of revenue per day' - the y-intercept 2000 is the starting baseline.
- For curved data the slope changes along the curve; the slope AT a point is the tangent line's slope (this is the derivative in M34).

cards.front: What is a function?
cards.back: A rule where each input x produces exactly one output y, written y = f(x). Same input always gives the same output.

cards.front: Is y = +/- sqrt(x) a function of x?
cards.back: No. Input 9 gives two outputs (3 and -3). A function allows exactly one output per input.

cards.front: What are domain and range?
cards.back: Domain = allowed inputs. Range = possible outputs. For 1/(x-4), domain is all x except 4.

cards.front: What three curve shapes matter most in data work?
cards.back: Linear (straight line, constant rate), quadratic (U-shape, rises then falls), exponential (doubling/halving each step).

cards.front: Slope formula and meaning?
cards.back: slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) = rise/run. It is the rate of change: output units per input unit.

cards.front: How do you spot an exponential from data points?
cards.back: Outputs multiply by a constant each step: (1,2),(2,4),(3,8),(4,16) doubles each time, so y = 2^x.

cards.front: In revenue = 125 * day + 2000, what do 125 and 2000 mean?
cards.back: 125 = slope = $125 revenue per day (rate). 2000 = y-intercept = baseline revenue at day 0.

cards.front: What does a negative slope tell you about a trend?
cards.back: The output decreases as the input increases - a declining trend, e.g. churn rising as satisfaction falls.

quiz.q: If f(x) = 2x + 7, what is f(5)?
Which relation is NOT a function of x?
quiz.explain: y = +/- sqrt(x) gives two outputs for one input (e.g. x = 9 gives 3 and -3), violating the one-output rule. (Module 27)

quiz.q: What is the slope of the line through (1,3) and (5,11)?
Which function grows by doubling each step?
quiz.explain: Exponential functions multiply by a constant base each step (e.g. y = 2^x doubles). (Module 27)

quiz.q: What is the domain of g(x) = 1 / (x - 4)?
quiz.explain: Division by zero is forbidden: x - 4 = 0 when x = 4, so that input is excluded. (Module 27)

quiz.q: The points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9) fit which shape?
quiz.explain: Outputs are 1^2, 2^2, 3^2 - that is y = x^2, a quadratic (U-shape). (Module 27)

quiz.q: What does a negative slope mean for a trend?
quiz.explain: Negative slope = output falls as input rises: a decreasing trend. (Module 27)

quiz.q: In revenue = 125 * day + 2000, how much revenue is added per day?
quiz.explain: The slope 125 is the rate: $125 of revenue per day. 2000 is just the day-0 baseline. (Module 27)

modules.title: Exponents & Logarithms
modules.summary: Master exponent rules, meet the logarithm as the 'un-exponent', and learn why log-scale charts turn explosive growth into readable straight lines. You need this for -> growth math, doubling times, and correctly reading log-axis revenue charts in downstream modules.
objectives: Apply exponent rules (product, quotient, power, negative, zero) to simplify expressions.
Explain a logarithm as the inverse of exponentiation: log asks '10 to what power?'.
Convert between exponential and logarithmic form and evaluate common logs by hand.
Read log-scale charts: explain why equal vertical distances mean equal RATIOS, not equal differences.

notes.title: Exponent rules
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** growth math: compound growth, doubling times, and the log-scale charts that make exponential growth readable.
- Product rule: x^a * x^b = x^(a+b). Quotient rule: x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). Power rule: (x^a)^b = x^(a*b).
- Negative exponents flip: x^-2 = 1 / x^2. Zero exponent: x^0 = 1 (for x != 0).
- WORKED EXAMPLE:
```
x^3 * x^4 = x^(3+4) = x^7
(x^5)^2   = x^(5*2)  = x^10
2^4 / 2^6 = 2^(4-6)  = 2^-2 = 1/4
```
- (2^4)^3 = 2^12, NOT 2^7: multiplying exponents under a power, not adding. The #1 exponent mistake.

notes.title: Logarithms are un-exponents
notes.body:
- log_b(x) answers: 'b to WHAT POWER gives x?' So log_10(1000) = 3 because 10^3 = 1000.
- Exponential form 2^5 = 32 converts to logarithmic form log_2(32) = 5. Same fact, two notations.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: log_2(32). Ask: 2 to what power is 32? 2^1=2, 2^2=4, 2^3=8, 2^4=16, 2^5=32. Answer: 5.
- log_10(10,000) = 4 (four zeros). ln(x) is log base e (~2.718), the natural log used in growth formulas.
- A logarithm turns multiplication into addition: doubling the input adds a constant to the log. That is the whole reason log scales exist.

notes.title: Log scales on charts
notes.body:
- On a log10 y-axis, the ticks go 10, 100, 1000, 10000 with EQUAL spacing: each step multiplies by 10. Equal vertical distance = equal RATIO, not equal difference.
- A straight line on a log-y chart means constant PERCENTAGE growth (exponential), because log turns multiplication into addition.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: a startup's revenue: year 1 = 10K, year 2 = 20K, year 3 = 40K.
```
Linear chart: the line curves upward - growth looks like it is 'accelerating'.
log10 chart:  log10(10K)=4, log10(20K)~4.3, log10(40K)~4.6
              Equal gaps (0.3 each) -> a STRAIGHT line.
Conclusion: steady 2x/year growth. The log chart reveals the constant rate
that the linear chart hides behind its exploding curve.
```
- Flat-then-exploding linear charts mislead stakeholders; the log view answers 'is growth speeding up or steady?' instantly.

notes.title: Log rules
notes.body:
- log(a * b) = log a + log b. log(a / b) = log a - log b. log(a^n) = n * log a.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (base 10): log(100) + log(1000) = 2 + 3 = 5 = log(100 * 1000) = log(100,000). Check: 10^5 = 100,000.
- Change of base: log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b). Rarely needed by hand, but it is how calculators compute any base.
- log(1) = 0 for any base (b^0 = 1). log_b(b) = 1.
- Inverse pairs cancel: 10^(log_10(x)) = x and log_10(10^x) = x. The log is literally the undo button for powers of 10.

cards.front: Simplify x^3 * x^4.
cards.back: x^7. Product rule: add exponents when multiplying same-base powers.

cards.front: What does log_10(1000) mean and equal?
Evaluate log_2(32).
cards.back: 5, because 2^5 = 32. Count doublings: 2,4,8,16,32.

cards.front: On a log10 chart, what does equal vertical spacing mean?
cards.back: Equal RATIOS (multiples of 10), not equal differences. 10->100 and 100->1000 are the same gap.

cards.front: Why do revenue charts go log?
cards.back: Exponential growth explodes on a linear axis and hides the rate. On log-y it becomes a straight line, so steady vs accelerating growth is visible at a glance.

cards.front: Simplify (2^4)^3.
cards.back: 2^12. Power rule: multiply exponents. (Not 2^7.)

cards.front: What is log(100) + log(1000) in base 10?
cards.back: 5. log(a*b) = log a + log b, so log(100000) = 5.

cards.front: What are 2^-3 and 5^0?
cards.back: 2^-3 = 1/8 (negative flips to the denominator). 5^0 = 1 (any nonzero base to the zero power).

quiz.q: Simplify x^5 * x^3.
quiz.explain: Product rule: add exponents. 5 + 3 = 8, so x^8. (Module 28)

quiz.q: What is log_10(10,000)?
quiz.explain: '10 to what power is 10,000?' 10^4 = 10,000, so the answer is 4. (Module 28)

quiz.q: Simplify (2^4)^3.
quiz.explain: Power rule: multiply exponents. 4 * 3 = 12, so 2^12 (= 4096, but 2^12 is the exact form). (Module 28)

quiz.q: On a log10 chart, equal vertical gaps represent what?
quiz.explain: Each equal gap multiplies by 10: 10->100 and 100->1000 are the same distance. (Module 28)

quiz.q: What is 5^0?
quiz.explain: Any nonzero base to the zero power is 1. (Module 28)

quiz.q: What is 2^-3?
quiz.explain: Negative exponent flips: 2^-3 = 1/2^3 = 1/8. (Module 28)

quiz.q: What is log(100) + log(1000) in base 10?
quiz.explain: log(a) + log(b) = log(a*b) = log(100,000) = 5. (Module 28)

quiz.q: If log_3(x) = 4, what is x?
quiz.explain: '3 to what power is x?' 3^4 = 81, so x = 81. (Module 28)

modules.title: Summation Notation
modules.summary: Read sigma notation, expand sums, apply the three sum rules, and connect it all to SQL SUM(), AVG(), and COUNT(). You need this for -> reading statistics formulas, writing correct aggregations, and understanding what AVG() actually computes downstream.
objectives: Read sigma notation: identify the index, lower/upper bounds, and the term being summed.
Expand a sigma sum into its individual terms and evaluate small sums by hand.
Apply the three sum rules: constant multiple, sum of sums, sum of constants.
Map sigma sums to SQL: SUM(), AVG() as sum/n, and COUNT() over grouped rows.

notes.title: Reading sigma notation
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** reading statistics formulas (means, variances) and writing correct aggregations: AVG(revenue) is literally sigma(revenue_i) / n.
- sum_{i=1}^{4} 2i reads: 'sum over i, from i = 1 to 4, of 2i'. i is the index, 1 is the lower bound, 4 the upper bound, 2i the term.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: expand and evaluate.
```
sum_{i=1}^{4} 2i = 2(1) + 2(2) + 2(3) + 2(4)
                 = 2 + 4 + 6 + 8
                 = 20
```
- sum_{i=1}^{3} (i + 1) = (1+1) + (2+1) + (3+1) = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.
- The index letter is a dummy: sum_{k=1}^{3} k and sum_{i=1}^{3} i are the same sum (both = 6).

notes.title: The three sum rules
notes.body:
- Rule 1 (constants factor out): sum c*x_i = c * sum x_i. Pull multipliers out front.
- Rule 2 (sums split): sum (x_i + y_i) = sum x_i + sum y_i.
- Rule 3 (constant sums): sum_{i=1}^{n} c = n * c. Adding c exactly n times.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: sum_{i=1}^{4} (3i - 1). Split (rule 2): sum 3i - sum 1. Factor (rule 1): 3 * sum i = 3 * 10 = 30. Constant (rule 3): 4 terms of 1 = 4. Result: 30 - 4 = 26.
- Sanity check by expansion: (3-1) + (6-1) + (9-1) + (12-1) = 2 + 5 + 8 + 11 = 26. Matches.
- These rules are why SUM(3 * price) = 3 * SUM(price) in SQL: the engine uses the same algebra.

notes.title: Sigma meets SQL
notes.body:
- SUM(revenue) is sum_{i=1}^{n} revenue_i over the table's n rows. COUNT(*) is sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n (rule 3: n ones).
- AVG(revenue) = (1/n) * sum revenue_i = SUM(revenue) / COUNT(*). The mean is a scaled sigma.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: daily signups 12, 18, 20 over 3 days.
```
SUM = 12 + 18 + 20 = 50
AVG = 50 / 3 = 16.67
GROUP BY turns one big sum into many small sums, one per group.
```
- AVG(AVG(x)) is NOT AVG(x) across groups: averaging group averages without weighting by group size is the classic sigma mistake. Weight by n.
- DISTINCT inside an aggregate changes the index set: SUM(DISTINCT x) sums each value once, like summing over a set instead of a multiset.

notes.title: Double sums and pivot tables
notes.body:
- A double sum sum_{i=1}^{2} sum_{j=1}^{2} (i + j) adds every combination: expand the inner sum for each outer i.
- WORKED EXAMPLE:
```
i = 1: j = 1 -> 2,  j = 2 -> 3   (subtotal 5)
i = 2: j = 1 -> 3,  j = 2 -> 4   (subtotal 7)
Total = 5 + 7 = 12
```
- This is a pivot table's grand total: rows i, columns j, each cell (i+j), summed over everything.
- Order does not matter: summing rows-first or columns-first gives the same grand total (Fubini for finite sums).
- GROUPING SETS / ROLLUP in SQL compute sums at multiple groupings at once: the same nested-sum idea, automated.

cards.front: In sum_{i=1}^{4} 2i, what are i, 1, 4, and 2i?
cards.back: i = index, 1 = lower bound, 4 = upper bound, 2i = the term being summed. Expand: 2+4+6+8 = 20.

cards.front: State the three sum rules.
cards.back: 1) sum c*x_i = c * sum x_i. 2) sum (x_i + y_i) = sum x_i + sum y_i. 3) sum_{i=1}^{n} c = n*c.

cards.front: Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{3} i.
How is AVG(x) expressed with sigma?
cards.back: AVG(x) = (1/n) * sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = SUM(x) / COUNT(*). The mean is a scaled sum.

cards.front: What does COUNT(*) equal in sigma terms?
cards.back: sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n: adding 1 once per row.

cards.front: Why is AVG of group AVGs usually wrong?
cards.back: Group averages need weighting by group size. AVG(AVG(x)) treats a 2-row group and a 2000-row group equally - weight by n.

cards.front: Evaluate the double sum sum_{i=1}^{2} sum_{j=1}^{2} (i+j).
cards.back: i=1: 2+3=5; i=2: 3+4=7; total 12. It is a pivot table's grand total.

cards.front: Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{4} (3i - 1) using the sum rules.

quiz.q: Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{3} i.
Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{4} 2i.
What is sum_{i=1}^{n} c for a constant c?
quiz.explain: Rule 3: adding the constant c exactly n times gives n*c. (Module 29)

quiz.q: Which SQL equals (1/n) * sum(x_i)?
quiz.explain: AVG(x) = SUM(x) / COUNT(*): the mean is a scaled sigma sum. (Module 29)

quiz.q: Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{3} (i + 1).
Evaluate sum_{k=1}^{3} 3k.
quiz.explain: Factor out 3 (rule 1): 3 * (1+2+3) = 3 * 6 = 18. (Module 29)

quiz.q: COUNT(*) over a table is sigma-equivalent to:
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) = sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n: one per row. (Module 29)

quiz.q: Evaluate sum_{i=1}^{2} sum_{j=1}^{2} (i+j).

modules.title: Set Theory & Logic
modules.summary: Learn sets, unions/intersections/complements, Venn diagrams, AND/OR/NOT truth tables, and see JOINs as set operations and WHERE clauses as Boolean logic. You need this for -> correct JOIN reasoning, filter logic, and deduplication in downstream SQL modules.
objectives: Define sets, elements, and subsets; use union, intersection, complement, and difference notation.
Draw and read Venn diagrams for two and three overlapping sets.
Build AND/OR/NOT truth tables and evaluate compound conditions.
Translate JOIN types to set operations and WHERE clauses to Boolean logic.

notes.title: Sets and membership
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** thinking in JOINs and filters: a table is a set of rows, WHERE carves out a subset, and JOIN types are union/intersection/difference wearing SQL syntax.
- A set is a collection of distinct elements: customers = {A, B, C}. Order does not matter, duplicates collapse: {1, 2, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3}.
- x in S means x is a member; x not in S means it is not. A subset B of A means every member of B is in A.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: customers = {A, B, C, D}, premium = {B, D}. premium is a subset of customers. A (in customers, not premium) vs B (in both) differ in exactly one membership fact.
- The empty set {} has zero members. Every set's subset list includes the empty set and itself.

notes.title: Unions, intersections, complements
notes.body:
- A UNION B: everything in A or B (or both). A INTERSECT B: only what is in BOTH. A - B (difference): in A but not B.
- The complement of S (within a universe U) is everything in U not in S: 'non-churned customers' = all customers minus churned.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {3, 4, 5}.
```
A UNION B     = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}   (3 and 4 appear once - no double count)
A INTERSECT B = {3, 4}
A - B         = {1, 2}
B - A         = {5}
```
- Inclusion-exclusion: |A UNION B| = |A| + |B| - |A INTERSECT B|. The overlap is subtracted because it was counted twice.
- 60 bought A, 50 bought B, 30 bought both: at least one = 60 + 50 - 30 = 80.

notes.title: AND/OR/NOT truth tables
notes.body:
- AND is TRUE only when both sides are TRUE. OR is TRUE when at least one side is TRUE. NOT flips TRUE to FALSE and back.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (the full truth table):
```
A     | B     | A AND B | A OR B
TRUE  | TRUE  | TRUE    | TRUE
TRUE  | FALSE | FALSE   | TRUE
FALSE | TRUE  | FALSE   | TRUE
FALSE | FALSE | FALSE   | FALSE

NOT TRUE = FALSE,  NOT FALSE = TRUE
```
- AND narrows (more conditions = fewer rows pass), OR widens (more conditions = more rows pass). This single fact debugs most broken WHERE clauses.
- De Morgan's laws: NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B); NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B). Negation flips the operator.

notes.title: JOINs are set operations; WHERE is Boolean logic
notes.body:
- INNER JOIN on customer_id: rows whose keys are in the INTERSECTION of both tables' key sets.
- LEFT JOIN: every row of the left set, matched where possible (left set plus the intersection).
- FULL OUTER JOIN: the UNION of both key sets. Anti-join (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL): the DIFFERENCE, left minus right.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: WHERE country = 'US' AND plan = 'Pro' returns customers in the intersection of {US customers} and {Pro customers} - both conditions must hold.
- Translating with De Morgan: 'NOT (churned OR delinquent)' = 'NOT churned AND NOT delinquent' = active AND in-good-standing. Say it either way; the logic is identical.
- UNION in SQL is set union (deduped); UNION ALL keeps duplicates - it is a multiset, not a true set operation.

cards.front: What is {1,2,3} UNION {3,4}?
cards.back: {1,2,3,4}. Union takes everything from either set; 3 appears only once.

cards.front: What is {1,2,3} INTERSECT {3,4}?
cards.back: {3}. Intersection takes only what is in both.

cards.front: State the inclusion-exclusion formula.
cards.back: |A UNION B| = |A| + |B| - |A INTERSECT B|. Subtract the overlap because it was counted twice.

cards.front: Write the AND truth table.
cards.back: T AND T = T; T AND F = F; F AND T = F; F AND F = F. TRUE only when both are TRUE.

cards.front: State De Morgan's laws.
cards.back: NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B). Negation flips the operator.

cards.front: Which JOIN is the intersection of key sets?
cards.back: INNER JOIN: only rows whose keys exist in BOTH tables.

cards.front: What does a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL return?
cards.back: The set DIFFERENCE: left-table rows with no match - left minus right.

cards.front: Does AND narrow or widen a filter? What about OR?
cards.back: AND narrows (fewer rows pass). OR widens (more rows pass).

quiz.q: What is {1,2,3} UNION {3,4}?
quiz.explain: Union takes everything from either set; 3 appears once. (Module 30)

quiz.q: What is {1,2,3} INTERSECT {3,4}?
quiz.explain: Only 3 is in both sets. (Module 30)

quiz.q: What is TRUE AND FALSE?
quiz.explain: AND is TRUE only when both sides are TRUE. (Module 30)

quiz.q: INNER JOIN returns rows whose keys:
choices: exist in the left table only
exist in the right table only
quiz.explain: INNER JOIN is the intersection of the two key sets. (Module 30)

quiz.q: The complement of 'churned customers' within 'all customers' is:
quiz.explain: Complement = universe minus the set: everyone who did not churn. (Module 30)

quiz.q: By De Morgan, NOT (A OR B) equals:
quiz.explain: Negation flips OR to AND: NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). (Module 30)

quiz.q: A FULL OUTER JOIN is closest to which set operation?
quiz.explain: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps keys from either side: the union of key sets. (Module 30)

quiz.q: A AND B is TRUE only when:
quiz.explain: AND requires both operands TRUE. (Module 30)

modules.title: Descriptive Statistics from First Principles
modules.summary: Compute mean, median, and mode by hand, learn why each one misleads, derive variance and standard deviation step-by-step, and read percentiles and quartiles. You need this for -> every dashboard summary, distribution check, and outlier decision in downstream analytics modules.
objectives: Compute mean, median, and mode by hand and explain when each measure misleads.
Compute variance and standard deviation step-by-step from a small dataset.
Interpret standard deviation as 'typical distance from the mean'.
Define quartiles and percentiles and read a five-number summary.

notes.title: Mean, median, mode
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** every dashboard summary you will ever write: picking the wrong center measure (mean on skewed revenue data) silently lies to stakeholders.
- MEAN: sum / count. MEDIAN: the middle value when sorted (average the two middles if even count). MODE: the most frequent value.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: salaries 40, 45, 50, 55, 500 (CEO included, in thousands).
```
Mean   = (40 + 45 + 50 + 55 + 500) / 5 = 690 / 5 = 138
Median = the middle of [40, 45, 50, 55, 500] = 50
Mode   = none (no repeats)
The CEO drags the mean to 138K while a typical employee earns 50K.
```
- Report the median (or both) when outliers dominate; report the mean when every value should count equally, like total/average revenue.

notes.title: Why each center misleads
notes.body:
- The MEAN is dragged by outliers: one billionaire in the room makes the 'average' person a millionaire. Useless for skewed pay, revenue, or home prices.
- The MEDIAN hides the shape: two teams can share median 50K while one spans 45-55K and the other 10-500K. Same center, wildly different risk.
- The MODE is useless on continuous data (no two revenues match exactly) and can be multimodal: two humps mean two different populations mixed together.
- Simpson-style caution: an overall mean can reverse subgroup patterns (e.g. higher overall conversion despite lower conversion in every segment) when group sizes differ. Always segment before trusting a single number.
- Rule of thumb for dashboards: show mean AND median on skewed metrics; the gap between them is itself a signal of skew.

notes.title: Variance and standard deviation, computed by hand
notes.body:
- Variance = average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation = its square root, back in original units.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (population variance) on 2, 4, 6, 8, 10:
```
Step 1: mean = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6
Step 2: deviations from mean = -4, -2, 0, 2, 4
Step 3: squared deviations = 16, 4, 0, 4, 16
Step 4: sum of squares = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40
Step 5: variance = 40 / 5 = 8   (population: divide by n)
Step 6: std dev = sqrt(8) ~ 2.83
```
- Squaring makes deviations positive and punishes far outliers (a deviation of 4 contributes 16). The square root at the end restores original units: dollars, days, tickets.
- Sample variance divides by n-1 (Bessel's correction) because a sample mean underestimates spread; population variance divides by n.

notes.title: Percentiles and quartiles
notes.body:
- The p-th percentile is the value with p% of data at or below it. The median is the 50th percentile.
- Quartiles split sorted data into quarters: Q1 = 25th percentile, Q2 = median, Q3 = 75th percentile. IQR = Q3 - Q1, the spread of the middle 50%.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: response times (minutes) sorted: 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18.
```
Median (Q2) = average of 4th and 5th values = (7 + 9) / 2 = 8
Q1 = median of lower half [2, 3, 5, 7] = (3 + 5) / 2 = 4
Q3 = median of upper half [9, 11, 14, 18] = (11 + 14) / 2 = 12.5
IQR = 12.5 - 4 = 8.5 minutes
Five-number summary: min 2, Q1 4, median 8, Q3 12.5, max 18.
```
- 'Top 10%' = above the 90th percentile. Box plots draw exactly this five-number summary.

cards.front: Compute mean, median of 40, 45, 50, 55, 500.
cards.back: Mean = 690/5 = 138. Median = middle of sorted list = 50. The outlier CEO drags the mean.

cards.front: When should you report the median instead of the mean?
cards.back: On skewed data with outliers (pay, revenue, home prices) - the median resists the drag of extreme values.

cards.front: What is variance, in plain words?
cards.back: Average squared distance of values from the mean. Bigger variance = more spread.

cards.front: Compute population variance of 2,4,6,8,10.
cards.back: Mean 6; squared deviations 16,4,0,4,16 sum to 40; 40/5 = 8.

cards.front: How do you get standard deviation from variance?
cards.back: Take the square root. sqrt(8) ~ 2.83 here - it restores the original units (dollars, days).

cards.front: What is the IQR?
cards.back: Q3 - Q1: the spread of the middle 50% of data. Resistant to outliers, unlike the full range.

cards.front: What percentile is the median?
cards.back: The 50th percentile: half the values are at or below it.

cards.front: What is a five-number summary?
cards.back: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Exactly what a box plot draws.

quiz.q: What is the mean of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10?
What is the median of 3, 1, 4, 1, 5?
quiz.explain: Sorted: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5. The middle value is 3. (Module 31)

quiz.q: What is the population variance of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10?
quiz.explain: Squared deviations 16,4,0,4,16 sum to 40; divide by n=5: 40/5 = 8. (Module 31)

quiz.q: What is the standard deviation of that dataset?
quiz.explain: Std dev = sqrt(variance) = sqrt(8) ~ 2.83, back in original units. (Module 31)

quiz.q: Which center measure is most dragged by outliers?
quiz.explain: The mean uses every value, so one extreme value pulls it hard. The median resists. (Module 31)

quiz.q: Being at the 75th percentile means:
choices: 75% of values are at or below it
you are in the top 25 values
quiz.explain: The p-th percentile has p% of data at or below it. (Module 31)

quiz.q: What is the IQR?
quiz.explain: IQR = Q3 - Q1: the spread of the middle 50% of data. (Module 31)

quiz.q: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7?
quiz.explain: Mode = most frequent value: 3 appears twice, everything else once. (Module 31)

modules.title: Probability Foundations
modules.summary: Learn events and sample spaces, conditional probability, independence, Bayes' theorem on a fraud example, and the law of total probability. You need this for -> fraud/churn risk scoring, interpreting model precision, and segment-weighted rates in downstream modules.
objectives: Define sample space, events, and compute probabilities as favorable over total outcomes.
Compute conditional probability P(A|B) and test whether two events are independent.
Apply Bayes' theorem to update beliefs with new evidence (worked fraud example).
Use the law of total probability to combine subgroup rates into an overall rate.

notes.title: Sample spaces and events
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** risk and likelihood questions: fraud rates, churn rates, and A/B-test 'chance of winning' are all probability dressed as business questions.
- The SAMPLE SPACE is all possible outcomes; an EVENT is a subset of outcomes. Probability = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes), between 0 and 1.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: 1000 customers, 80 churned this quarter. Sample space = all 1000 customers; event = 'churned'. P(churn) = 80 / 1000 = 0.08 = 8%.
- Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). P(retained) = 1 - 0.08 = 0.92.
- Probabilities are long-run frequencies: 8% churn means ~8 of every 100 similar customers churn, not that THIS customer has an 8% dial inside them.

notes.title: Conditional probability and independence
notes.body:
- P(A|B) = 'probability of A GIVEN B happened' = P(A and B) / P(B). Restrict to the B-world, then measure A inside it.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: 1000 users; 200 on the annual plan; 20 of those annual users churn.
```
P(churn | annual) = (annual users who churn) / (all annual users)
                   = 20 / 200 = 0.10 = 10%
Overall churn is 8%, but INSIDE the annual-plan segment it is 10%.
The condition changed the probability - that is the whole point.
```
- INDEPENDENCE: A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A). Knowing B tells you nothing about A.
- Test it: if P(churn|annual) != P(churn), plan type and churn are NOT independent - plan carries signal.

notes.title: Bayes' theorem: the fraud-model example
notes.body:
- Bayes flips a conditional: P(fraud | flagged) = P(flagged | fraud) * P(fraud) / P(flagged). Turn 'how well the model catches fraud' into 'how likely a flagged transaction is fraud'.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: 1% of transactions are fraud. The model flags 90% of fraud (true positive) but also 5% of legit transactions (false positive).
```
P(flagged) = P(flagged|fraud)*P(fraud) + P(flagged|legit)*P(legit)
           = 0.90 * 0.01 + 0.05 * 0.99
           = 0.009 + 0.0495
           = 0.0585
P(fraud | flagged) = 0.009 / 0.0585 ~ 0.154 = 15.4%
```
- The model is 90% sensitive, yet a flagged transaction is only 15.4% likely fraud: rare events stay rare even after strong evidence. This is the base-rate fallacy, and it bites every fraud/churn model review.
- Prior (1% base rate) times likelihood, normalized: that is Bayes in one sentence.

notes.title: Law of total probability
notes.body:
- Overall rate = weighted average of segment rates: P(churn) = sum over segments of P(churn | segment) * P(segment).
- WORKED EXAMPLE: mobile users are 30% of the base with 5% churn; desktop users are 70% with 10% churn.
```
P(churn) = P(churn|mobile)*P(mobile) + P(churn|desktop)*P(desktop)
         = 0.05 * 0.30 + 0.10 * 0.70
         = 0.015 + 0.070
         = 0.085 = 8.5%
```
- This is the correct way to roll segment dashboards into one company number: weight by segment SIZE, never take a plain average of the rates.
- It also runs backward: if overall churn moved, decompose the move into segment-rate changes vs segment-mix changes - the start of real churn diagnostics.

cards.front: What is P(churn) if 80 of 1000 customers churn?
cards.back: 80/1000 = 0.08 = 8%. Probability = favorable outcomes / total outcomes.

cards.front: State the conditional probability formula.
cards.back: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Restrict to the B-world, measure A inside it.

cards.front: When are two events independent?
cards.back: When P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A). Knowing B tells you nothing about A.

cards.front: State Bayes' theorem.
cards.back: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B). It flips a conditional using the prior P(A).

cards.front: Fraud model: 90% sensitive, but a flagged transaction is only ~15% likely fraud. Why?
cards.back: Base rate: only 1% of transactions are fraud. Rare events stay rare even after strong evidence (base-rate fallacy).

cards.front: What is the law of total probability?
cards.back: Overall rate = weighted average of segment rates: sum of P(event|segment) * P(segment). Weight by segment size.

cards.front: What is the complement rule?
cards.back: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). P(retained) = 1 - P(churn).

cards.front: For mutually exclusive events, what is P(A or B)?
cards.back: P(A) + P(B). They cannot co-occur, so just add. (If they can overlap, subtract P(A and B).)

quiz.q: What is P(rolling a 6 on a fair die)?
quiz.explain: 1 favorable outcome out of 6: 1/6. (Module 32)

quiz.q: 20 of 200 annual-plan users churn. What is P(churn | annual)?
quiz.explain: Restrict to the annual world: 20/200 = 0.10 = 10%. (Module 32)

quiz.q: Two events are independent when:
quiz.explain: Independence means the joint probability factors: P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B). (Module 32)

quiz.q: Bayes' theorem lets you compute:
quiz.explain: Bayes flips P(flag|fraud) into P(fraud|flag) using the base rate P(fraud). (Module 32)

quiz.q: The law of total probability says the overall rate equals:
quiz.explain: Weight each segment's rate by the segment's share: sum of P(event|segment)*P(segment). (Module 32)

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) =
quiz.explain: Mutually exclusive events cannot co-occur, so add their probabilities. (Module 32)

quiz.q: What is P(not A) in terms of P(A)?
quiz.explain: Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). (Module 32)

quiz.q: In the fraud example (1% base rate, 90% flagged-if-fraud, 5% flagged-if-legit), P(fraud | flagged) is about:
quiz.explain: 0.009 / 0.0585 ~ 0.154: the rare base rate dominates despite 90% sensitivity. (Module 32)

modules.title: Linear Algebra Essentials
modules.summary: Meet vectors as arrows and lists, dot products as similarity scores, matrices as tables of vectors, and matrix multiplication as chained transformations. You need this for -> regression math, NumPy vectorization, and similarity/recommendation logic in downstream modules.
objectives: Represent data rows as vectors (lists of numbers) and interpret them geometrically as arrows.
Compute dot products by hand and interpret them as similarity scores.
Read a matrix as a stacked table of vectors and identify its shape (rows x columns).
Perform small matrix multiplications and explain them as chained transformations / weighted sums.

notes.title: Vectors: lists of numbers, arrows in space
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** NumPy, feature rows in ML, and similarity math: every row of your dataframe is already a vector, and 'similar customers' is vector geometry.
- A vector is an ordered list: v = [3, 4]. Geometrically it is an arrow from the origin to the point (3, 4).
- Magnitude (length) = sqrt(sum of squares): |[3,4]| = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: customer feature vector [5, 1] = buys 5 coffees, 1 tea per week. Another customer [4, 2] = 4 coffees, 2 teas. Each customer's row is one arrow in 'purchase space'.
- Adding vectors adds component-wise: [2, 0] + [0, 3] = [2, 3]. Scaling multiplies each component: 2 * [1, 5] = [2, 10].

notes.title: Dot products as similarity
notes.body:
- Dot product: multiply component-wise, then add: [1, 2] . [3, 4] = 1*3 + 2*4 = 3 + 8 = 11.
- Meaning: large positive = pointing the same direction (similar); zero = perpendicular (unrelated); negative = pointing opposite (opposite tastes).
- WORKED EXAMPLE: customer A [5, 1] (coffee-heavy), customer B [4, 2].
```
A . B = 5*4 + 1*2 = 20 + 2 = 22   (large positive -> similar buyers)
Customer C [1, 5] (tea-heavy): A . C = 5*1 + 1*5 = 10  (less similar)
```
- This is the engine of 'customers like you also bought': high dot product = similar rows.
- Cosine similarity is the dot product normalized by magnitudes: it measures the ANGLE between arrows, ignoring how big the baskets were.

notes.title: Matrices as tables of vectors
notes.body:
- A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers: rows x columns. A dataframe IS a matrix (plus labels).
- Shape is always 'rows x columns': a 3x2 matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns (6 entries).
- WORKED EXAMPLE: two customers, two features (coffee, tea):
```
        coffee  tea
A  ->  [  5      1  ]
B  ->  [  4      2  ]
This is a 2x2 matrix. Each ROW is a customer vector;
each COLUMN is one feature across customers.
```
- Transpose flips rows and columns: the 2x2 above transposed is still 2x2; a 3x2 transposed becomes 2x3.
- Matrix addition and scaling work entry-by-entry, exactly like vector addition.

notes.title: Matrix multiplication as chained transformations
notes.body:
- C = A @ B: entry (i, j) of C is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Inner dimensions must match: (2x3) @ (3x2) -> 2x2.
- WORKED EXAMPLE (2x2 @ 2x2):
```
[1 2]   [5 6]   [1*5+2*7  1*6+2*8]   [19 22]
[3 4] @ [7 8] = [3*5+4*7  3*6+4*8] = [43 50]
Row 1 . Column 1 = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19, and so on for each cell.
```
- Think of it as chained transformations: B transforms the data, then A transforms the result. Order matters: A @ B is usually NOT B @ A.
- Why analysts meet this: linear regression solves Xw = y for the weight vector w (the data matrix X times weights gives predictions y). NumPy replaces slow Python loops with these vectorized operations.

cards.front: What is a vector, in data terms?
cards.back: An ordered list of numbers - one row of your dataframe. Geometrically, an arrow from the origin.

cards.front: Compute the magnitude of [3, 4].

cards.back: 1*3 + 2*4 = 3 + 8 = 11. Multiply component-wise, then add.

cards.front: What does a dot product of 0 mean? Of a large positive?
cards.back: 0 = perpendicular, unrelated. Large positive = pointing the same direction, similar.

cards.front: What shape is a 3x2 matrix?
cards.back: 3 rows, 2 columns, 6 entries. Shape is always rows x columns.

cards.front: How do you compute entry (i,j) of A @ B?
cards.back: Dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Inner dimensions must match: (2x3)@(3x2) -> 2x2.

cards.front: In regression's Xw = y, what is w?
cards.back: The weight vector: the coefficients the model learns. X is the data matrix, y the targets.

cards.front: Why does NumPy matter for linear algebra in data work?
cards.back: It replaces slow Python loops with vectorized matrix/vector operations - the same math, thousands of times faster.

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of [3, 4]?
quiz.explain: sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5. (Module 33)

quiz.q: A 3x2 matrix has:
quiz.explain: Shape is rows x columns: 3 rows, 2 columns. (Module 33)

quiz.q: A dot product of 0 means the vectors are:
quiz.explain: Zero dot product = 90-degree angle = perpendicular = unrelated. (Module 33)
Add component-wise: [2+0, 0+3] = [2, 3]. (Module 33)

quiz.q: In Xw = y for linear regression, w is:
quiz.explain: w holds the learned coefficients; X times w produces the predictions. (Module 33)

quiz.q: What is the shape of (2x3) @ (3x2)?
quiz.explain: Inner dimensions (3) match; outer dimensions give 2x2. (Module 33)

quiz.q: Compute 2 * [1, 5].
quiz.explain: Scaling multiplies every component: [2*1, 2*5] = [2, 10]. (Module 33)

modules.title: Calculus Concepts for Analysts
modules.summary: Learn what a derivative really means (instantaneous rate of change), what an integral really means (cumulative total), and how optimization finds the minimum of a cost curve - no proofs, just intuition. You need this for -> growth-rate questions, cumulative metrics, and understanding how ML models learn in downstream modules.
objectives: Explain the derivative as the instantaneous rate of change (the slope of the curve at a point).
Explain the integral as accumulated area under a curve (a cumulative total).
Use optimization intuition: a minimum or maximum sits where the derivative crosses zero.
Recognize growth, decay, and diminishing-returns shapes in business data.

notes.title: The derivative: how fast, right now
notes.body:
- **You need this for ->** rate questions your dashboards answer daily: 'how fast is revenue growing TODAY' is a derivative; gradient descent in ML literally follows derivatives downhill.
- The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the curve THERE: the tangent line's slope, the instantaneous rate of change.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: distance d(t) = 5t^2 (meters after t seconds).
```
Average speed from t=1 to t=3:
  (d(3) - d(1)) / (3 - 1) = (45 - 5) / 2 = 40 / 2 = 20 m/s
Instantaneous speed at t=2 (the derivative):
  d'(t) = 10t, so d'(2) = 10 * 2 = 20 m/s
The derivative is the speedometer reading at one instant.
```
- Power rule shortcut: if f(x) = x^n then f'(x) = n*x^(n-1). So (x^2)' = 2x, (x^3)' = 3x^2.
- Positive derivative = rising, negative = falling, zero = flat moment (peak, valley, or plateau).

notes.title: The integral: adding up everything
notes.body:
- The integral is accumulation: area under the rate curve = total. If the derivative is the speedometer, the integral is the odometer.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: sales rate is a flat 100 units/day for 5 days.
```
Total = area of the rectangle under the rate line
      = rate * time = 100 units/day * 5 days = 500 units
As an integral: integral from 0 to 5 of 100 dt = 500
```
- Cumulative revenue curves are integrals of daily revenue: each day's bar stacks onto the running total.
- The fundamental link: integrating a rate recovers the total; differentiating a total recovers the rate. They undo each other.
- In dashboards, any 'cumulative' or 'running total' line is an integral of the underlying daily series.

notes.title: Optimization: finding the bottom of the valley
notes.body:
- At a smooth minimum or maximum, the curve is momentarily flat: derivative = 0. So: take the derivative, set it to zero, solve.
- WORKED EXAMPLE: cost curve C(x) = x^2 - 10x + 50, where x = production batch size.
```
Step 1: derivative: C'(x) = 2x - 10
Step 2: set to zero: 2x - 10 = 0
Step 3: solve: 2x = 10, so x = 5
Step 4: check shape: x^2 has a positive coefficient, so the
         parabola opens UPWARD -> x = 5 is a MINIMUM.
Minimum cost = C(5) = 25 - 50 + 50 = 25.
```
- This is exactly how ML training works at scale: define a cost (error) function, follow the derivative downhill until it flattens - that is gradient descent.
- Second-derivative intuition: curving upward (positive) near the flat point = valley = minimum; curving downward = hill = maximum.

notes.title: Growth, decay, and diminishing returns
notes.body:
- EXPONENTIAL GROWTH (y = a*b^x, b > 1): the derivative grows WITH the function - viral signups, compounding. The bigger it gets, the faster it grows.
- EXPONENTIAL DECAY (b < 1): shrinks toward zero - activity of an aging user cohort, radioactive half-life, email open rates over days.
- DIMINISHING RETURNS: rising but flattening - each extra ad dollar buys less additional revenue than the last. Derivative positive but SHRINKING (concave down).
- WORKED EXAMPLE: ad spend vs revenue: $1K -> $10K revenue, $2K -> $15K (+5K), $3K -> $18K (+3K). The increments 10K, 5K, 3K shrink: positive but diminishing marginal return.
- Reading dashboards: steepening curve = accelerating (derivative rising); flattening curve = saturating (derivative falling toward zero).

cards.front: What does a derivative measure?
cards.back: The instantaneous rate of change: the slope of the curve at a single point (the tangent line's slope).

cards.front: What does an integral measure?
cards.back: Accumulation: the area under a rate curve, i.e. the cumulative total. Speedometer vs odometer.

cards.front: How do you find the minimum of a smooth cost curve?
cards.back: Take the derivative, set it to zero, solve. For C(x) = x^2 - 10x + 50: 2x - 10 = 0 gives x = 5.

cards.front: What is the power rule for derivatives?
cards.back: If f(x) = x^n then f'(x) = n*x^(n-1). So (x^2)' = 2x.

cards.front: What does a zero derivative at a point tell you?
cards.back: The curve is momentarily flat there: a peak, a valley, or a plateau. Check the curvature to tell which.

cards.front: How is gradient descent related to derivatives?
cards.back: ML training defines a cost function and repeatedly steps in the direction the derivative points downhill, until the derivative flattens near a minimum.

cards.front: What shape shows diminishing returns?
cards.back: Rising but flattening: derivative positive but shrinking. Each extra input dollar buys less additional output.

cards.front: What does exponential decay describe in business data?
cards.back: Shrinking toward zero: aging-cohort activity, email open rates over days, anything with a half-life pattern.

quiz.q: What does a derivative measure?
quiz.explain: The derivative is the slope of the curve at a point: how fast the value is changing right now. (Module 34)

quiz.q: What does an integral measure?
quiz.explain: Integrating a rate accumulates it: area under the curve = cumulative total. (Module 34)

quiz.q: At a smooth minimum of a cost curve, the derivative is:
quiz.explain: The curve is momentarily flat at a min or max, so the derivative is zero there. (Module 34)

quiz.q: If d(t) = t^2, what is d'(t)?
quiz.explain: Power rule: (t^2)' = 2*t^(2-1) = 2t. (Module 34)

quiz.q: Diminishing returns means each extra dollar:
quiz.explain: Marginal return shrinks: the curve rises but flattens (derivative positive but falling). (Module 34)

quiz.q: A steeper curve at a point means:
quiz.explain: Steepness IS the derivative: steeper = larger rate of change. (Module 34)

quiz.q: To find the minimum of C(x) = x^2 - 10x + 50, you:
quiz.explain: Derivative zero: 2x - 10 = 0 gives x = 5; upward-opening parabola confirms a minimum. (Module 34)

quiz.q: Exponential decay best describes:
choices: shrinking activity of an aging cohort
quiz.explain: Decay shrinks toward zero over time: cohort activity fade, half-life patterns. (Module 34)

modules.title: Advanced SQL: Window Functions, CTEs & Optimization
modules.summary: Master analytic SQL: ranking, offsets, running totals, and frames via window functions; readable multi-step logic with recursive and non-recursive CTEs; and the optimization habits (EXPLAIN, indexes, SARGable predicates) that keep warehouse queries fast.
objectives: Write ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() queries and explain how ties and PARTITION BY change results
Use LAG()/LEAD() and frame clauses for period-over-period change, running totals, and moving averages
Structure complex logic with non-recursive CTEs and solve hierarchical problems with guarded recursive CTEs
Read an EXPLAIN plan, choose indexes, keep predicates SARGable, and avoid SELECT * and functions on indexed columns

notes.title: Ranking window functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
notes.body:
- **Window functions** - compute over a set of rows without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does; detail rows survive
- **OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)** - PARTITION BY slices rows into independent groups; ORDER BY orders within each group
- **ROW_NUMBER()** - assigns 1, 2, 3 with no ties; use it when you need exactly one row per group
- **RANK()** - leaves gaps after ties (1, 2, 2, 4); **DENSE_RANK()** - no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3)
- **Top-N per group** - rank in a CTE, then filter rank <= N in the outer query; window functions cannot appear in WHERE
- **Classic dedupe** - keep the latest row per customer:
```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
```

notes.title: Offsets and frames: LAG/LEAD, running totals, moving averages
notes.body:
- **LAG(col, n, default)** - looks n rows back inside the ordered window; **LEAD(col, n, default)** looks forward; the default fills edge rows
- **Running total** - SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
- **Frame default trap** - with ORDER BY present, the default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW; RANGE treats duplicate ORDER BY values as peers, so prefer ROWS for running totals
- **Moving average** - AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) gives a 7-day average
- **Period-over-period** - (cur - LAG(cur)) / NULLIF(LAG(cur), 0) avoids divide-by-zero
```sql
SELECT dt, revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY dt) AS wow_change,
       AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7
FROM daily_revenue;
```

notes.title: CTEs: non-recursive structure and recursive traversal
notes.body:
- **Non-recursive CTEs** - WITH q AS (...) names intermediate result sets; stack them filter -> join -> aggregate -> rank so logic reads top-down instead of nesting inward
- **Recursive CTE shape** - anchor member (base rows) UNION ALL recursive member referencing the CTE, plus a termination condition
- **Use cases** - org-chart chains, bill-of-materials explosion, date-series generation, graph traversal
- **Termination guard** - always bound depth (WHERE lvl < 10) or rely on the engine's recursion limit; cyclic data without a guard loops until it is killed
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, name, 1 AS lvl
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, e.name, r.lvl + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
  WHERE r.lvl < 10
)
SELECT * FROM reports;
```

notes.title: Optimization: EXPLAIN, indexes, SARGability
notes.body:
- **EXPLAIN (QUERY) PLAN** - shows the optimizer's path; red flags are full scans on large tables, nested loops over big inputs, and sorts that suggest a missing index
- **Composite indexes** - index on (customer_id, order_ts) serves filters and ORDER BY on those columns; put equality columns first, then range/order columns
- **SARGable** - the column stands alone so the optimizer can seek: WHERE order_ts >= '2026-01-01' is SARGable; WHERE YEAR(order_ts) = 2026 wraps the column in a function and forces a scan
- **Avoid SELECT *** - fetches unneeded columns (I/O plus network), breaks on schema change, and defeats covering-index-only scans
- **Filter early** - push selective filters into the first CTE; never use SELECT DISTINCT to hide row multiplication caused by a bad join - fix the join

cards.front: ROW_NUMBER() vs RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() on values 10, 20, 20, 30
cards.back: ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4 (no ties). RANK: 1, 2, 2, 4 (gap after tie). DENSE_RANK: 1, 2, 2, 3 (no gap).

cards.front: What does PARTITION BY do inside OVER()?
cards.back: Splits rows into independent groups; the window function restarts for each partition - like a GROUP BY that keeps the detail rows.

cards.front: Why can't a window function appear in WHERE?
cards.back: Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> window functions. Compute the window in a CTE or subquery, then filter in the outer WHERE.

cards.front: LAG vs LEAD
cards.back: LAG(col, n, default) looks n rows back in the ordered window; LEAD looks n rows forward. The default fills the first/last edge rows.

cards.front: Default frame when ORDER BY is present in OVER()
cards.back: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For running totals with duplicate sort values, prefer ROWS to avoid peer-row surprises.

cards.front: The three parts of a recursive CTE
cards.back: Anchor member (base rows), UNION ALL, recursive member referencing the CTE - plus a termination condition such as a depth guard.

cards.front: What makes a predicate SARGable?
cards.back: The column stands alone against constants (order_ts >= '2026-01-01') so the optimizer can do an index seek. Wrapping it in a function forces a scan.

cards.front: Why avoid SELECT * in analytics queries?
cards.back: Pulls unneeded columns (I/O and network cost), breaks when schemas change, and prevents covering-index-only scans.

quiz.q: You need exactly one row per customer: the most recent order. Which belongs in the CTE?
choices: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC), then filter rn = 1
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC), then filter rnk = 1
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC), then filter dr = 1
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id), then filter cnt = 1
quiz.explain: ROW_NUMBER guarantees exactly one row even with tied timestamps; RANK and DENSE_RANK can return several rows on ties. (Module 8)

quiz.q: Scores 90, 80, 80, 70 with RANK() ORDER BY score DESC produce:
quiz.explain: RANK leaves a gap after ties (the next rank is 4, not 3). DENSE_RANK would give 1, 2, 2, 3. (Module 8)

quiz.q: LAG(revenue, 1, 0) evaluated on the first row of the window returns:
choices: the revenue of the second row
quiz.explain: The third argument is the default returned when no preceding row exists, so the first row gets 0. (Module 8)

quiz.q: For a running total that must count every row even when dt has duplicates, the correct frame is:
choices: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
quiz.explain: ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE treats duplicate ORDER BY values as peers and can double-count or skip them. (Module 8)

quiz.q: A recursive CTE on an employee-manager table runs forever. The most likely cause:
choices: missing termination condition (or cyclic data with no depth guard)
using UNION instead of UNION ALL
quiz.explain: Without a depth guard, cycles in manager_id keep the recursion expanding indefinitely. (Module 8)

quiz.q: Which predicate is SARGable?
quiz.explain: The column stands alone against constants, so the optimizer can do an index range seek; the others wrap columns in functions or arithmetic. (Module 8)

quiz.q: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a 50M-row fact table for a query filtering on customer_id. First thing to check:
choices: add more RAM to the warehouse
whether a usable index (or sort/cluster key) exists on customer_id
split the query into smaller CTEs
quiz.explain: A full scan for a selective filter usually means no usable index or sort key on the filter column; fix the access path before reaching for hardware. (Module 8)

quiz.q: SELECT x FROM t WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x) = 1 fails because:
choices: window functions are not allowed with aggregates
window functions evaluate after WHERE in logical query order
quiz.explain: Compute the window in a CTE or subquery, then filter on it in the outer WHERE clause. (Module 8)

modules.title: Python for Analytics: pandas & NumPy at Scale
modules.summary: Write fast, memory-safe analytics Python: disciplined CSV ingestion with explicit dtypes, vectorized pandas/NumPy operations, correct joins and reshapes, deliberate missing-data strategy, chunked processing for big files, and quick profiling.
objectives: Ingest CSVs efficiently with explicit dtypes, date parsing, and column selection
Replace Python row loops with vectorized pandas/NumPy operations and explain the speed difference
Choose correctly between merge, join, and concat, and reshape with melt/pivot without corrupting grain
Handle missing data deliberately, chunk files that exceed RAM, and profile memory and runtime

notes.title: read_csv like a professional
notes.body:
- **dtype=** - declare types up front: prevents bad inference (IDs with leading zeros becoming numbers), and shrinks memory (int32 vs int64, category for low-cardinality strings)
- **usecols=** - read only the columns you need; **parse_dates=** - parse timestamps at load instead of converting later
- **low_memory=False** - only when mixed-type warnings actually appear; do not set it blindly
- **Verify after load** - df.dtypes and df.memory_usage(deep=True) before assuming anything
```python
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.read_csv(
    'orders.csv',
    dtype={'order_id': 'string', 'customer_id': 'string', 'qty': 'int32'},
    parse_dates=['order_ts'],
    usecols=['order_id', 'customer_id', 'qty', 'order_ts'],
)
```

notes.title: Vectorization beats loops
notes.body:
- **Why faster** - vectorized ops run in compiled C/NumPy code over whole arrays; iterrows/itertuples pay Python interpreter overhead per row, typically 10-100x slower on millions of rows
- **Prefer** - df['x'] * 2, np.where(cond, a, b), the .str accessor, the .dt accessor, pd.cut/pd.qcut for binning
- **Demote** - .apply(lambda row: ...) is still a Python-level loop; iterrows is the slowest option and also returns copies
- **Filter with masks** - boolean Series plus .loc keeps everything vectorized
```python
import numpy as np
df['revenue'] = df['qty'] * df['unit_price']
df['tier'] = np.where(df['revenue'] >= 1000, 'high', 'std')
recent = df.loc[df['order_ts'].dt.year == 2026]
```

notes.title: groupby/agg and joins that do not corrupt grain
notes.body:
- **Named aggregation** - df.groupby('region').agg(total=('revenue', 'sum'), n=('order_id', 'nunique')) names outputs and functions in one call
- **merge** - inner/left/right/outer; always pass validate='many_to_one' or 'one_to_one' when you expect it - it raises on unexpected fan-out instead of silently multiplying rows
- **join vs concat** - join aligns on indexes; concat stacks frames (axis=0 rows, axis=1 columns)
- **melt vs pivot** - melt goes wide to long (columns become rows); pivot/pivot_table goes long to wide; pivot needs unique index+column pairs or an aggfunc
```python
m = customers.merge(orders, on='customer_id', how='left', validate='one_to_many')
long = wide.melt(id_vars='month', var_name='channel', value_name='spend')
```

notes.title: Missing data, chunking, and profiling
notes.body:
- **Decide per column** - drop when tiny and random, median/mode imputation for skewed/symmetric numerics, forward-fill for time series, or add an is_missing indicator when missingness itself is informative
- **Never silently fillna(0)** - on a revenue column it drags down means and hides data-quality problems
- **Chunking** - pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=100_000) yields a TextFileReader; aggregate per chunk, then combine the partial aggregates - the file never fully sits in RAM
- **Profile first** - df.info(memory_usage='deep') and %timeit on the hot path; optimize the biggest cost first (usually I/O, dtypes, or a hidden Python loop)
```python
totals = {}
for chunk in pd.read_csv('huge.csv', chunksize=100_000, usecols=['region', 'revenue']):
    s = chunk.groupby('region')['revenue'].sum()
    for k, v in s.items():
        totals[k] = totals.get(k, 0) + v
```

cards.front: Why pass dtype= and usecols= to read_csv?
cards.back: Explicit dtypes prevent bad inference (IDs losing leading zeros, int64 bloat) and cut memory; usecols skips unneeded columns entirely - faster loads, smaller RAM.

cards.front: Why is vectorized pandas faster than iterrows?
cards.back: Vectorized ops run in compiled C/NumPy over whole arrays; iterrows pays Python interpreter overhead per row - typically 10-100x slower.

cards.front: What does np.where(df['revenue'] >= 1000, 'high', 'std') do?
cards.back: Vectorized conditional column: 'high' where revenue >= 1000, else 'std'. Prefer it over .apply(lambda) row functions.

cards.front: What does merge(validate='many_to_one') buy you?
cards.back: It asserts the right frame has unique keys and raises if violated - catching accidental many-to-many fan-out before it multiplies rows.

cards.front: melt vs pivot
cards.back: melt: wide to long (columns become rows). pivot/pivot_table: long to wide. Watch grain: pivot needs unique index+column pairs or an aggfunc.

cards.front: When is fillna(0) dangerous?
cards.back: On measures like revenue it drags down means and masks missing-data problems. Use median/mode, forward-fill for series, or an is_missing indicator.

cards.front: How do you process a 20 GB CSV that exceeds RAM?
cards.back: pd.read_csv(chunksize=...) yields chunks; compute partial aggregates per chunk and combine. The whole file never loads into memory.

cards.front: First step before optimizing slow pandas code?
cards.back: Profile: df.info(memory_usage='deep') and %timeit the hot path. Fix the biggest cost first - usually I/O, dtypes, or a hidden Python loop.

quiz.q: Fastest way to add a revenue column from qty and unit_price on 10M rows?
choices: for i, r in df.iterrows(): df.at[i, 'revenue'] = r.qty * r.unit_price
quiz.explain: Element-wise vectorized multiply runs in compiled code; the loop and apply options pay per-row Python overhead. (Module 9)

quiz.q: A merge unexpectedly doubles the row count. Best first check?
choices: check key uniqueness and use validate='many_to_one' (or 'one_to_one')
quiz.explain: Duplicate keys on the 'one' side cause fan-out; validate asserts the expected cardinality instead of hiding the problem. (Module 9)

quiz.q: customer_id '00123' must keep its leading zero when read from CSV. Correct dtype?
quiz.explain: Numeric dtypes drop leading zeros; identifiers with significant zeros must stay as string. (Module 9)

quiz.q: Which reshapes wide format (one column per month) into long format?
quiz.explain: melt unpivots columns into rows; pivot goes the other direction, long to wide. (Module 9)

quiz.q: A 20 GB CSV exceeds RAM. The correct approach?
choices: pd.read_csv with chunksize, aggregating per chunk
read it fully, then drop columns
quiz.explain: Chunked reading bounds memory per chunk; partial aggregates combine exactly without loading the whole file. (Module 9)

quiz.q: A revenue column is 5% missing and the missingness looks random. Reasonable treatment?
quiz.explain: Median preserves center without the downward bias of fillna(0); document the choice so it is auditable. (Module 9)

quiz.q: df.groupby('region').agg(total=('revenue', 'sum')) does what?
choices: creates a 'total' column with sum of revenue per region
quiz.explain: Named aggregation sets the output column name and aggregation function per group in one call. (Module 9)

quiz.q: A notebook is slow on 5M rows. First diagnostic step?
choices: profile with df.info(memory_usage='deep') and %timeit the hot path
quiz.explain: Measure before optimizing; dtypes, I/O, and hidden Python loops are the usual culprits. (Module 9)

modules.title: Statistics & Probability for Analysts
modules.summary: The statistical foundations behind every dashboard: distributions, center and spread, sampling, confidence intervals, correlation vs causation, and regression intuition - including the misreadings that most often fool analysts.
objectives: Recognize normal, binomial, and Poisson situations and choose the right model for counts vs measurements
Summarize center and spread with mean/median/mode, variance, and standard deviation, and read skew from their relationship
Interpret confidence intervals correctly and identify sampling bias in real datasets
Distinguish correlation from causation and explain linear regression as fitted conditional means

notes.title: Distributions: normal, binomial, Poisson
notes.body:
- **Normal** - bell-shaped, defined by mean and standard deviation; many measurements (heights, errors) approximate it; 68/95/99.7% of values fall within 1/2/3 standard deviations of the mean
- **Binomial** - number of successes in n fixed trials with constant p (conversions out of 1000 visitors)
- **Poisson** - count of events in a fixed interval at a constant rate (support tickets per hour); mean equals variance equals lambda
- **Choosing** - fixed trials with yes/no outcomes -> binomial; rate over time or space -> Poisson; continuous measurement -> approximately normal
- **Simulate to build intuition** - sampling from a distribution beats memorizing its formula
```python
import numpy as np
samples = np.random.normal(loc=50, scale=10, size=10000)
print(samples.mean(), samples.std())  # near 50 and 10
```

notes.title: Center, spread, and skew
notes.body:
- **Mean** - arithmetic average, sensitive to outliers; **median** - middle value, robust; **mode** - most frequent value
- **Right skew** - long tail of high values (income): mean > median; **left skew** - mean < median
- **Variance** - average squared deviation from the mean (units squared); **standard deviation** - its square root, back in original units, the interpretable one
- **Reporting rule** - median plus IQR for skewed data; mean plus standard deviation for roughly symmetric data
- **IQR** - interquartile range (Q3 - Q1); the 1.5xIQR rule flags outliers for investigation, not automatic deletion

notes.title: Confidence intervals and sampling bias
notes.body:
- **Correct 95% CI reading** - if we repeated the sampling procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true parameter; it is NOT a 95% chance that this specific interval contains it
- **Width math** - CI width shrinks with 1/sqrt(n): quadrupling the sample size halves the width
- **Sampling bias** - the sample differs systematically from the population: opt-in surveys, only logged-in users, survivorship bias (studying only the startups that survived)
- **Random sampling plus large n** - beats clever modeling on biased data; always ask who is missing from the dataset before modeling who is in it

notes.title: Correlation vs causation and regression intuition
notes.body:
- **Correlation** - measures linear association from -1 to 1; **causation** - needs a mechanism plus ruling out confounders, or an experiment
- **Classic traps** - reverse causation, common-cause confounders (ice-cream sales vs drownings, driven by heat), Simpson's paradox (a trend reverses inside subgroups)
- **Simple linear regression** - fits the line minimizing squared residuals; the slope is the expected change in y per one-unit change in x
- **R-squared** - fraction of y's variance explained by the model; a high R-squared with a confounded x is still not causal
- **Residual check** - plot residuals vs fitted values; patterns (funnels, curves) mean the linear model is misspecified

cards.front: Binomial vs Poisson - when to use each
cards.back: Binomial: successes in n fixed trials with constant p. Poisson: events in a fixed interval at a constant rate; mean equals variance.

cards.front: The 68-95-99.7 rule
cards.back: For normal data: about 68% within 1 std dev of the mean, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3.

cards.front: mean > median tells you what?
cards.back: Right skew - a long tail of high values (like income) pulls the mean up. Prefer the median for center.

cards.front: Variance vs standard deviation
cards.back: Variance is mean squared deviation (units squared); std dev is its square root, back in original units - the interpretable one.

cards.front: Correct reading of a 95% confidence interval
cards.back: About 95% of intervals from repeated sampling would contain the true parameter. Not a 95% probability for this specific interval.

cards.front: How does quadrupling n change a confidence interval?
cards.back: Halves its width - standard error scales with 1/sqrt(n).

cards.front: Correlation is 0.9. Can you claim causation?
cards.back: No. Confounders, reverse causation, or coincidence can produce strong correlation. Causation needs a mechanism or an experiment.

cards.front: What does a regression slope mean?
cards.back: Expected change in y for a one-unit change in x, holding other model variables fixed - descriptive, not automatically causal.

quiz.q: Support tickets arrive at roughly 12 per hour at a fairly constant rate. Best model for tickets in the next hour?
quiz.explain: Counts of events in a fixed interval at a constant rate are the Poisson situation. (Module 10)

quiz.q: Income data: mean $95k, median $62k. The distribution is:
quiz.explain: mean > median means a high-value tail pulls the mean up: right skew. (Module 10)

quiz.q: A 95% CI for conversion lift is [+0.2%, +1.1%]. Correct interpretation?
choices: there is a 95% chance the true lift is in this range
95% of users saw a lift in this range
the procedure produces intervals containing the true lift about 95% of the time
quiz.explain: Confidence intervals describe the long-run procedure, not a probability attached to this specific interval. (Module 10)

quiz.q: Ice-cream sales correlate 0.85 with drownings. Best conclusion?
choices: a confounder (hot weather) likely drives both
quiz.explain: Common-cause confounding is the classic trap; correlation alone never establishes causation. (Module 10)
