quiz.q: Which situation fits a binomial model?
choices: number of conversions among 500 ad clicks with stable click behavior
quiz.explain: Fixed n trials, binary outcome, constant p: the binomial setup. (Module 10)

quiz.q: Standard deviation of delivery times is 2 days. Variance is:
quiz.explain: Variance is std dev squared: 4, in squared units. (Module 10)

quiz.q: You want to halve the width of a confidence interval. You must:
choices: switch to a 90% interval and halve n
quiz.explain: Width scales with 1/sqrt(n); halving the width needs 4x the data. (Module 10)

quiz.q: A survey of your app's power users shows 90% satisfaction. The main risk?
choices: sampling bias: power users are not representative
quiz.explain: Opt-in power-user samples systematically differ from the full user base. (Module 10)

modules.title: Hypothesis Testing & A/B Testing
modules.summary: Run trustworthy experiments: the hypothesis-testing framework done right, power and sample sizing, randomization with SRM checks, and the classic A/B pitfalls - peeking, novelty/primacy effects, and missing guardrail metrics.
objectives: State null and alternative hypotheses and interpret p-values without the common misreadings
Explain Type I/II errors, power, and how sample size, effect size, and variance trade off
Design randomized experiments with the right unit of randomization and validate with SRM checks
Avoid peeking, account for novelty/primacy effects, and pair primary metrics with guardrail metrics

notes.title: The framework: H0, p-values, Type I/II
notes.body:
- **H0 (null)** - no effect or difference; **H1/Ha (alternative)** - the effect you are testing for; you never 'prove' H0, you fail to reject it
- **p-value** - probability of seeing results this extreme (or more) IF H0 were true; small p is evidence against H0
- **p is NOT** - the probability H0 is true, the probability your result replicates, or a measure of effect size
- **Type I error (alpha)** - false positive: rejecting a true H0; **Type II error (beta)** - false negative: missing a real effect; **power** = 1 - beta
- **Decision rule** - reject H0 when p < alpha (commonly 0.05); alpha is the false-positive rate you accept when H0 is true

notes.title: Power and sample size
notes.body:
- **Power rises with** - bigger true effect, bigger sample, lower variance, higher alpha
- **Size BEFORE launch** - pick the minimum detectable effect (MDE, the smallest lift worth shipping), baseline rate, variance, alpha 0.05, power 0.8
- **MDE math** - required n scales with 1/MDE^2: halving the MDE quadruples the sample size
- **Underpowered tests waste traffic** - a 'non-significant' result may just mean n was too small, not that the effect is zero
```python
# sizing intuition for two proportions:
# n per variant grows with p*(1-p) and shrinks with MDE^2
# use a power calculator in practice; the discipline that matters
# is sizing BEFORE launch, not the formula itself
```

notes.title: Randomization and SRM checks
notes.body:
- **Unit of randomization** - the entity assigned to a variant: user-level for UX changes (safest, avoids carryover), session/page-level only when effects cannot carry over
- **Analysis must match** - randomize by user but analyze by pageview and your variance estimates are wrong
- **SRM (sample ratio mismatch)** - expected 50/50 split shows 53/47 with p < 0.001: randomization or tracking is broken; do not trust the result
- **Invariant metrics** - check things the test cannot move (pre-period revenue, browser mix); if they differ between variants, something is wrong
- **One primary metric** - decided in advance; everything else is secondary or guardrail

notes.title: Peeking, novelty/primacy, guardrails
notes.body:
- **Peeking problem** - checking significance daily and stopping when p < 0.05 inflates false positives far above 5%; fix with a fixed horizon or sequential methods (alpha spending) designed for interim looks
- **Novelty effect** - users click the new shiny thing, then revert; **primacy effect** - existing users resist change, then adapt; run 1-2 full weekly cycles minimum so both wash out
- **Guardrail metrics** - things you must not break (latency, error rate, revenue per user); a primary-metric win with a broken guardrail is not shippable
- **Segment peeks** - slicing by mobile/desktop multiplies comparisons; pre-register segments or adjust for multiplicity, or treat them as exploratory

cards.front: p-value in one sentence
cards.back: Probability of results this extreme or more, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Small p = evidence against H0 - not P(H0 is true).

cards.front: Type I vs Type II error
cards.back: Type I (alpha): false positive, rejecting a true null. Type II (beta): false negative, missing a real effect. Power = 1 - beta.

cards.front: What is MDE?
cards.back: Minimum detectable effect - the smallest lift worth detecting and shipping. Smaller MDE needs much larger samples (n scales with 1/MDE^2).

cards.front: Sample ratio mismatch (SRM)
cards.back: Observed split differs significantly from the designed split (e.g., 53/47 vs 50/50) - signals broken randomization or tracking. Invalidate the test.

cards.front: Unit of randomization
cards.back: The entity assigned to a variant (user, session, page). It must match the analysis unit; user-level is safest for UX changes to avoid carryover.

cards.front: The peeking problem
cards.back: Repeatedly checking p < 0.05 and stopping early inflates false positives. Use a fixed horizon or sequential testing with alpha spending.

cards.front: Novelty vs primacy effects
cards.back: Novelty: temporary lift from the new thing. Primacy: temporary dip from change resistance. Run 1-2 full weekly cycles to let both wash out.

cards.front: Guardrail metrics
cards.back: Metrics the experiment must not harm (latency, errors, revenue per user). A primary-metric win with a broken guardrail is not shippable.

quiz.q: p = 0.03. Correct statement?
choices: if the null were true, results this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
there is a 97% chance the result replicates
quiz.explain: p is computed under the assumption H0 is true; it is not P(H0), says nothing about replication, and is not an effect size. (Module 11)

quiz.q: You check the dashboard daily and ship the moment p < 0.05. The risk:
choices: inflated Type I error from peeking; use a fixed horizon or sequential method
quiz.explain: Repeated interim looks without adjustment make false positives far more likely than 5%. (Module 11)

quiz.q: A 50/50 test shows 53/47 with p < 0.001 on the split itself. You should:
choices: ship the winner - the split barely matters
quiz.explain: Sample ratio mismatch means the experiment machinery is broken; the results are untrustworthy. (Module 11)

quiz.q: Primary metric up +5%, but the checkout error rate doubled. Decision?
choices: ship - the primary metric is what counts
run it longer to confirm the win
do not ship; the guardrail metric blocks it
quiz.explain: Guardrails exist to veto wins that break the product; investigate the error rate first. (Module 11)

quiz.q: Power = 0.8 means:
choices: an 80% chance of detecting a true effect of the assumed size
quiz.explain: Power = 1 - beta: probability of rejecting H0 when the assumed effect is real. (Module 11)

quiz.q: Halving the MDE roughly ___ the required sample size.
quiz.explain: n scales with 1/MDE^2, so halving the MDE needs about 4x the sample. (Module 11)

quiz.q: Novelty effect threatens a test because:
choices: users get bored and stop clicking
the control group sees the variant
an early lift from 'newness' fades, overstating the long-run effect
quiz.explain: Run through 1-2 weekly cycles so novelty washes out before you read the result. (Module 11)

quiz.q: Best unit of randomization for a checkout redesign?
quiz.explain: User-level assignment avoids the same user seeing both variants across sessions (carryover and contamination). (Module 11)

modules.title: Data Modeling & Warehousing
modules.summary: Model data for analytics: star vs snowflake schemas, facts/dimensions/grain, slowly changing dimensions, dbt-style staging and marts, surrogate keys, and when to denormalize.
objectives: Design star schemas with fact tables, dimension tables, and a declared grain
Contrast snowflake schemas and explain the query-simplicity tradeoff
Implement SCD Types 1 and 2 and justify surrogate keys over natural keys
Organize dbt-style staging/intermediate/marts layers and justify denormalization for analytics

notes.title: Facts, dimensions, grain, star vs snowflake
notes.body:
- **Fact table** - measurements and events (orders, clicks) with foreign keys to dimensions; usually long and narrow
- **Dimension table** - descriptive attributes (customer, product, date); wide, far fewer rows
- **Grain** - the lowest level of detail in a fact (one row per order line); declare it first, and every measure must be additive at the grain or aggregations lie
- **Star schema** - dimensions denormalized into single tables around the fact: fewer joins, BI-tool friendly, the analytics default
- **Snowflake schema** - dimensions normalized into sub-tables: less redundancy, more joins per query, harder BI SQL

notes.title: SCD Types 1/2 and surrogate keys
notes.body:
- **SCD Type 1** - overwrite the old value, no history; use for corrections and typos
- **SCD Type 2** - insert a new versioned row with effective dates plus a current flag; preserves full as-was history
- **Surrogate keys** - warehouse-generated integers, stable when source natural keys change format, compact for joins, and required for SCD2 where one natural key maps to many history rows
```sql
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_sk BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,  -- surrogate key
  customer_id VARCHAR,              -- natural key from source
  name VARCHAR, segment VARCHAR,
  valid_from DATE, valid_to DATE, is_current BOOLEAN
);
```

notes.title: dbt-style layers: staging, intermediate, marts
notes.body:
- **Staging** - 1:1 with source tables, light cleaning only (rename, cast, dedupe); no business logic, no joins
- **Intermediate** - reusable building blocks (joined, lightly aggregated components) shared by multiple marts
- **Marts** - business-facing wide tables per domain (mart_orders, mart_marketing) with declared grain, documentation, and tests
- **Tests live with the models** - unique and not-null on keys, freshness checks on staging sources, accepted-values on categories; a failing test blocks the refresh

notes.title: Normalization vs denormalization for analytics
notes.body:
- **OLTP normalizes** (3NF) to protect write integrity; **analytics denormalizes** because reads dominate: fewer joins means faster, simpler queries
- **Cost trade** - storage is cheap; repeated join compute at query time is expensive; wide marts trade disk for speed and clarity
- **Conformed dimensions** - one shared dim_customer and dim_date across marts so every team's metrics join to identical definitions
- **Document grain and metric definitions** - a mart without a documented grain is a footgun; two teams will aggregate it two ways and disagree

cards.front: Fact table vs dimension table
cards.back: Fact: measurements/events with foreign keys (long, narrow). Dimension: descriptive attributes (wide, fewer rows). Facts join to dims on surrogate keys.

cards.front: What is grain?
cards.back: The lowest level of detail in a table (e.g., one row per order line). Declare it first; measures must be additive at the grain or aggregations lie.

cards.front: Star vs snowflake schema
cards.back: Star: denormalized dims, fewer joins, BI-friendly. Snowflake: normalized dims, less redundancy, more joins. Analytics favors star.

cards.front: SCD Type 1 vs Type 2
cards.back: Type 1 overwrites (no history - corrections). Type 2 adds a new versioned row with effective dates (full history).

cards.front: Why surrogate keys?
cards.back: Stable when source natural keys change, compact integer joins, and required for SCD Type 2 where one natural key maps to many history rows.

cards.front: dbt staging vs marts
cards.back: Staging: 1:1 with sources, light cleaning only. Marts: business-facing wide tables with declared grain, docs, and tests.

cards.front: Why denormalize for analytics?
cards.back: Reads dominate: fewer joins means faster, simpler queries. Storage is cheap; repeated join compute at query time is not.

cards.front: Conformed dimension
cards.back: A dimension shared unchanged across marts (one dim_customer, one dim_date) so every team's metrics join to the same definitions.

quiz.q: 'One row per order line' in fact_orders declares the:
quiz.explain: Grain is the lowest detail level; everything aggregated from the fact must respect it. (Module 12)

quiz.q: Marketing wants a customer's segment as it was at purchase time vs today. You need:
choices: a wider fact table with no history
quiz.explain: Type 2 versions history so you can query as-was; Type 1 overwrites and loses it. (Module 12)

quiz.q: A source system changes customer_id from INT to VARCHAR. What breaks least?
choices: fact tables keyed on natural customer_id
quiz.explain: Surrogate keys insulate the warehouse from source key changes; only the mapping updates. (Module 12)

quiz.q: Snowflake schema's main cost versus star:
choices: more joins per query, harder BI SQL
quiz.explain: Normalized dimensions mean extra joins for every question; star keeps one join per dimension. (Module 12)

quiz.q: Where does business logic (e.g., the revenue definition) belong in dbt-style layers?
choices: intermediate and mart models, tested and documented
quiz.explain: Staging stays 1:1 with sources; business logic lives downstream where it is tested and documented. (Module 12)

quiz.q: Two teams report different revenue because each built their own customer dimension. Fix:
choices: a conformed dim_customer shared by both marts
quiz.explain: Conformed dimensions give every mart identical join keys and definitions. (Module 12)

quiz.q: A Type 1 SCD is appropriate when:
quiz.explain: Type 1 overwrites: fine for corrections, wrong whenever history matters. (Module 12)

quiz.q: Analysts complain every question needs 9 joins. Best modeling response?
choices: build a denormalized star mart with conformed dims
quiz.explain: Analytics favors fewer joins; a purpose-built mart trades cheap storage for fast, simple queries. (Module 12)

modules.title: ETL/ELT Pipelines & Orchestration
modules.summary: Build pipelines that do not wake you up: ETL vs ELT, batch vs streaming, incremental loads with watermarks, idempotent reruns, DAG orchestration concepts, data-quality tests, and failure triage.
objectives: Choose between ETL and ELT and between batch and streaming for a given use case
Design incremental loads with high-watermark tracking and handle late-arriving data
Make pipelines idempotent so reruns are safe, and explain DAG scheduling concepts
Add null/unique/freshness data-quality tests and triage failures systematically

notes.title: ETL vs ELT, batch vs streaming
notes.body:
- **ETL** - transform before load in a separate engine; **ELT** - load raw first, transform inside the warehouse using warehouse compute, keeping raw history
- **ELT dominates modern analytics** - the raw/bronze layer is preserved, transformations are versioned SQL, and replays are cheap
- **Batch** - scheduled runs (hourly/daily) over bounded data; simpler and cheaper; fine when latency tolerance is hours
- **Streaming** - continuous processing for seconds-level latency (fraud, monitoring); real operational cost; choose it only when the decision genuinely needs it

notes.title: Incremental loads and watermarks
notes.body:
- **Full refresh** - reload everything: simple, expensive; **incremental** - load only new/changed rows since the last run
- **High watermark** - store max(updated_at) processed; next run filters WHERE updated_at > watermark; add a lookback window for late-arriving data
- **CDC (change data capture)** - read the source's transaction log for inserts, updates, AND deletes; the robust way to catch changes, including hard deletes a watermark can never see
- **Merge/upsert** - on the business key so reruns update rather than duplicate
```sql
MERGE INTO mart_orders AS t
USING (SELECT * FROM stg_orders WHERE updated_at > :watermark) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.amount = s.amount, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, amount, updated_at)
VALUES (s.order_id, s.amount, s.updated_at);
```

notes.title: Idempotency and DAG concepts
notes.body:
- **Idempotent** - rerunning the same job produces the same result: merge/upsert on keys, or overwrite the run's partition, never blind append
- **DAG (directed acyclic graph)** - tasks with dependencies; the orchestrator runs them in topological order, retries failures, and alerts
- **Core concepts** - schedule/interval, backfill (rerun past intervals to repair history), sensors (wait for upstream data), SLAs on task duration
- **Partitioned writes** - one partition per run date makes reruns surgical: overwrite the partition, not the table

notes.title: Data quality tests and failure triage
notes.body:
- **Test categories** - not-null on keys, unique on primary keys, accepted values on categories, referential integrity, freshness (source updated within SLA), row-count/volume anomaly detection
- **Tests as gates** - run them as pipeline tasks that BLOCK downstream on failure; a failed test should stop the mart refresh, not just log a warning
- **Triage order** - (1) is the source late or empty? (2) did the schema change? (3) is it real data drift or a bad threshold? (4) infra issue (warehouse, queue)?
- **Alert with context** - include the watermark, row counts, and the failing test in the alert, not a bare 'job failed'

cards.front: ETL vs ELT
cards.back: ETL transforms before loading in an external engine. ELT loads raw first, then transforms inside the warehouse - keeps raw history and uses warehouse compute.

cards.front: When is batch enough vs streaming?
cards.back: Batch (hourly/daily) when decisions tolerate hours of latency - simpler and cheaper. Streaming only when seconds-level latency drives a decision (fraud, alerts).

cards.front: High-watermark incremental load
cards.back: Store max(updated_at) from the last run; next run loads only rows newer than the watermark. Add a lookback window for late-arriving data.

cards.front: CDC
cards.back: Change data capture: reads the source database's transaction log to capture inserts, updates, AND deletes - the robust incremental pattern.

cards.front: Idempotent pipeline
cards.back: Rerunning produces the same result: merge/upsert on business keys or overwrite the run's partition instead of blind-appending.

cards.front: DAG in orchestration
cards.back: Directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies; the scheduler runs them in order, retries failures, and supports backfill and sensors.

cards.front: Five data-quality test types
cards.back: Not-null keys, unique keys, accepted values, referential integrity, and freshness/volume checks. Failures should block downstream, not just log.

cards.front: Pipeline failure triage order
cards.back: 1) source late/empty? 2) schema change? 3) real data drift vs bad threshold? 4) infra issue? Include watermark and counts in the alert.

quiz.q: A daily job blind-appends, and a rerun after a partial failure duplicates rows. The fix:
choices: make the load idempotent: merge on business key or overwrite the run partition
run it twice to be safe
delete the whole table each run
append with an extra timestamp column
quiz.explain: Idempotent writes make reruns converge to the same state instead of duplicating. (Module 13)

quiz.q: Deletes in the source must propagate to the warehouse. A watermark on updated_at will:
choices: miss deletes - use CDC or a delete flag
quiz.explain: Hard deletes leave no updated_at row behind; CDC reads the transaction log including deletes. (Module 13)

quiz.q: Raw data must be preserved for replay and transforms should be versioned SQL. Choose:
choices: classic ETL with transforms in a black-box tool
ELT: load raw, transform in the warehouse
quiz.explain: ELT keeps the bronze/raw layer and puts logic in versioned, testable SQL. (Module 13)

quiz.q: A mart refreshes before its upstream staging finishes. Orchestration fix:
choices: model the dependency in the DAG (or a sensor on upstream)
quiz.explain: Explicit dependencies and sensors guarantee ordering; schedules alone race. (Module 13)

quiz.q: Late-arriving events (up to 2 days) break a strict watermark filter. Best adjustment?
choices: add a 3-day lookback window and merge on key
quiz.explain: Lookback re-reads the late window; merge/upsert keeps the rerun idempotent. (Module 13)

quiz.q: Which test catches 'the source feed stopped arriving'?
choices: freshness test on max(updated_at) vs SLA
quiz.explain: Freshness asserts recency; the others check content, not arrival. (Module 13)

quiz.q: Backfill means:
choices: rerunning the pipeline for past intervals to repair history
quiz.explain: Backfill replays historical runs - safe only if the pipeline is idempotent. (Module 13)

quiz.q: A streaming pipeline is proposed for an executive dashboard refreshed daily. Verdict?
choices: use both batch and streaming always
batch is sufficient - streaming adds cost without decision value
quiz.explain: Match latency to the decision cadence; daily decisions do not need seconds-level data. (Module 13)

modules.title: Cloud Data Platforms, Vendor-Neutral
modules.summary: Understand modern cloud warehouses without vendor lock-in: columnar storage, partitioning and clustering, separated compute and storage, elastic compute concepts, cost drivers, and when a warehouse beats a transactional database. Independent prep - no vendor affiliation.
objectives: Explain columnar storage and why it accelerates analytic scans
Use partitioning, clustering, and sort/distribution concepts to prune data and avoid shuffles
Describe separated compute and storage and elastic scaling patterns
Control warehouse cost and choose correctly between a warehouse and a transactional database

notes.title: Columnar storage and compression
notes.body:
- **Row stores** keep whole rows together (good for single-record lookups); **columnar stores** keep each column together - analytic queries scanning few columns over many rows read far less data
- **Per-column compression** - run-length, dictionary, and delta encoding shrink scans further; sorted columns compress best
- **Result** - full-table aggregations over billions of rows finish in seconds on columnar engines
- **Tradeoff** - single-row writes and updates are expensive; columnar warehouses are built for bulk loads, not OLTP

notes.title: Partitioning, clustering, sort and distribution
notes.body:
- **Partitioning** - physically group rows by a column (usually date) so queries filtering on it skip the rest: partition pruning
- **Clustering/sort keys** - order rows within storage so range filters and merge joins skip blocks (some engines call these micro-partitions with min/max metadata)
- **Distribution keys** - co-locate join keys on the same compute node to avoid shuffling large tables across the network
- **Rule of thumb** - partition/cluster by the columns you filter on most (event date); distribute by the keys you join on most

notes.title: Separated compute and storage, elastic compute
notes.body:
- **Separation** - storage lives in cheap shared object storage; compute clusters scale or suspend independently; you pay for compute while it runs, storage always
- **Elastic compute** - resize up for heavy jobs, down or suspended when idle; isolate workloads (ELT vs BI vs data science) on separate pools so one runaway query cannot starve dashboards
- **Generic pattern** - whether a platform calls them slots, warehouses, or clusters, the idea is identical: independently scalable compute over shared storage
- **Topic references only** - Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, and Snowflake are managed columnar warehouses named here as neutral examples; this course is independent and unaffiliated with any vendor

notes.title: Cost awareness and warehouse vs database
notes.body:
- **Cost drivers** - compute time (size x duration), bytes scanned, storage volume, data egress/transfer
- **Cost habits** - filter early for partition pruning, avoid SELECT *, aggregate before exporting, suspend idle compute, right-size for the workload
- **Warehouse wins** - analytic scans over large history, many concurrent BI readers, ELT transforms at scale
- **Transactional database (OLTP) wins** - single-row CRUD, low-latency transactions, high write throughput; use each for its strength and replicate/ELT between them

cards.front: Why is columnar storage faster for analytics?
cards.back: Queries typically touch few columns over many rows; columnar layouts read only those columns (plus per-column compression), slashing I/O versus row stores.

cards.front: Partition pruning
cards.back: Rows physically grouped by a filter column (often date); the engine skips partitions outside the filter instead of scanning them.

cards.front: Sort/cluster keys vs distribution keys
cards.back: Sort/cluster keys order rows to skip blocks on range filters and speed merge joins. Distribution keys co-locate join keys on the same node to avoid network shuffles.

cards.front: Separated compute and storage
cards.back: Storage lives in cheap shared object storage; compute clusters scale and suspend independently. Pay for compute while running, storage always.

cards.front: Elastic compute pattern (slots/warehouses/clusters)
cards.back: Resize compute up for heavy jobs, down or suspended when idle; isolate workloads on separate pools so ELT cannot starve BI.

cards.front: Top warehouse cost drivers
cards.back: Compute time (size x duration), bytes scanned, storage volume, and egress. Prune partitions, avoid SELECT *, suspend idle compute.

cards.front: Warehouse vs transactional database
cards.back: Warehouse: bulk analytic scans, BI concurrency, ELT at scale. Database (OLTP): single-row CRUD, low-latency transactions, high write throughput.

cards.front: Why suspend idle compute?
cards.back: You pay for compute while it runs. Idle clusters burn budget with zero work; auto-suspend converts that to near-zero cost.

quiz.q: A query aggregates 3 columns over 2B rows. Columnar storage wins because:
choices: it reads only the 3 needed columns instead of full rows
it stores more rows per page
quiz.explain: Columnar I/O is proportional to columns touched, not row width. (Module 14)

quiz.q: Queries almost always filter on event_date. Best physical design:
choices: partition (or cluster) by event_date for pruning
quiz.explain: Date partitioning lets the engine skip irrelevant partitions entirely. (Module 14)

quiz.q: Two 500M-row tables join on customer_id daily and the join shuffles heavily. Fix:
quiz.explain: Co-locating join keys on the same node removes the network shuffle. (Module 14)

quiz.q: Overnight ELT starves morning dashboards on one shared cluster. Fix:
choices: separate compute pools for ELT and BI
quiz.explain: Workload isolation prevents noisy-neighbor contention; each pool scales independently. (Module 14)

quiz.q: The biggest surprise line item on a first warehouse bill is usually:
quiz.explain: Idle compute and unpruned scans dominate; storage is comparatively cheap. (Module 14)

quiz.q: Use case: 50k single-row order writes/sec with millisecond lookups. Choose:
quiz.explain: High-throughput single-row CRUD is OLTP's strength; warehouses optimize bulk scans. (Module 14)

quiz.q: Micro-partitions (in engines that use them) help queries by:
choices: storing min/max metadata that lets the engine skip irrelevant blocks
quiz.explain: Per-block min/max metadata enables pruning without reading the data. (Module 14)

quiz.q: This course names Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake. The correct framing is:
choices: they are topic references only; the course is independent and unaffiliated
quiz.explain: Vendor names appear only as neutral topic references; all exposition is original and unaffiliated. (Module 14)

modules.title: BI & Visualization Mastery
modules.summary: Design dashboards that answer business questions in under five seconds using visual hierarchy, pre-attentive attributes, correct chart selection, and analytical modeling concepts like filter context and level-of-detail thinking. Learn to tell honest data stories and strip chartjunk.
objectives: Apply the 5-second rule and visual hierarchy to lay out dashboards so the primary KPI and its trend are legible instantly
Choose the correct chart type for comparison, trend, distribution, and composition questions
Explain filter context, CALCULATE-style evaluation, and level-of-detail thinking in BI tools
Identify chartjunk, dual-axis traps, and truncated-axis deception and rebuild flawed visuals

notes.title: Dashboard Design: The 5-Second Rule and Hierarchy
notes.body:
- **5-second rule** -- a viewer should grasp the dashboard's main message within five seconds; put the headline KPI and its trend in the top-left where the eye lands first
- **Visual hierarchy** -- size, position, color, and whitespace signal importance; biggest element = most important, everything else recedes
- **Z-pattern / F-pattern** -- western readers scan top-left to top-right then diagonally down; place supporting detail along those paths
- **Progressive disclosure** -- summary first, filters and drill-throughs for detail; never dump 20 charts on one screen
- **Whitespace is free** -- crowding charts kills comprehension; group related visuals in cards with clear titles
- **Title the insight, not the chart** -- "Revenue grew 8% driven by the West region" beats "Bar chart of revenue"

notes.title: Pre-Attentive Attributes and Encoding
notes.body:
- **Pre-attentive attributes** -- color, size, position, orientation, and shape are processed in under 200ms before conscious thought; use them for the variable you want noticed
- **Length vs. area vs. angle** -- humans judge bar length accurately, circle area poorly, and angles worst; prefer bars over pies for precise comparison
- **Color as signal** -- use saturated color sparingly to highlight; gray out everything else; never use red/green alone (colorblindness)
- **Sequential vs. diverging palettes** -- sequential (light to dark) for one-directional magnitude; diverging (two hues around a neutral midpoint) for deviation from a target
- **Limit categorical colors** -- more than ~7 distinct hues becomes noise; combine small categories into "Other"
- **Annotations beat legends** -- label values directly on the marks instead of forcing the eye to bounce to a legend

notes.title: Choosing Chart Types and Avoiding Traps
notes.body:
- **Comparison across categories** -- vertical/horizontal bar charts (horizontal when labels are long)
- **Trend over time** -- line charts with a continuous x-axis; bars only if each period is a discrete bucket
- **Part-to-whole** -- stacked bars or treemaps; pie only with 2-4 slices and a clear "of total" question
- **Distribution** -- histograms for spread, box plots for comparing distributions across groups
- **Correlation** -- scatter plots; add trend lines and quadrant bands only when they clarify
- **Dual-axis trap** -- two scales on one chart can imply a false relationship; prefer two stacked charts with aligned axes
- **Truncated y-axis** -- starting bars above zero exaggerates differences; lines may be truncated ONLY if labeled and the delta is the story

notes.title: DAX Concepts, LOD Thinking, and Storytelling
notes.body:
- **Filter context** -- every cell in a BI report evaluates its formula under the filters applied by slicers, rows, columns; the same measure returns different values per cell
- **CALCULATE-style evaluation** -- functions that modify filter context (add/remove/override filters) let you compute "share of total" or "all-time" figures inside a filtered view
- **Time intelligence** -- year-to-date, same-period-last-year, and rolling averages need a proper date table; never hardcode date logic
- **Level-of-detail thinking** -- decide the grain first: one row per customer per month? per order? Then build aggregations to match; grain errors silently inflate totals
- **Story structure** -- hook (the change), context (why it matters), evidence (the visual), implication (what to do)
- **Chartjunk to kill** -- 3D effects, gradient fills, decorative icons, excessive gridlines, and drop shadows add zero information

cards.front: What is the 5-second rule in dashboard design?
cards.back: A viewer should grasp the dashboard's main message within five seconds. Put the headline KPI and its trend in the top-left where the eye lands first.

cards.front: Name four pre-attentive attributes.
cards.back: Color, size, position, and orientation (also shape). They are processed in under 200ms before conscious thought.

cards.front: Which visual encodings do humans judge most accurately, in order?
cards.back: Position/length first (bars), then area (circles), then angle (pie slices) last. Prefer bars over pies for precise comparison.

cards.front: What is filter context in BI tools?
cards.back: The set of filters applied by slicers, rows, and columns that determines what data each formula cell evaluates against -- the same measure returns different values per cell.

cards.front: When should you use a sequential vs. diverging color palette?
cards.back: Sequential (light-to-dark) for one-directional magnitude; diverging (two hues around a neutral midpoint) for deviation from a target or baseline.

cards.front: What is the dual-axis trap?
cards.back: Two different scales on one chart can imply a false relationship between series. Prefer two stacked charts with aligned axes.

cards.front: What is level-of-detail (grain) thinking and why does it matter?
cards.back: Decide the grain first (one row per customer per month, per order, etc.) and build aggregations to match. Grain errors silently inflate or deflate totals.

cards.front: Give three examples of chartjunk to remove.
cards.back: 3D effects, gradient fills, decorative icons, excessive gridlines, drop shadows -- anything that adds zero information.

quiz.q: A dashboard viewer should understand the main message within five seconds. Where should the headline KPI go?
choices: Top-left, where the eye lands first
Hidden behind a filter for interactivity
Randomly placed since layout does not matter
quiz.explain: The 5-second rule puts the headline KPI and its trend top-left on the eye's first landing path. (Module 15)

quiz.q: Which encoding should you use to compare precise values across categories?
quiz.explain: Humans judge length most accurately, area poorly, and angle worst -- bars beat pies for precise comparison. (Module 15)

quiz.q: What does filter context determine in a BI report?
choices: The color theme of the dashboard
What data each formula cell evaluates against, based on slicers/rows/columns
The refresh schedule of the dataset
The user permissions for the report
quiz.explain: Filter context is the set of applied filters under which each measure cell evaluates -- the same measure differs per cell. (Module 15)

quiz.q: A single diverging palette is most appropriate when the visual shows:
choices: Deviation from a target or baseline
A simple count of orders by month
quiz.explain: Diverging palettes (two hues around a neutral midpoint) encode deviation from a target; sequential palettes encode magnitude. (Module 15)

quiz.q: Which practice best fixes a misleading dual-axis chart?
choices: Add a third axis for more context
Use 3D columns to separate the series
Split into two stacked charts with aligned axes
Truncate both axes to exaggerate the trend
quiz.explain: Dual axes imply false relationships; two aligned stacked charts let each series keep its own honest scale. (Module 15)

quiz.q: Why does deciding the grain (level of detail) come before building aggregations?
choices: It determines the dashboard color scheme
It is required by the chart legend
Grain errors silently inflate or deflate totals
quiz.explain: If the grain (one row per what?) does not match your aggregation logic, totals are wrong with no error raised. (Module 15)

quiz.q: A line chart of monthly revenue starts its y-axis at $900K instead of $0. This is acceptable only if:
choices: The chart uses a red color
The truncation is labeled and the delta is the actual story
There are at least 12 data points
quiz.explain: Truncating a y-axis exaggerates differences; it is only defensible when labeled and the change itself is the point. (Module 15)

quiz.q: Which of the following is chartjunk?
choices: A labeled trend line on a scatter plot
A descriptive chart title stating the insight
quiz.explain: 3D effects, gradients, and decoration add zero information and are classic chartjunk; the others aid comprehension. (Module 15)

modules.title: Excel & Sheets Power Skills
modules.summary: Master modern lookup and reference functions, pivot tables, Power Query transformations, array formulas, and the Google Sheets QUERY function so spreadsheets become a serious analysis engine rather than a data graveyard.
objectives: Use XLOOKUP and INDEX-MATCH (and legacy VLOOKUP safely) to join data across tables without brittle column indexing
Build pivot tables with correct aggregation, grouping, and calculated fields for fast ad-hoc analysis
Transform and automate data cleaning with Power Query / Get & Transform steps
Write array formulas and the Sheets QUERY function to filter, aggregate, and reshape data in place

notes.title: Lookups: XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and VLOOKUP Safely
notes.body:
- **XLOOKUP** -- the modern default: =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]); searches any direction, returns whole rows
- **INDEX-MATCH** -- =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0)); immune to column insertions that break VLOOKUP's column index
- **VLOOKUP safely** -- always use exact match (FALSE/0) as the last argument; prefer table column names over hardcoded indexes
- **Approximate match danger** -- omitting the match argument defaults to approximate and requires sorted data; it silently returns wrong values otherwise
- **IFNA wrapping** -- =IFNA(XLOOKUP(...), "Not found") keeps reports clean instead of showing #N/A
- **Two-way lookups** -- MATCH on rows and columns inside INDEX for matrix lookups (e.g., price by product and region)

notes.title: Pivot Tables for Fast Ad-Hoc Analysis
notes.body:
- **Rows vs. columns vs. values vs. filters** -- dimensions go in rows/columns, facts (numbers) go in values, high-level cuts go in filters/slicers
- **Aggregation choice** -- SUM for additive facts, COUNT/COUNT DISTINCT for volume, AVERAGE only when the denominator is correct; never average pre-averaged numbers
- **Grouping** -- group dates by month/quarter/year and numbers into bins directly in the pivot; do not pre-bucket in source data
- **Show values as** -- "percent of row/column/grand total" answers share questions instantly without helper columns
- **Calculated fields** -- add ratio metrics (margin = profit/revenue) inside the pivot so they aggregate at the displayed grain
- **Refresh discipline** -- pivots do not auto-refresh; right-click refresh (or Data > Refresh All) after source data changes

notes.title: Power Query / Get & Transform
notes.body:
- **Repeatable ETL in Excel** -- each step (promote headers, change types, filter rows, merge queries) is recorded as an M-code recipe you replay on new files
- **Merge = join** -- use Home > Merge Queries with left/anti joins to combine tables instead of fragile VLOOKUP columns
- **Unpivot columns** -- turn wide monthly columns (Jan, Feb, Mar) into a tall Month/Value table for pivoting
- **Type discipline** -- set column types explicitly at the start; type errors caught early beat silent wrong results later
- **Applied Steps list** -- every transformation is a named, editable, reorderable step; click any step to inspect intermediate state
- **Parameters for file paths** -- store the source folder path as a parameter so the query survives folder moves

notes.title: Array Formulas, Validation, Formatting, and Sheets QUERY
notes.body:
- **Dynamic arrays** -- FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, and SEQUENCE spill results automatically; one formula replaces hundreds of copied formulas
- **FILTER example** -- =FILTER(A2:D1000, C2:C1000="West") returns matching rows live with no refresh
- **Data validation** -- dropdown lists and input rules prevent bad entries at the source; pair with conditional formatting to flag violations
- **Conditional formatting for analysis** -- color scales, data bars, and icon sets surface outliers; use sparingly and consistently
- **Sheets QUERY** -- =QUERY(A1:D, "select A, sum(C) where B > 100 group by A", 1) runs SQL-like queries over ranges; the third argument marks header rows
- **QUERY clauses** -- select, where, group by, order by, limit, label, and pivot mirror SQL; dates need date literals like date '2026-01-01'

cards.front: What is the XLOOKUP syntax and why is it better than VLOOKUP?
cards.back: =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). It searches in any direction and is immune to column insertions that break VLOOKUP's column index.

cards.front: What does =INDEX(A:A, MATCH("x", B:B, 0)) do?
cards.back: Finds "x" in column B with an exact MATCH and returns the corresponding value from column A -- a two-column lookup that survives column insertions.

cards.front: Why must you pass FALSE (0) as VLOOKUP's last argument?
cards.back: Omitting it defaults to approximate match, which requires sorted data and silently returns wrong values. Exact match is almost always what you want.

cards.front: Where do dimensions and facts go in a pivot table?
cards.back: Dimensions in rows/columns, numeric facts in values, high-level cuts in filters or slicers.

cards.front: What is Power Query's "Applied Steps" list?
cards.back: Every transformation recorded as a named, editable, reorderable step in the M-code recipe -- click any step to inspect the data at that point.

cards.front: What does unpivoting do in Power Query?
cards.back: Turns wide columns (Jan, Feb, Mar...) into a tall table with Month and Value columns so the data can be pivoted and aggregated.

cards.front: Name three dynamic array functions and what they do.
cards.back: FILTER (returns matching rows), SORT (sorts a range), UNIQUE (deduplicates values). Results spill automatically with no copied formulas.

cards.front: What is the Google Sheets QUERY function?
cards.back: =QUERY(range, "select A, sum(C) where ... group by A", 1) -- runs SQL-like queries (select, where, group by, order by, limit) over a range; the final 1 marks the header row.

quiz.q: A VLOOKUP returns wrong values after a colleague inserts a column in the lookup table. The best fix is:
choices: Switch to XLOOKUP or INDEX-MATCH, which do not depend on column position
Add more rows to the table array
Change the font size of the results
quiz.explain: VLOOKUP's hardcoded column index breaks on insertions; XLOOKUP and INDEX-MATCH reference ranges, not positions. (Module 16)

quiz.q: In a pivot table, you want each region's share of total revenue. The fastest correct method is:
choices: Manually compute percentages in a helper column
Use Show Values As > % of Grand Total
Export and calculate in another sheet
quiz.explain: Show Values As computes share-of-total at the pivot's grain instantly, no helper columns needed. (Module 16)

quiz.q: In Power Query, turning wide monthly columns (Jan-Dec) into Month/Value rows is called:
quiz.explain: Unpivot converts wide attribute columns into tall rows so the data can be aggregated. (Module 16)

quiz.q: Which formula returns all rows where column C equals "West", updating live?
quiz.explain: FILTER is a dynamic array that spills matching rows live; the others return single values. (Module 16)

quiz.q: What does the final argument "1" mean in =QUERY(A1:D, "select A", 1)?
choices: The first row is a header row
quiz.explain: The third QUERY argument declares how many header rows the range has. (Module 16)

quiz.q: You need to join two tables in Excel without adding fragile lookup columns. The Power Query feature is:
quiz.explain: Merge Queries performs joins (left, inner, anti) as a repeatable recorded step. (Module 16)

quiz.q: A margin metric (profit / revenue) shown inside a pivot table should be built as:
choices: A typed number in the source data
A calculated field, so it aggregates at the displayed grain
quiz.explain: Calculated fields compute the ratio from summed components at the pivot's grain; averaging pre-averaged margins is mathematically wrong. (Module 16)

quiz.q: Why wrap lookups in IFNA, e.g. =IFNA(XLOOKUP(...), "Not found")?
choices: It replaces ugly #N/A errors with a clean message for unmatched keys
quiz.explain: IFNA catches the #N/A from unmatched lookups and shows a readable fallback instead. (Module 16)

modules.title: Data Governance, Privacy & Ethics
modules.summary: Understand the data quality dimensions, lineage and cataloging practices, PII/PHI handling, and the core concepts of GDPR/CCPA that shape what analysts may collect, store, and report -- plus how bias creeps into data and how to practice responsible analytics.
objectives: Assess datasets against the six data quality dimensions and document defects before analysis
Explain data lineage and cataloging and why governed definitions beat tribal knowledge
Apply PII/PHI handling rules: minimization, masking, access control, and retention
Recognize sampling, measurement, and algorithmic bias and communicate their limits honestly

notes.title: Data Quality Dimensions
notes.body:
- **Accuracy** -- values reflect reality; validate against known totals and spot-check source records
- **Completeness** -- no missing critical fields; track null rates per column as a data health metric
- **Consistency** -- the same entity is represented the same way everywhere (one customer ID scheme, one date format)
- **Timeliness** -- data is fresh enough for the decision; a 24-hour lag kills intraday trading decisions but not monthly reporting
- **Validity** -- values conform to expected formats and domains (emails match a pattern, ages are non-negative)
- **Uniqueness** -- no unintended duplicates; define the natural key and test for violations
- **Profile first** -- before any analysis, run null rates, distinct counts, min/max, and distribution checks; fix or flag defects in the write-up

notes.title: Lineage, Cataloging, and Governed Definitions
notes.body:
- **Data lineage** -- the documented path from source systems through transformations to the final report; answers "where did this number come from?"
- **Data catalog** -- a searchable inventory of datasets with owners, descriptions, update cadence, and quality scores
- **Business glossary** -- one governed definition per metric ("What exactly counts as an active user?"); ambiguity here causes dueling dashboards
- **Certified datasets** -- governed, reviewed sources analysts should prefer over ad-hoc extracts
- **Ownership** -- every dataset needs a named owner accountable for quality and access decisions
- **Documentation habit** -- record assumptions, filters, and exclusions in the report itself; future-you and auditors will thank you

notes.title: PII/PHI Handling for Analysts
notes.body:
- **PII** -- personally identifiable information: names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, SSNs, device IDs, and combinations that identify someone
- **PHI** -- protected health information: health data tied to an individual; handled under stricter rules (HIPAA in the US)
- **Minimization** -- collect and query only the fields the analysis needs; never SELECT * on customer tables out of habit
- **Masking and tokenization** -- replace direct identifiers with tokens or masked values in analysis and test environments
- **Access control** -- work in the smallest-privilege environment; never export PII to personal devices or email
- **Retention** -- keep personal data only as long as the stated purpose requires, then delete per policy

notes.title: GDPR/CCPA Concepts, Consent, Bias, and Responsible Analytics
notes.body:
- **GDPR (EU)** -- core concepts: lawful basis for processing, purpose limitation, data minimization, and individual rights (access, erasure, portability)
- **CCPA/CPRA (California)** -- consumer rights to know, delete, and opt out of sale/sharing of personal information
- **Consent** -- processing must rest on a valid basis; for analysts this usually means working only with data collected under a stated purpose
- **Sampling bias** -- data that over-represents one group (e.g., app users) cannot speak for everyone; name the population your data actually covers
- **Measurement bias** -- proxies mismeasure the target (arrest records as a proxy for crime); question what the metric really captures
- **Responsible practice** -- disaggregate results by relevant groups when fair, report confidence and limits, never present a model's output as objective truth without caveats

cards.front: Name the six data quality dimensions.
cards.back: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness. Profile every dataset against them before analysis.

cards.front: What is data lineage?
cards.back: The documented path from source systems through transformations to the final report -- it answers "where did this number come from?"

cards.front: What is a business glossary and why does it matter?
cards.back: One governed definition per metric (e.g., "active user"). Without it, teams build dueling dashboards that disagree on the same KPI.

cards.front: What counts as PII?
cards.back: Personally identifiable information: names, emails, phones, addresses, SSNs, device IDs -- and combinations that can identify someone.

cards.front: What is data minimization?
cards.back: Collecting and querying only the fields the analysis needs -- never SELECT * on customer tables out of habit.

cards.front: What rights do GDPR and CCPA give individuals over their data?
cards.back: GDPR: lawful-basis processing, purpose limitation, and rights of access, erasure, portability. CCPA/CPRA: rights to know, delete, and opt out of sale/sharing.

cards.front: Give an example of sampling bias and its consequence.
cards.back: Analyzing only app users over-represents tech-comfortable customers; conclusions cannot be generalized to all customers. Name the population your data actually covers.

cards.front: What is measurement bias?
cards.back: When a proxy mismeasures the real target -- e.g., using arrest records as a proxy for crime. Always question what the metric truly captures.

quiz.q: A customer table has 12% null emails and three different date formats. Which quality dimensions are violated?
quiz.explain: Nulls hit completeness; mixed formats hit consistency. Profile both before analysis. (Module 17)

quiz.q: Two teams report different "active user" counts for the same month. The root fix is:
choices: Establish one governed definition in a business glossary
quiz.explain: Ambiguous metric definitions cause dueling dashboards; a governed glossary gives one answer. (Module 17)

quiz.q: An analyst needs customer ages for a segmentation study. Following minimization, they should:
choices: Query full names, emails, and addresses too, just in case
Download the table to a personal laptop
Query only the age field (and keys needed for the join)
Share the raw extract with the vendor
quiz.explain: Minimization means taking only the fields the analysis needs, never SELECT * out of habit. (Module 17)

quiz.q: Under GDPR concepts, an analyst should be most concerned with:
choices: Having a lawful basis, stated purpose, and honoring erasure/access requests
The color palette of the report
The number of rows in the export
quiz.explain: GDPR centers on lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimization, and individual rights. (Module 17)

quiz.q: A churn model trained only on customers who called support will:
choices: Suffer sampling bias -- it only saw the complainers
quiz.explain: Training on a non-representative slice bakes in sampling bias; name the population the data actually covers. (Module 17)

quiz.q: Which is the best practice when emailing an analysis containing customer emails?
choices: CC the whole company for transparency
Mask or tokenize identifiers before sharing, and use approved channels
quiz.explain: Direct identifiers must be masked/tokenized and shared only through approved, access-controlled channels. (Module 17)

quiz.q: Data lineage is most useful when:
choices: Someone asks where a reported number came from
quiz.explain: Lineage documents the source-to-report path, answering provenance questions and enabling audits. (Module 17)

quiz.q: A metric defined as "arrests per neighborhood" is used as a measure of crime. The risk is:
choices: Timeliness -- the data is too fresh
Measurement bias -- arrests proxy policing intensity, not just crime
quiz.explain: Proxies mismeasure their targets; arrest rates reflect enforcement patterns as well as crime. (Module 17)

modules.title: Stakeholder Management & Analytics Communication
modules.summary: Turn vague requests into scoped, deliverable analyses: use the 5-whys to discover real requirements, scope work and say no with alternatives, lead with BLUF executive summaries, present insights that drive decisions, and manage revisions without endless rework.
objectives: Run a 5-whys discovery to convert vague requests into a concrete business question and decision
Scope an analysis with explicit in/out boundaries and decline or defer work with alternatives
Write BLUF executive summaries that lead with the answer, not the methodology
Present insights using the hook-context-evidence-implication arc and handle revisions professionally

notes.title: Requirements Discovery: The 5-Whys for Vague Requests
notes.body:
- **"Can you pull some data?" is not a requirement** -- it is a symptom; your job is to find the decision behind it
- **5-whys technique** -- ask "why" (politely reframed as "what decision will this inform?") repeatedly until you reach the action the analysis enables
- **The three discovery questions** -- (1) What decision will this inform? (2) What will you do differently based on each possible answer? (3) When do you need it and what does "good" look like?
- **Identify the real stakeholder** -- the requester may be a proxy; find who owns the decision and confirm the question with them
- **Surface hidden assumptions** -- "compare to last quarter" assumes last quarter is the right baseline; confirm it
- **Write it back** -- restate the agreed question, scope, and deadline in writing before starting; misalignment caught here is cheap

notes.title: Scoping and Saying No
notes.body:
- **Define in/out explicitly** -- "In: US retail orders, 2024-2026. Out: wholesale, returns analysis, forecasting." Scope creep dies at the boundary
- **Say no with alternatives** -- never a flat no: "I cannot do the full forecast by Friday, but I can give you the trend drivers by Friday and the forecast next week"
- **Trade the triangle** -- scope, speed, quality: when a stakeholder demands all three, ask which one flexes
- **Park the parking lot** -- capture out-of-scope ideas visibly so stakeholders feel heard without derailing the current work
- **Estimate honestly** -- pad for data cleaning (it always takes longer); a credible date beats an optimistic one
- **Push back on proxy metrics** -- if the requested metric cannot answer the real question, propose the one that can and explain why

notes.title: BLUF Executive Summaries
notes.body:
- **BLUF = Bottom Line Up Front** -- lead with the answer and recommendation; methodology goes last or in an appendix
- **The 3-sentence formula** -- (1) the finding, (2) the business implication, (3) the recommended action
- **One page maximum** -- if an executive needs more, link the appendix; the summary itself stays tight
- **Quantify the so-what** -- "Churn rose 2 points, costing ~$400K ARR" beats "Churn increased"
- **State confidence and caveats** -- "based on 90 days of complete data; West region under-reported by ~5%" builds trust
- **Headline every section** -- each heading should state a conclusion, so skimming the headings tells the story

notes.title: Presenting Insights and Managing Revisions
notes.body:
- **Hook-context-evidence-implication arc** -- open with the change, give just enough context, show the visual proof, land the implication
- **Influencing without authority** -- frame recommendations around the stakeholder's goals and incentives, not your analysis effort
- **Pre-wire big findings** -- share surprising or political results 1:1 before the group meeting; no ambushes
- **Revision policy** -- batch feedback into rounds; distinguish "new question" (new scope) from "correction" (your fix, fast)
- **Version discipline** -- date and version every deliverable; keep the changelog so "final_v2_FINAL" chaos never starts
- **Close the loop** -- after delivery, ask what decision was made; it calibrates your judgment and builds the relationship

cards.front: What are the three discovery questions for a vague request?
cards.back: (1) What decision will this inform? (2) What will you do differently based on each possible answer? (3) When do you need it and what does "good" look like?

cards.front: What is the 5-whys technique in analytics?
cards.back: Asking "why" (framed as "what decision will this inform?") repeatedly until you reach the action the analysis enables -- converting "pull some data" into a real business question.

cards.front: How do you say no to a stakeholder without damaging the relationship?
cards.back: Say no with alternatives: offer what you CAN deliver and when ("trend drivers Friday, forecast next week"), and trade scope/speed/quality explicitly.

cards.front: What does BLUF stand for and what is its structure?
cards.back: Bottom Line Up Front: lead with the answer and recommendation. The 3-sentence formula: finding, business implication, recommended action.

cards.front: What is a "parking lot" in scoping?
cards.back: A visible list capturing out-of-scope ideas so stakeholders feel heard without derailing the current analysis.

cards.front: What is pre-wiring and when do you do it?
cards.back: Sharing surprising or politically sensitive findings 1:1 with key stakeholders before the group meeting -- no ambushes.

cards.front: How do you distinguish a revision that is a correction from one that is new scope?
cards.back: A correction fixes your error or agreed requirement (fix fast); a new question expands scope (re-scope, re-estimate). Batch feedback into rounds.

cards.front: Why quantify the "so-what" in an executive summary?
cards.back: "Churn rose 2 points, costing ~$400K ARR" drives action; "Churn increased" does not. Numbers tied to business impact get decisions made.

quiz.q: A stakeholder asks you to "pull some data on sales." Your first move should be:
choices: Ask what decision the data will inform and what "good" looks like
Pull last 12 months of sales immediately
Build a full dashboard to cover all possibilities
Decline the request as too vague
quiz.explain: Discovery first: find the decision behind the request before touching data. (Module 18)

quiz.q: A stakeholder demands full scope, by Friday, with perfect quality. You should:
choices: Ask which of scope, speed, or quality flexes
Deliver whatever is done Friday with no explanation
quiz.explain: Trade the triangle explicitly -- one of scope, speed, or quality must flex. (Module 18)

quiz.q: Which opening follows BLUF for an executive summary?
choices: "We used a left join on the orders table..."
"Recommendation: pause the West campaign; it drove a $400K ARR churn increase"
quiz.explain: BLUF leads with the answer and recommendation; methodology goes last or in an appendix. (Module 18)

quiz.q: Your analysis shows the CEO's pet project is failing. Before the group meeting you should:
choices: Present it cold for maximum impact
Pre-wire the finding 1:1 with key stakeholders
Soften the numbers to avoid conflict
quiz.explain: Pre-wiring surprising or political findings 1:1 prevents ambushes and keeps trust. (Module 18)

quiz.q: After delivery, the stakeholder asks for "one more cut by region." This is best handled as:
choices: A new question -- confirm scope and re-estimate
A reason to rebuild the whole analysis
quiz.explain: New cuts are new scope, not corrections; confirm and re-estimate rather than absorbing silently. (Module 18)

quiz.q: Writing the agreed question, scope, and deadline back to the stakeholder before starting is valuable because:
choices: It creates paperwork for its own sake
Misalignment caught in writing is cheap; caught after delivery is expensive
quiz.explain: Written confirmation surfaces misunderstandings when they cost nothing to fix. (Module 18)

quiz.q: Which headline best follows the "headline the conclusion" rule?
choices: "West region drove 70% of Q3 revenue growth"
quiz.explain: Headings should state conclusions so skimming the headings tells the story. (Module 18)

quiz.q: To influence without authority, frame your recommendation around:
choices: How much effort your analysis took
quiz.explain: Recommendations land when tied to what the stakeholder cares about, not your effort. (Module 18)

modules.title: R Essentials for Data Analysts (Google Track Coverage)
modules.summary: The Google Data Analytics track includes R programming; this module covers the R essentials an analyst needs: data frames, dplyr verbs, ggplot2 visualization, and R Markdown reporting — mapped concept-for-concept to the Python skills in Module 9.
objectives: Read, inspect, and clean tabular data in R using data frames and the tidyverse.
Transform data with dplyr verbs: filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarise, and group_by.
Build publication-quality charts with ggplot2 using the grammar-of-graphics layering model.
Produce reproducible reports with R Markdown and translate any pandas workflow into R.

notes.title: R basics and data frames
notes.body:
- **Data frame** — R's core tabular structure; think pandas DataFrame with 1-based indexing.
- **Assignment** — `<-` is idiomatic (`x <- 5`); `=` also works in most contexts.
- **Vectors** — the atomic unit: `c(1, 2, 3)`; everything in R is a vector.
- **Reading data** — `read.csv('sales.csv')` returns a data frame; `readr::read_csv()` is faster and never coerces strings to factors.
- **Inspection** — `head()`, `str()`, `summary()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()` mirror pandas' `head/info/describe/shape`.

notes.title: dplyr: the grammar of data manipulation
notes.body:
- **filter()** — keep rows: `filter(df, amount > 100)` (= pandas query/boolean mask).
- **select()** — keep columns: `select(df, customer_id, amount)`.
- **mutate()** — new columns: `mutate(df, tax = amount * 0.08)`.
- **arrange()** — sort: `arrange(df, desc(order_date))`.
- **summarise() + group_by()** — aggregation: `df %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(revenue = sum(amount))`.
- **The pipe** — `%>%` (magrittr) or native `|>` chains verbs left-to-right, like method chaining in pandas.

notes.title: Joins, tidying, and missing data
notes.body:
- **Joins** — `inner_join()`, `left_join()`, `full_join()` take `by = 'key'`; semantics match SQL joins.
- **tidyr** — `pivot_longer()` / `pivot_wider()` reshape data (= pandas melt/pivot).
- **Missing data** — `NA` is R's null; `is.na()`, `na.omit()`, `tidyr::drop_na()`, `replace_na()`.
- **Factors** — categorical type; `factor()` with explicit `levels=` prevents alphabetical surprises in plots and models.
- **Dates** — `as.Date()`, `lubridate::ymd()` parse strings; date arithmetic returns difftime objects.

notes.title: ggplot2 and R Markdown reporting
notes.body:
- **Grammar of graphics** — `ggplot(df, aes(x = date, y = revenue)) + geom_line()`: data + aesthetics + geometry layers.
- **Common geoms** — `geom_col()` bars, `geom_point()` scatter, `geom_histogram()` distributions, `geom_boxplot()` spreads.
- **Faceting** — `facet_wrap(~ region)` small multiples; `labs()` titles; `theme_minimal()` clean look.
- **R Markdown** — `.Rmd` mixes prose and executable chunks (```{r}); knit to HTML/PDF for reproducible reports.
- **Translation rule** — every pandas verb has an R twin: `groupby().agg()` ↔ `group_by() %>% summarise()`; learn the mapping once, work in either language.

cards.front: dplyr verb for filtering rows
cards.back: filter(): filter(df, amount > 100) keeps rows meeting the condition — the R twin of a pandas boolean mask.

cards.front: dplyr verb for creating new columns
cards.back: mutate(): mutate(df, tax = amount * 0.08) adds or transforms columns, like pandas assign().

cards.front: dplyr verb for aggregation by group
cards.back: group_by() %>% summarise(): df %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(revenue = sum(amount)) — the R twin of pandas groupby().agg().

cards.front: R pipe operators
cards.back: %>% (magrittr) and |> (native R 4.1+) chain operations left-to-right, equivalent to pandas method chaining.

cards.front: ggplot2 layering model
cards.back: ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_*(): data plus aesthetic mappings plus one or more geometry layers; add labs(), theme, and facets.

cards.front: R representation of missing values
cards.back: NA. Detect with is.na(), drop with na.omit()/drop_na(), fill with tidyr::replace_na().

cards.front: tidyr reshaping verbs
cards.back: pivot_longer() (wide → long, like pandas melt) and pivot_wider() (long → wide, like pandas pivot).

cards.front: R Markdown purpose
cards.back: Reproducible reporting: .Rmd files interleave narrative prose with executable R chunks and knit to HTML/PDF.

quiz.q: Which dplyr pipeline computes total revenue per region?
quiz.explain: group_by() sets the grouping, then summarise() aggregates within each group — the dplyr equivalent of pandas groupby().agg(). (Module 25)

quiz.q: In ggplot2, what does aes() specify?
choices: The aesthetic mappings from data columns to visual properties
quiz.explain: aes() maps data variables to aesthetics (x, y, color, size); geoms then render those mappings. (Module 25)

quiz.q: How does R represent missing values, and how do you detect them?
quiz.explain: R uses NA for missing data; is.na() detects it elementwise. NULL is the empty object, distinct from NA. (Module 25)

quiz.q: Which tidyr verb converts wide data to long format?
quiz.explain: pivot_longer() stacks multiple columns into key-value pairs (like pandas melt); pivot_wider() does the reverse. (Module 25)

quiz.q: What does the magrittr pipe %>% do?
choices: Passes the left-hand result as the first argument of the right-hand function
quiz.explain: x %>% f() is f(x); it chains dplyr verbs into readable left-to-right pipelines, like pandas method chaining. (Module 25)

quiz.q: Which read function avoids coercing strings to factors and is fastest for CSVs?
quiz.explain: readr::read_csv() is faster, never creates factors, and reports column-type guesses; base read.csv() is fine for small files. (Module 25)

quiz.q: In an R Markdown document, executable R code lives in:
quiz.explain: Rmd chunks (```{r}) execute on knit; the YAML header holds metadata like title and output format. (Module 25)

quiz.q: pandas df.groupby('region')['amount'].sum() translates to which dplyr pipeline?
quiz.explain: Both the group_by/summarise pipeline and the newer .by argument work; tapply() is base-R but returns a named vector, not a data frame. (Module 25)

modules.title: Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate: Domains & Study Plan
modules.summary: Maps the eight-course Google certificate onto the six-phase analytics workflow (ask, prepare, process, analyze, share, act), with heavy emphasis on case studies, SQL, R, and a portfolio capstone project.
objectives: Describe the eight-course structure and the six analytics phases it teaches
Explain why case studies and the capstone portfolio carry the most weight for hiring
Identify the SQL, R, spreadsheet, and Tableau skills each course targets
Build a realistic weekly study plan and exam-readiness checklist

notes.title: The six phases (ask to act)
notes.body:
- **Ask** - define the business problem and stakeholders before touching data
- **Prepare** - collect, store, and organize data from sources
- **Process** - clean and check data for integrity
- **Analyze** - organize, format, and draw insights
- **Share** - communicate findings with visuals and narratives
- **Act** - recommend data-driven actions and next steps

notes.title: Eight courses, one arc
notes.body:
- **Foundations** - data life cycle, toolboxes, fairness concepts
- **Ask** - problem types, scope of work, SMART questions
- **Prepare** - data types, formats, credibility, BigQuery basics
- **Process** - data integrity, cleaning techniques, SQL for cleaning
- **Analyze** - sorting, filtering, R basics, aggregation, validation
- **Share** - visualization principles, dashboards, storytelling with Tableau
- **Act (capstone)** - optional case-study track, full end-to-end project
- **Capstone** - portfolio project: pick a case study, document every phase

notes.title: Case-study emphasis and assessment style
notes.body:
- **Ungraded practice** - quizzes check recall; hands-on activities build muscle
- **Case studies** - graded scenario work mirrors real analyst requests
- **Peer review** - capstone graded against a rubric by other learners
- **Fairness checks** - explicit bias and sampling checks are scored concepts

notes.title: Portfolio capstone and study plan
notes.body:
- **One project, six phases** - show ask through act in a single README-documented project
- **Public artifact** - publish on GitHub or a portfolio site with charts and SQL
- **Study cadence** - 5-8 hours/week finishes in roughly 3-6 months
- **Readiness gate** - you can explain every phase, write joins and aggregations from scratch, and defend your capstone choices

cards.front: Name the six phases of the data analysis process in order.

cards.front: What is a SMART question in the Ask phase?
cards.back: Specific, measurable, action-oriented, relevant, time-bound.

cards.front: Which two programming/data tools are taught for analysis in the certificate?
cards.back: SQL (BigQuery) and R.

cards.front: What visualization tool is featured in the Share course?
cards.back: Tableau, for dashboards and storytelling visuals.

cards.front: Why are fairness and bias concepts graded in this program?
cards.back: Because flawed sampling or biased data produces misleading business decisions.

cards.front: What is a typical completion pace for the certificate?
cards.back: 5-8 hours per week over about 3 to 6 months.

Prepare, ask, analyze, process, act, share

quiz.explain: The program uses SQL (BigQuery) and R for analysis work. (Module 1)

quiz.explain: SMART stands for specific, measurable, action-oriented, relevant, time-bound. (Module 1)
