modules.title: Microsoft PL-300: Power BI Data Analyst Domains
modules.summary: Covers the PL-300 exam domains: preparing data with Power Query, modeling with relationships and DAX over star schemas, building reports and dashboards, and deploying and maintaining Power BI assets.
objectives: Outline the four PL-300 domains and their approximate exam weights
Describe Power Query shaping steps: connecting, transforming, and loading data
Explain star schema modeling, relationships, and core DAX patterns
Summarize report design, dashboard, and deployment/maintenance responsibilities

notes.title: Exam domains and weights
notes.body:
- **Prepare the data (15-20%)** - connect, profile, clean, transform, load in Power Query
- **Model the data (30-35%)** - relationships, DAX, star schema, performance
- **Visualize and analyze (25-30%)** - reports, dashboards, interactive analysis
- **Deploy and maintain (20-25%)** - workspaces, sharing, refresh, security

notes.title: Power Query preparation
notes.body:
- **Connectors** - files, databases, web, and online services as sources
- **Applied steps** - each transformation is recorded and replayable in M
- **Data profiling** - column quality, distribution, and profile views catch issues early
- **Merge vs append** - merge joins tables side by side; append stacks rows

notes.title: Modeling: star schema and DAX
notes.body:
- **Star schema** - central fact table joined to dimension tables; preferred for performance
- **Relationship cardinality** - one-to-many is standard; avoid bi-directional filters unless needed
- **Measures vs calculated columns** - measures compute at query time; calculated columns at refresh
- **CALCULATE** - the core DAX function that modifies filter context for measures

notes.title: Visualize, deploy, maintain
notes.body:
- **Report vs dashboard** - reports are multi-page and interactive; dashboards pin key visuals to one page
- **Drillthrough and tooltips** - focused detail views without cluttering the main page
- **Gateways and refresh** - on-premises data needs a gateway for scheduled refresh
- **Row-level security** - DAX filter roles restrict rows per user or group

cards.front: What are the four PL-300 exam domains?
cards.back: Prepare the data; model the data; visualize and analyze the data; deploy and maintain deliverables.

cards.front: What is a star schema?
cards.back: A model with a central fact table connected to dimension tables, optimized for analytics.

cards.front: What does DAX CALCULATE do?
cards.back: It evaluates an expression under modified filter context, the foundation of most measures.

cards.front: Difference between a Power BI report and a dashboard?
cards.back: Reports are multi-page interactive documents; dashboards pin key visuals onto a single page.

cards.front: What is the role of an on-premises data gateway?
cards.back: It enables scheduled refresh of datasets sourced from on-premises data.

cards.front: Merge vs append in Power Query?
cards.back: Merge joins tables side by side (like a join); append stacks rows (like a union).

cards.front: What is row-level security (RLS)?
cards.back: DAX-based roles that filter which rows each user or group can see.

cards.front: Measures vs calculated columns?
cards.back: Measures evaluate at query time in context; calculated columns compute once at refresh and store values.

quiz.q: Which PL-300 domain carries the largest exam weight?
quiz.explain: Model the data is weighted 30-35%, the largest of the four domains. (Module 2)

quiz.q: In Power Query, stacking rows from two tables with the same columns is called:
quiz.explain: Append stacks rows; merge joins tables side by side. (Module 2)

quiz.q: The preferred modeling pattern for Power BI performance is:
quiz.explain: A star schema with one-to-many relationships is the recommended pattern. (Module 2)

quiz.q: CALCULATE in DAX primarily:
choices: Modifies filter context for an expression
quiz.explain: CALCULATE evaluates an expression under modified filter context. (Module 2)

quiz.q: A Power BI dashboard differs from a report because it:
choices: Pins key visuals onto a single page
quiz.explain: Dashboards are single-page collections of pinned visuals. (Module 2)

quiz.q: Scheduled refresh for on-premises sources requires:
quiz.explain: An on-premises data gateway bridges cloud refresh to local sources. (Module 2)

quiz.q: Row-level security is implemented with:
quiz.explain: RLS uses DAX-based roles to filter rows per user or group. (Module 2)

quiz.q: A calculated column differs from a measure because it:
choices: Computes once at refresh and stores the value
quiz.explain: Calculated columns compute at refresh time; measures compute at query time. (Module 2)

modules.title: Tableau Certified Data Analyst: Domains & Study Plan
modules.summary: Maps the Tableau Certified Data Analyst exam: connecting and preparing data, exploring and analyzing, calculations including LOD expressions, and sharing insights through published dashboards.
objectives: List the Tableau Certified Data Analyst exam domains and question style
Describe data connection, joins/unions, and data preparation options
Explain dimensions, measures, and level-of-detail (LOD) calculation concepts
Plan dashboard design, publishing, and a study schedule

notes.title: Exam domains and format
notes.body:
- **Connect to and prepare data** - connectors, joins, unions, data interpreter
- **Explore and analyze data** - sorting, grouping, sets, forecasting basics
- **Create calculations** - row-level, aggregate, table calculations, LOD
- **Share insights** - dashboards, stories, publishing, permissions
- **Format** - multiple choice plus hands-on lab items in a virtual environment

notes.title: Connecting and preparing data
notes.body:
- **Live vs extract** - live queries the source; extracts snapshot data into .hyper for speed
- **Joins** - combine tables side by side on keys (inner, left, right, full outer)
- **Unions** - stack tables with matching columns, including wildcard unions
- **Data interpreter** - cleans messy Excel headers and subtotals on connect

notes.title: Analysis building blocks
notes.body:
- **Dimensions vs measures** - dimensions slice (categorical); measures aggregate (numeric)
- **Continuous vs discrete** - green pills aggregate; blue pills create headers
- **Sets and groups** - custom subsets for cohort and comparative analysis
- **Bins and histograms** - turn continuous measures into distribution views

notes.title: Calculations, LOD, and sharing
notes.body:
- **LOD expressions** - FIXED, INCLUDE, EXCLUDE compute at a chosen granularity
- **Table calculations** - run across the viz layout (running total, percent of total)
- **Parameters** - user-controlled inputs that swap measures, dimensions, or thresholds
- **Publishing** - workbooks go to Tableau Cloud/Server with projects and permissions

cards.front: What are the four Tableau Certified Data Analyst domains?
cards.back: Connect to and prepare data; explore and analyze data; create calculations; share insights.

cards.front: Live connection vs extract?
cards.back: Live queries the source directly; an extract snapshots data for faster performance.

cards.front: What do FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE do?
cards.back: They are LOD expressions that compute aggregations at a specified level of detail.

cards.front: Dimensions vs measures?
cards.back: Dimensions are categorical fields that slice data; measures are numeric fields that aggregate.

cards.front: What is a table calculation?
cards.back: A calculation computed across the visualization layout, e.g., running total or percent of total.

cards.front: What is a parameter used for?
cards.back: A user-controlled input that can swap measures, dimensions, or thresholds in the view.

cards.front: Joins vs unions?
cards.back: Joins combine tables side by side on keys; unions stack rows from tables with matching columns.

cards.front: Where are published workbooks managed?
cards.back: Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server, organized in projects with permissions.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a Tableau Certified Data Analyst exam domain?
quiz.explain: The four domains are connect/prepare, explore/analyze, calculations, and share insights. (Module 3)

quiz.q: An extract differs from a live connection because it:
choices: Queries the source on every interaction
quiz.explain: Extracts snapshot data into .hyper for speed; live queries the source. (Module 3)

quiz.q: FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE are:
quiz.explain: They are the three level-of-detail expression keywords. (Module 3)

quiz.q: A running total across months in a view is an example of:
quiz.explain: Table calculations operate across the viz layout, like running totals. (Module 3)

quiz.q: Blue pills vs green pills in Tableau indicate:
quiz.explain: Blue = discrete (headers), green = continuous (axes); the color maps to the field role. (Module 3)

quiz.q: Stacking monthly sales files with identical columns uses:
quiz.explain: Unions stack rows from tables with matching columns. (Module 3)

quiz.q: Parameters are most useful for:
choices: Letting users swap measures or thresholds interactively
quiz.explain: Parameters give users control over inputs like measures or thresholds. (Module 3)

quiz.q: Published Tableau workbooks are organized using:
quiz.explain: Publishing goes to Tableau Cloud/Server with projects and permission rules. (Module 3)

modules.title: CompTIA Data+ (DA0-002): Domains & Study Plan
modules.summary: Covers the CompTIA Data+ DA0-002 domains: data concepts and environments, data mining, data analysis, visualization, and data governance and quality, with the vendor-neutral multiple-choice format.
objectives: Name the five DA0-002 domains and their emphasis
Contrast data mining techniques with confirmatory analysis
Describe common visualizations and when each fits the data
Explain governance, quality dimensions, and basic compliance duties

notes.title: Five domains, vendor-neutral
notes.body:
- **Data concepts and environments** - types, schemas, storage, ETL/ELT basics
- **Data mining** - extraction, profiling, discovery techniques
- **Data analysis** - descriptive statistics, hypothesis framing, common methods
- **Visualization** - chart selection, dashboard principles
- **Data governance and quality** - stewardship, lineage, quality dimensions

notes.title: Data concepts and environments
notes.body:
- **Structured vs unstructured** - tables and schemas vs text, images, logs
- **Schemas** - star and snowflake patterns for warehouses; wide vs normalized
- **ETL vs ELT** - transform before load vs load raw then transform in the warehouse
- **Data lake vs warehouse** - raw multi-format storage vs curated analytic store

notes.title: Mining and analysis methods
notes.body:
- **Data mining** - exploratory discovery of patterns in large datasets
- **Descriptive statistics** - mean, median, mode, variance, percentiles summarize data
- **Correlation vs causation** - related movement does not prove one causes the other
- **Sampling** - representative subsets; watch for selection and survivorship bias

notes.title: Visualization and governance
notes.body:
- **Chart fit** - bars for categories, lines for trends, scatter for relationships, histograms for distributions
- **Dashboard discipline** - one screen, clear hierarchy, consistent scales
- **Quality dimensions** - accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity
- **Governance basics** - stewardship roles, lineage, access control, retention rules

cards.front: Name the five CompTIA Data+ DA0-002 domains.
cards.back: Data concepts and environments; data mining; data analysis; visualization; data governance and quality.

cards.front: ETL vs ELT?
cards.back: ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw data then transforms inside the warehouse.

cards.front: Name the five data quality dimensions.
cards.back: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity.

cards.front: When do you use a scatter plot?
cards.back: To show the relationship between two numeric variables.

cards.front: What is survivorship bias?
cards.back: Drawing conclusions from only the survivors/successes while ignoring failures that dropped out.

cards.front: Data lake vs data warehouse?
cards.back: A lake stores raw multi-format data; a warehouse stores curated, schema-defined analytic data.

cards.front: What does data lineage track?
cards.back: The origin, movement, and transformations of data over its lifetime.

cards.front: Correlation vs causation?
cards.back: Correlation is co-movement; causation requires evidence one variable drives the other.

quiz.q: Which is a CompTIA Data+ DA0-002 domain?
quiz.explain: Data governance and quality is one of the five DA0-002 domains. (Module 4)

quiz.q: Transforming data after loading it raw into the warehouse describes:
quiz.explain: ELT loads raw first, then transforms inside the warehouse. (Module 4)

quiz.q: Which quality dimension asks whether data arrived on time?
quiz.explain: Timeliness measures whether data is available when needed. (Module 4)

quiz.q: A histogram is the right chart for:
quiz.explain: Histograms show the distribution shape of continuous data. (Module 4)

quiz.q: Analyzing only successful startups to find success factors risks:
quiz.explain: Ignoring failures that dropped out is survivorship bias. (Module 4)

quiz.q: Data lineage primarily documents:
quiz.explain: Lineage tracks where data came from and how it changed. (Module 4)

quiz.q: Two variables moving together without proof of influence is:
quiz.explain: Correlation is co-movement; it does not establish causation. (Module 4)

quiz.q: A curated, schema-defined store optimized for analytics is a:
quiz.explain: Warehouses hold curated analytic data; lakes hold raw multi-format data. (Module 4)

modules.title: IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate: Domains

objectives: Sequence the IBM certificate's tool progression from Excel to Python
Describe the SQL and relational-database skills the program targets

Plan the capstone project arc from question to presentation

notes.title: Tool arc: Excel to Python

notes.title: Excel and SQL foundations

cards.front: What is the tool progression of the IBM certificate?

notes.title: Six domains in pipeline order
notes.body:

- **Storage and data management** - lakes, warehouses, catalogs, lifecycle rules

- **Analysis and visualization** - query engines and BI for insight

notes.title: Collection patterns
notes.body:
- **Batch ingestion** - scheduled loads of files or database snapshots
- **Streaming ingestion** - continuous event flows with low latency
- **Schema on write vs read** - enforced at ingest vs applied at query time
- **Ordering and durability** - streams trade strict ordering for throughput; buffers protect against loss

notes.title: Storage and processing
notes.body:
- **Data lake** - cheap object storage for raw, multi-format data at any scale
- **Data warehouse** - structured, query-optimized storage for BI workloads
- **Catalogs** - metadata registries that make lake data discoverable and queryable
- **Distributed processing** - cluster frameworks split transforms across many nodes

notes.title: Analysis, visualization, security, study plan
notes.body:

- **BI services** - managed dashboards with SPICE-like in-memory acceleration concepts
- **Security layers** - encryption at rest/in transit, IAM policies, audit trails
- **Study plan** - learn one representative service per domain, then practice cross-service scenarios

modules.title: Palantir Bar I: Advanced SQL Under Interview Pressure
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir. Chain 3+ CTEs, write window functions with explicit frames, use set operations safely, and handle ties and duplicates so your SQL is correct on the whiteboard the first time.
objectives: Chain three or more CTEs into readable multi-stage pipelines under time pressure.
Write window functions with explicit ROWS/RANGE frames for running totals, moving averages, and peer comparisons.
Apply EXCEPT, INTERSECT, and UNION correctly under real constraints: duplicates, NULLs, and column-order rules.
Handle ties and duplicates with ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK and NOT EXISTS, and use timed problem-solving tactics that produce correct-first-time SQL.

notes.title: Chaining CTEs like an assembly line
notes.body:
- **One CTE, one job** - name each CTE for its stage (base_orders, monthly_rev, ranked). An interviewer should read your query top to bottom like a pipeline.
- **Three-stage shape** - filter/shape rows, aggregate, then window or rank. Resist the urge to do everything in one SELECT.
- **Materialization caution** - some engines materialize CTEs (older Postgres), others inline them; never rely on CTEs for performance, only for readability.
- **Worked example** - top-10 customers per month, built in three stages:

```sql
WITH base_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS m, amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01'
),
monthly_rev AS (
  SELECT customer_id, m, SUM(amount) AS rev
  FROM base_orders
  GROUP BY 1, 2
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, m, rev,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY m ORDER BY rev DESC) AS rnk
  FROM monthly_rev
)
SELECT customer_id, m, rev
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 10
ORDER BY m, rnk;
```

notes.title: Window frames: ROWS, RANGE, and peer comparisons
notes.body:
- **Frame anatomy** - `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` = running total. Omitting the frame gives you the default (RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW), which is a classic bug source.
- **ROWS vs RANGE** - ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups rows with equal ORDER BY values (peers). With duplicate sort keys, RANGE collapses ties into one peer group.
- **Moving averages** - `AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` is a 7-day trailing average.
- **Worked example** - running total plus 7-day moving average of daily revenue:

```sql
SELECT day,
       SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day
                     ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
       AVG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day
                     ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_revenue
ORDER BY day;
```

notes.title: Set operations under interview constraints
notes.body:
- **UNION vs UNION ALL** - UNION dedupes (extra sort cost); UNION ALL keeps duplicates. Default to UNION ALL unless the problem asks for distinct rows.
- **INTERSECT / EXCEPT** - INTERSECT returns rows present in both sets; EXCEPT returns rows in the first set but not the second. Both dedupe like UNION.
- **NULL trap** - `WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y ...)` returns NOTHING if the subquery contains a single NULL. EXCEPT treats NULLs as equal, so it behaves; for anti-joins, prefer `NOT EXISTS`.
- **Column rules** - same number of columns, in the same order, with compatible types. Names come from the first SELECT.
- **Worked example** - customers who ordered but never returned anything:

```sql
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM returns;
-- Equivalent anti-join, NULL-safe:
-- SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM orders o
-- WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM returns r
--                   WHERE r.customer_id = o.customer_id);
```

notes.title: Ties, duplicates, and first-time-right tactics
notes.body:
- **ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK** - on values 100, 100, 90: ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3 (arbitrary tie-break); RANK gives 1,1,3 (gap); DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2 (no gap). Pick the one the question actually asks for.
- **Top-N per group with ties** - use RANK/DENSE_RANK in a subquery, then filter `rnk <= N`. ROW_NUMBER silently drops tied rows.
- **Dedup pattern** - `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY natural_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` then keep rn = 1; deterministic and auditable, unlike DISTINCT on wide rows.
- **Timed tactics** - (1) restate the question in one sentence before writing; (2) name CTEs before filling them; (3) write clauses in order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, window, final SELECT; (4) reserve the last 60 seconds to re-read the question and check ties, NULLs, and off-by-one dates.
- **Worked example** - latest event per user, ties broken by highest priority:

```sql
WITH deduped AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_type, event_ts,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                            ORDER BY event_ts DESC, priority DESC) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_type, event_ts
FROM deduped
WHERE rn = 1;
```

cards.front: What is a CTE, and why chain several of them in an interview answer?
cards.back: A Common Table Expression (WITH x AS (...)) names an intermediate result. Chaining 3+ CTEs turns one unreadable mega-query into an assembly line - filter, aggregate, rank - that the interviewer can follow stage by stage.

cards.front: Which window frame produces a running total?
cards.back: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, inside SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY day ...). UNBOUNDED PRECEDING starts the frame at the partition start; CURRENT ROW ends it at the current row.

cards.front: ROWS vs RANGE in a window frame - what is the difference?
cards.back: ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups rows whose ORDER BY values are equal (peers) into one frame edge. With duplicate sort keys, RANGE treats tied rows as a single unit while ROWS counts each one.

cards.front: On values 100, 100, 90: what ranks do ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK assign?
cards.back: ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3 (arbitrary tie-break). RANK: 1,1,3 (ties share a rank, then a gap). DENSE_RANK: 1,1,2 (ties share a rank, no gap). Use RANK/DENSE_RANK when ties must be kept for top-N-per-group.

cards.front: Why does WHERE x NOT IN (subquery) sometimes return zero rows?
cards.back: If the subquery returns even one NULL, the NOT IN comparison becomes UNKNOWN for every row, so nothing matches. Use NOT EXISTS or EXCEPT instead - both handle NULLs correctly.

cards.front: UNION vs UNION ALL - which is faster and why?
cards.back: UNION ALL is faster because it skips the dedupe sort. UNION removes duplicates. Default to UNION ALL unless the question explicitly needs distinct rows.

cards.front: What does EXCEPT do, and how does it treat NULLs?
cards.back: EXCEPT returns rows in the first query that are absent from the second. Unlike NOT IN, it treats NULLs as equal to each other, so it is NULL-safe - handy for 'in A but not B' questions.

cards.front: What is the 'name your CTEs before filling them' tactic?
cards.back: Under time pressure, write the WITH skeleton with stage names (base, agg, ranked) first, then fill each stage. It forces the pipeline structure, prevents one giant SELECT, and lets you narrate while you write.

quiz.q: Which window frame computes a running total of rev ordered by day?
choices: SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING)
quiz.explain: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW grows the frame row by row, accumulating the total. The second choice sums the future; the RANGE version is a sliding peer window. (Module 35)

quiz.q: A subquery used with NOT IN returns one NULL. What does the outer query return?
choices: Zero rows, because every comparison becomes UNKNOWN
All rows except the NULL one
quiz.explain: NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery evaluates to UNKNOWN for every candidate row, so the WHERE clause filters everything out. Use NOT EXISTS or EXCEPT. (Module 35)

quiz.q: Values 100, 100, 90 ranked with DENSE_RANK produce:
quiz.explain: DENSE_RANK shares the rank across ties with no gap: both 100s get 1, then 90 gets 2. RANK would give 1,1,3; ROW_NUMBER would give 1,2,3. (Module 35)

quiz.q: How does EXCEPT handle NULL values compared to NOT IN?
choices: EXCEPT treats NULLs as equal to each other, so it is NULL-safe; NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing
EXCEPT throws an error on NULLs
NOT IN treats NULLs as equal
quiz.explain: Set operators consider NULLs equal for dedupe and matching, so EXCEPT works; NOT IN's three-valued logic breaks on a single NULL. (Module 35)

quiz.q: You need rows in table A that have no match in table B, and B.id may contain NULLs. Safest choice?
choices: WHERE a.id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM B)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.id = A.id)
quiz.explain: NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and expresses the anti-join directly; NOT IN breaks on NULLs, and the join options do not express anti-join semantics. (Module 35)

quiz.q: INTERSECT returns:
choices: All rows from both queries including duplicates
Rows in the first query only
Distinct rows present in both queries
Rows present in exactly one query
quiz.explain: INTERSECT is the set intersection: rows appearing in both inputs, deduplicated. For 'exactly one', use symmetric difference via (A EXCEPT B) UNION (B EXCEPT A). (Module 35)

quiz.q: Which pattern returns exactly one latest event per user with deterministic tie-breaking?
choices: SELECT DISTINCT user_id, MAX(event_ts) FROM events GROUP BY 1
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC), keep rank = 1
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, priority DESC), keep rn = 1
quiz.explain: ROW_NUMBER with a full tie-break ordering yields exactly one row per user deterministically; MAX loses the event_type, RANK can return multiple tied rows, and the HAVING version drops users with several events. (Module 35)

quiz.q: Best first-time-right tactic when the clock starts on a hard SQL question?
choices: Start writing the SELECT immediately to save time
Write the whole query as nested subqueries for compactness
Guess the expected row count and tune toward it
Restate the question in one sentence, name the CTE stages, then fill them in clause order
quiz.explain: Restating catches misreads, named CTE stages force pipeline structure, and clause order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, window, SELECT) prevents the most common syntax slips. (Module 35)

modules.title: Palantir Bar II: Python, Probability & Product Sense
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir. Wrangle data with pandas under time pressure, solve probability brainteasers in classic interview form, estimate anything with Fermi methods, and structure ambiguous product-sense questions around measurable success.
objectives: Wrangle tabular data in pandas under time pressure using idiomatic one-liners: groupby-agg, query, assign, merge, pivot_table.
Solve classic probability brainteasers by defining the sample space and conditioning explicitly.
Break any Fermi estimation problem into defensible segments anchored on known numbers.
Structure ambiguous product questions: clarify, define a success metric, add guardrails, and reason about trade-offs.

notes.title: pandas one-liners under the clock
notes.body:
- **Named aggregation** - `df.groupby('region').agg(revenue=('amount','sum'), orders=('order_id','nunique'))` produces clean column names in one pass; faster than renaming after.
- **query() for filters** - `df.query('amount > 100 and region == "west"')` reads like the business question and avoids chained boolean masks.
- **merge with validate** - `pd.merge(a, b, on='id', validate='one_to_one')` fails loudly on unexpected duplicates instead of silently exploding row counts.
- **pivot_table for cross-tabs** - `df.pivot_table(index='month', columns='plan', values='revenue', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)` is the interview go-to for "show me X by Y".
- **Worked example** - monthly revenue per region with order counts, top region first:

```python
import pandas as pd

out = (
    df.query('order_date >= "2025-01-01"')
      .assign(month=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d['order_date']).dt.to_period('M'))
      .groupby(['region', 'month'])
      .agg(revenue=('amount', 'sum'), orders=('order_id', 'nunique'))
      .reset_index()
      .sort_values(['month', 'revenue'], ascending=[True, False])
)
top_per_month = out.groupby('month').head(1)
```

notes.title: Probability brainteasers, classic interview form
notes.body:
- **Method first** - write the sample space, write the conditioning event, count. Interviewers score the reasoning path, not just the final fraction.
- **Conditioning shrinks the space** - 'given at least one 6' removes all 25 no-six outcomes from 36, leaving 11 equally likely outcomes; only one is (6,6).
- **Independence check** - ask 'does knowing X change the probability of Y?' If no, multiply marginals; if yes, condition.
- **Bayes shape** - P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B); use it when the question gives you the 'reverse' conditional (e.g., test accuracy given disease status).
- **Worked example** - two fair dice; given at least one die shows 6, what is P(both are 6)?

```python
from fractions import Fraction

total = 36
no_six = 5 * 5            # outcomes with neither die a 6
conditioned = total - no_six   # 11 outcomes with at least one 6
favorable = 1             # only (6, 6)
print(Fraction(favorable, conditioned))  # 1/11, NOT 1/6
# The trap answer 1/6 treats 'a specific die is 6' (conditioned space of 6)
# as 'at least one die is 6' (conditioned space of 11).
```

notes.title: Fermi estimation: order-of-magnitude thinking
notes.body:
- **Segment, anchor, multiply** - break the unknown into pieces, anchor each piece on a number you know, multiply, then sanity-check the magnitude.
- **Know your anchors** - US population ~340M, households ~130M, labor force ~170M, hours in a year ~9,000, seconds in a year ~30M.
- **State assumptions aloud** - every assumption is a chance for the interviewer to agree or redirect; silent math gets no partial credit.
- **Sanity-check the tail** - compare your answer to a known adjacent quantity. If your estimate of data analysts exceeds total software workers, a segment is off.
- **Worked example** - how many data analysts work in the US?

```python
us_workers   = 170_000_000   # labor force
tech_share   = 0.05          # ~5% in tech-ish roles (assumption)
tech_workers = us_workers * tech_share            # 8.5M
analyst_share = 0.10         # ~10% of tech workers are data analysts (assumption)
estimate = tech_workers * analyst_share           # ~850K
# Sanity check: BLS-adjacent figures put ops-research/data roles in the
# high hundreds of thousands - same order of magnitude. Ship it.
print(f'{estimate:,.0f}')
```

notes.title: Product sense: measuring success for a feature
notes.body:
- **Structure** - clarify the goal and user, pick a north-star metric, list input (leading) metrics, add guardrails, then name trade-offs and counter-metrics.
- **North-star vs input** - north-star measures the ultimate goal (e.g., weekly retained savers); input metrics are levers you can move this quarter (save rate, revisit rate).
- **Guardrails** - metrics that must not regress (page latency, support tickets, unsubscribe rate). A feature that wins its goal but tanks a guardrail is a failure.
- **Trade-off talk** - explicitly say what you would sacrifice and what you would not; senior candidates name the cost.
- **Worked example** - 'How would you measure success for a save-for-later feature?'

```python
# Metrics tree for the save-for-later case
metrics = {
  'north_star': 'weekly users who return to a saved item within 7 days',
  'inputs': ['save rate per session', 'saved-item revisit rate',
             'share rate from saved items'],
  'guardrails': ['median page latency (must not regress)',
                 'unsubscribe / notification opt-out rate',
                 'support tickets mentioning saves'],
  'segments': ['by device', 'by new vs returning', 'by content category'],
  'tradeoff': 'Optimize revisits, not raw saves - a save nobody revisits is clutter.',
}
```

cards.front: pandas one-liner: total revenue and unique orders per region with clean column names.
cards.back: df.groupby('region').agg(revenue=('amount','sum'), orders=('order_id','nunique')) - named aggregation gives readable columns in a single pass.

cards.front: What does validate='one_to_one' do in pd.merge?
cards.back: It asserts each key appears at most once on each side and raises on violations. Use it in interviews to show you check join cardinality instead of silently exploding row counts.

cards.front: Two fair dice; given at least one shows 6, what is P(both are 6)?
cards.back: 1/11. Conditioning removes the 25 no-six outcomes from 36, leaving 11 equally likely outcomes, of which only (6,6) is favorable. The trap answer 1/6 confuses 'a specific die is 6' with 'at least one die is 6'.

cards.front: State Bayes' theorem and when you reach for it in an interview.
cards.back: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B). Use it when the question hands you the reverse conditional - e.g., test accuracy given disease status - but asks for the probability given a positive test.

cards.front: Name the three Fermi steps and two anchor numbers.
cards.back: Segment the unknown, anchor each segment on a known number, multiply then sanity-check. Anchors: US population ~340M, labor force ~170M, households ~130M, ~9,000 hours/year.

cards.front: What is a north-star metric, and how does it differ from an input metric?
cards.back: The north-star measures the ultimate goal (e.g., weekly users returning to saved items). Input metrics are levers you move this quarter (save rate, revisit rate) that feed the north-star.

cards.front: What is a guardrail metric in a product case?
cards.back: A metric that must not regress while you optimize the goal - e.g., page latency, unsubscribe rate, support tickets. A feature that wins its goal but tanks a guardrail is a failure.

cards.front: Give the 5-step structure for an ambiguous product-sense question.
cards.back: Clarify the goal and user; pick a north-star metric; list input (leading) metrics; add guardrails and segments; name trade-offs and counter-metrics explicitly.

quiz.q: Which pandas one-liner gives revenue and unique order counts per region with clean names?
quiz.explain: Named aggregation computes both measures in one pass with readable column names. groupby().sum() aggregates every numeric column and gives no count; value_counts gives row counts only. (Module 36)

quiz.q: In a merge of customers to orders on customer_id, which argument fails loudly if a customer appears twice?
quiz.explain: validate='one_to_one' asserts key uniqueness on both sides and raises on violations, catching the silent row-count explosion that a plain merge would hide. (Module 36)

quiz.q: A test is 99% accurate and 1% of people have the condition. Roughly, P(condition | positive test) is:
quiz.explain: Bayes: with a 1% base rate, true positives (~1%) roughly equal false positives (~1%), so a positive test means about a 50-50 chance. The 99% figure is the reverse conditional - the classic base-rate trap. (Module 36)

quiz.q: Monty Hall: you pick a door, the host opens a losing door, you may switch. Best strategy?
choices: Switch - it wins about 2/3 of the time
Ask the host for a hint
quiz.explain: Your first pick wins 1/3; the other two doors held 2/3 collectively, and the host's reveal concentrates that 2/3 on the remaining door. Switching doubles your odds. (Module 36)

quiz.q: Estimating US data analysts: 170M workers x 5% tech x 10% analysts = 850K. What is the last required step?
choices: Sanity-check against a known adjacent quantity
quiz.explain: Fermi answers must be magnitude-checked: compare 850K to adjacent knowns (e.g., total software workers) to catch a bad segment. Precision beyond order of magnitude is false accuracy. (Module 36)

quiz.q: Which is a valid Fermi anchor for US-scale estimation?
quiz.explain: The US population is about 340 million; there are ~8,760 hours and ~31.5 million seconds in a year. Anchors must be right to the order of magnitude or the whole chain drifts. (Module 36)

quiz.q: For a save-for-later feature, which is the best north-star metric?
choices: Weekly users who return to a saved item within 7 days
quiz.explain: The north-star must capture the goal - saved items actually revisited - not vanity activity. Raw saves can be gamed and never revisited; returning-to-saved measures real value. (Module 36)

quiz.q: Which belongs in the guardrail set for the save-for-later feature?
quiz.explain: Guardrails protect what must not regress: opt-out rate guards against notification spam from the feature. Save rate, revisit rate, and share rate are goal/input metrics, not guardrails. (Module 36)

modules.title: Palantir Bar III: Ontology & Pipeline Thinking
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir. Think in objects: define entities, relationships, and properties; turn messy operational tables into clean, decision-ready objects; and trace data lineage from source to dashboard.
objectives: Define an ontology-style object model: entity types, relationship (link) types, and typed properties.
Restructure messy operational tables into clean objects with stable identity keys and deterministic rules.
Describe pipeline stages from raw sources to decision-ready objects: ingest, clean, model, serve.
Trace data lineage at field level to explain where a metric came from and why it changed.

notes.title: Ontology thinking: entities, relationships, properties
notes.body:
- **Entities (objects)** - the nouns the business reasons about: Trade, Counterparty, Instrument, Account. Each entity type has a stable identity key, never a row number.
- **Relationships (links)** - named, directed connections: Trade EXECUTED_WITH Counterparty, Account HOLDS Instrument. Links carry their own meaning; 'related to' is not a link type.
- **Properties** - typed attributes on entities: trade.notional is a decimal, trade.trade_date is a date. Property types are contracts, not suggestions.
- **Interview move** - when handed a messy scenario, first name the entities, then the links, then the properties. The model falls out before any code.
- **Worked example** - mini object model for a settlement-operations question:

```
Entity:  Trade        | key: trade_id (stable, source-assigned)
         properties:  notional (decimal), trade_date (date),
                      status (enum: PENDING/SETTLED/FAILED)
Link:    Trade --SETTLES_INTO--> Account
Link:    Account --OWNED_BY--> Counterparty
Entity:  Counterparty | key: lei (Legal Entity Identifier)
         properties:  name (string), jurisdiction (string)
Rule:    a Trade links to exactly one Account; an Account links to
         one or more Counterparties through OWNED_BY.
```

notes.title: From messy rows to clean objects
notes.body:
- **Identity first** - pick a stable key per entity (trade_id, LEI, account number). If the source has none, derive one deterministically (hash of natural key) and document it.
- **One row, one truth** - dedupe to one row per entity instance before modeling properties; use ROW_NUMBER over the natural key ordered by source freshness.
- **Type the properties** - cast at the boundary: dates to dates, decimals to decimals, statuses to a controlled enum. Reject or quarantine rows that violate types.
- **Slowly changing properties** - when a property can change (counterparty jurisdiction), decide: overwrite (Type 1) or keep history (Type 2 with valid_from/valid_to).
- **Worked example** - build a clean Counterparty object from messy feed rows:

```sql
WITH deduped AS (
  SELECT lei, name, jurisdiction, source_ts,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lei ORDER BY source_ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM raw_counterparty_feed
  WHERE lei IS NOT NULL
),
clean AS (
  SELECT lei,
         MAX(name) AS name,                 -- most recent row already isolated
         MAX(jurisdiction) AS jurisdiction -- by rn = 1 below
  FROM deduped WHERE rn = 1 GROUP BY lei
)
SELECT lei,
       name,
       UPPER(TRIM(jurisdiction)) AS jurisdiction,  -- typed, normalized
       CASE WHEN jurisdiction ~ '^[A-Z]{2}$' THEN 'VALID' ELSE 'QUARANTINE' END AS quality_flag
FROM clean;
```

notes.title: Pipeline anatomy: raw to decision-ready
notes.body:
- **Four stages** - ingest (land raw, immutable), clean (type, dedupe, quarantine), model (build entities, links, aggregates), serve (dashboards, APIs, extracts).
- **Raw is immutable** - never edit the landing zone; every fix is a new pipeline run over the same raw data. Reproducibility is the whole game.
- **Idempotent by design** - re-running a stage over the same input must produce the same output; key on business dates and use merge/upsert, not blind appends.
- **Backfill plan** - any pipeline needs a documented way to reprocess history; 'we would have to rebuild everything' is a failing interview answer.
- **Worked example** - stage contract for the daily positions pipeline:

```
ingest:  land trades + prices as-is, partitioned by trade_date; no transforms
clean:   type casts, null-key quarantine, dedupe to one row per trade_id
model:   positions = sum(signed qty) per account/instrument (idempotent merge
         on business_date); P&L = position x price move (recomputed, not stored)
serve:   dashboard reads the positions table only; never raw
backfill: rerun model for any date range from immutable ingest; ~2h per year
```

notes.title: Data lineage reasoning
notes.body:
- **Field-level lineage** - for any dashboard number, answer: which source tables, which transforms, which filters produced it. 'The warehouse' is not an answer.
- **Impact analysis** - before changing a source or a transform, list every downstream object and report that consumes the field. Seniors do this reflexively.
- **'Why did the metric move?'** - debug in order: (1) did the source data change, (2) did a transform or filter change, (3) did the definition change, (4) is it real business movement.
- **Lineage as documentation** - each model stage records its inputs, logic version, and run timestamp; a number without provenance is a rumor.
- **Worked example** - tracing a sudden drop in reported daily P&L:

```
1. Check source: did the trades feed arrive? (row counts vs prior days)
2. Check transforms: did the price join change? (any new NULL prices?)
3. Check definition: did anyone edit the P&L model's filters or status enum?
4. Check business: are the remaining moves explained by market data?
Found: price feed switched to a new vendor code -> NULL prices ->
       positions valued at zero. Fix at the clean stage: map vendor codes,
       quarantine unmapped, alert on null-price rate > 0.5%.
```

cards.front: In ontology terms, what is an entity, a relationship, and a property?
cards.back: Entity: a business noun with a stable identity key (Trade, Counterparty). Relationship/link: a named, directed connection between entities (Trade SETTLES_INTO Account). Property: a typed attribute on an entity (trade.notional as decimal).

cards.front: Why must an entity have a stable identity key?
cards.back: Because everything downstream - links, history, dedupe, lineage - joins on identity. A row number or a generated surrogate that shifts between runs breaks links and makes history unmatchable.

cards.front: What is the difference between SCD Type 1 and Type 2?
cards.back: Type 1 overwrites the old property value (only current truth kept). Type 2 keeps history with valid_from/valid_to rows, so you can reconstruct what was true at any past date - required for auditability.

cards.front: What does it mean for a pipeline stage to be idempotent?
cards.back: Re-running it over the same input produces the same output - achieved with business-date keys and merge/upsert instead of blind appends. Without it, reruns double-count.

cards.front: What is a backfill, and why do interviewers ask about it?
cards.back: Reprocessing historical data through the pipeline after a fix or logic change. Interviewers ask because a pipeline that cannot reprocess history from immutable raw data is not production-grade.

cards.front: Name the four pipeline stages and what each owns.
cards.back: Ingest (land raw, immutable), clean (type, dedupe, quarantine), model (entities, links, aggregates), serve (dashboards, APIs, extracts). Raw is never edited; every fix is a new run.

cards.front: Walk through 'why did this metric move?' in order.
cards.back: (1) Did source data change? (2) Did a transform or filter change? (3) Did the definition change? (4) Is it real business movement? Check data and logic before concluding the business moved.

cards.front: What is field-level lineage and why does it matter?
cards.back: The exact chain - source tables, transforms, filters - that produced a specific field or metric. It lets you answer 'where did this number come from' and do impact analysis before changing anything upstream.

quiz.q: Which is a well-formed link type in an object model?
quiz.explain: Link types are named, directed, and semantically precise (SETTLES_INTO). 'Related to' and vague labels carry no meaning and cannot drive logic or lineage. (Module 37)

quiz.q: A source feed has no stable key for counterparties. Best approach?
choices: Derive a deterministic key from the natural key (e.g., hash of LEI + name) and document it
Use the row number as the key
Generate a random UUID per load
quiz.explain: A deterministic derived key is stable across reruns, so links and history stay joinable. Row numbers shift, random UUIDs break reruns, and names are not unique or stable. (Module 37)

quiz.q: SCD Type 2 is required when:
choices: You only need the current value
You must reconstruct what was true at any past date for audit or history
quiz.explain: Type 2 keeps history rows with valid_from/valid_to, enabling point-in-time reconstruction. If only current truth matters, Type 1 overwrite is simpler and cheaper. (Module 37)

quiz.q: A pipeline stage appends rows without a business-date key. Re-running it will:
choices: Double-count, because it is not idempotent
quiz.explain: Blind appends are not idempotent: each rerun adds the same rows again. Idempotency needs business keys plus merge/upsert semantics. (Module 37)

quiz.q: Why must the raw landing zone be immutable?
choices: So every fix is a reproducible rerun over the same raw data
quiz.explain: Immutable raw data means any pipeline fix or logic change can be replayed deterministically, including backfills. Editing raw destroys the ground truth you would reprocess. (Module 37)

quiz.q: Best backfill answer in an interview?
choices: We would rebuild everything from scratch
Rerun the model stage for the affected date range from immutable ingest; ~2h per year of history
quiz.explain: A production pipeline reprocesses a date range from immutable raw through the fixed logic with a known cost. 'Rebuild everything' or manual edits signal no real pipeline discipline. (Module 37)

quiz.q: Daily reported P&L suddenly drops. What do you check FIRST?
choices: Whether the business actually lost money
Whether the source feeds arrived completely (row counts vs prior days)
quiz.explain: Debug in order: source data, then transforms, then definitions, then business reality. Most 'metric moved' incidents are feed or logic issues, not real business moves. (Module 37)

quiz.q: Before changing a widely used transform, a senior analyst first does:
choices: Impact analysis: list every downstream object and report consuming the field
quiz.explain: Field-level lineage tells you everything downstream of a change; seniors check the blast radius before touching shared logic. The other options are how incidents are born. (Module 37)

modules.title: BNY Mellon Track I: Banking Data Domain
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by BNY Mellon. Learn the banking data domain: trades and positions, P&L attribution, Value-at-Risk as a concept with its limits, and how analysts find reconciliation breaks between systems.
objectives: Read trades and positions data: explain what each row means and how positions aggregate from trades.
Explain P&L attribution conceptually: decompose what moved the P&L into market moves, new activity, and carry/fees.
Describe Value-at-Risk conceptually: what a VaR statement means, what it does not mean, and its key limits.
Diagnose reconciliation breaks between systems: classify missing, mismatch, and timing breaks and trace them with SQL.

notes.title: Trades and positions: events vs state
notes.body:
- **Trades are events** - immutable rows: trade_id, instrument, signed quantity, price, trade_date, book. A trade never changes; corrections are new rows (cancels/rebooks).
- **Positions are state** - derived: net signed quantity per account/instrument, recomputed from trades. Positions answer 'what do we hold right now?'
- **Book** - the desk or portfolio a trade is booked to; P&L and risk are always reported per book.
- **Trade date vs settlement date** - trade date is when the deal was struck; settlement date is when cash/securities move. Positions often key off settlement.
- **Worked example** - net position per account and instrument from the trades table:

```sql
SELECT account_id, instrument_id,
       SUM(signed_qty) AS net_position,   -- buys positive, sells negative
       COUNT(*)        AS trade_count
FROM trades
WHERE status <> 'CANCELLED'
  AND settlement_date <= CURRENT_DATE     -- settled positions only
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING SUM(signed_qty) <> 0;              -- drop flat books
```

notes.title: P&L attribution: what moved the number
notes.body:
- **Attribution decomposes P&L** - 'we made $2M' is the start; attribution says how much came from market moves on prior positions, new trading activity, carry/interest, and fees.
- **Prior-position P&L** - yesterday's position times today's price move: the market did the work.
- **New-activity P&L** - intraday round-trips and new positions: the desk did the work.
- **Carry and fees** - interest, dividends, borrow costs, commissions: the structural drag or lift.
- **Why analysts do this** - a desk that 'made money' purely on market drift has a different story than one that made it on new flow; attribution separates luck from activity.
- **Worked example** - decompose daily P&L per book into components:

```sql
WITH px AS (
  SELECT instrument_id,
         SUM(qty * (close_px - prev_close_px)) AS market_pnl
  FROM prior_positions JOIN prices USING (instrument_id)
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT b.book,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.market_pnl), 0)            AS market_move_pnl,
       COALESCE(SUM(t.realized_pnl), 0)          AS new_activity_pnl,
       COALESCE(SUM(f.carry + f.fees), 0)       AS carry_and_fees
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN px p USING (instrument_id)
LEFT JOIN intraday_trades t USING (book)
LEFT JOIN funding f USING (book)
GROUP BY 1;
-- If market_move_pnl dominates, the story is 'the market moved';
-- if new_activity_pnl dominates, the story is 'the desk traded well'.
```

notes.title: Value-at-Risk, conceptually (not advice)
notes.body:
- **What a VaR statement means** - '1-day 99% VaR of $5M' means: under current conditions, we expect losses to exceed $5M on roughly 1 day out of 100. It is a quantile statement about the loss distribution, not a worst case.
- **What it is NOT** - not a maximum loss (the 1% tail can be far worse), not a guarantee, not valid outside the conditions it was estimated under.
- **Key limits** - (1) tail blindness: VaR says nothing about how bad the worst 1% gets; (2) assumption risk: it assumes the recent past resembles the near future; (3) regime change: in a crisis, correlations and volatilities break the model; (4) model risk: the number is only as good as the data and methods behind it.
- **How analysts use it** - VaR is a common language for comparing risk across books and a trigger for questions ('why did VaR jump?'), not a verdict. Educational concept only: nothing here is investment or risk advice, and VaR must never be used to size positions.
- **Interview framing** - 'VaR is a quantile of the loss distribution; its limits are the tail it ignores, the stationarity it assumes, and the model risk behind the estimate.'

notes.title: Reconciliation: finding breaks between systems
notes.body:
- **Why breaks happen** - front office (trading), middle office (risk), back office (settlement), and custodians each keep their own books; timing, feeds, and booking rules differ.
- **Three break types** - missing (in A, not in B), mismatch (in both, values differ), timing (settlement-date vs trade-date cutoffs make the same trade appear on different days).
- **Analyst workflow** - (1) pick the two sources and the key, (2) full-outer-join on the key, (3) classify: NULL on one side = missing; both present but unequal = mismatch; (4) bucket by cause before escalating.
- **Tolerances** - penny differences from rounding are noise; define a materiality threshold per break type and report only above it, with the raw detail attached.
- **Worked example** - reconcile internal positions against custodian positions:

```sql
WITH rec AS (
  SELECT COALESCE(i.account_id, c.account_id) AS account_id,
         COALESCE(i.instrument_id, c.instrument_id) AS instrument_id,
         i.qty AS internal_qty, c.qty AS custodian_qty
  FROM internal_positions i
  FULL OUTER JOIN custodian_positions c
    USING (account_id, instrument_id)
)
SELECT account_id, instrument_id, internal_qty, custodian_qty,
       CASE
         WHEN internal_qty IS NULL THEN 'MISSING_INTERNAL'
         WHEN custodian_qty IS NULL THEN 'MISSING_CUSTODIAN'
         WHEN ABS(internal_qty - custodian_qty) > 0.01 THEN 'MISMATCH'
         ELSE 'MATCHED'
       END AS break_type
FROM rec
WHERE internal_qty IS NULL OR custodian_qty IS NULL
   OR ABS(COALESCE(internal_qty,0) - COALESCE(custodian_qty,0)) > 0.01
ORDER BY break_type, account_id;
```

cards.front: Trades vs positions: which is the event and which is the state?
cards.back: Trades are immutable events (trade_id, signed qty, price, dates); positions are derived state (net qty per account/instrument), recomputed from trades. Corrections to trades are new rows, never edits.

cards.front: What is a book in banking data?
cards.back: The desk or portfolio a trade is booked to. P&L, positions, and risk are always reported per book - 'which book made/lost the money' is the first question after any P&L move.

cards.front: Trade date vs settlement date - why does the difference cause breaks?
cards.back: Trade date is when the deal was struck; settlement date is when cash/securities move. Systems keyed to different dates show the same trade on different days, creating timing breaks in reconciliation.

cards.front: What does P&L attribution decompose, and why?
cards.back: It splits P&L into market moves on prior positions, new trading activity, and carry/fees. It separates 'the market moved' from 'the desk traded well' - luck vs activity.

cards.front: State what '1-day 99% VaR of $5M' means.
cards.back: Under current conditions, losses are expected to exceed $5M on roughly 1 day out of 100. It is a quantile statement about the loss distribution - not a maximum loss, not a guarantee.

cards.front: Name three limits of Value-at-Risk.
cards.back: Tail blindness (says nothing about how bad the worst 1% gets), assumption risk (assumes the recent past resembles the near future), and regime change/model risk (correlations break in crises; the number is only as good as the model).

cards.front: Name the three reconciliation break types.
cards.back: Missing (in one system, not the other), mismatch (in both, values differ), timing (same trade on different days due to trade-date vs settlement-date cutoffs). Classify before escalating.

cards.front: What is the standard SQL shape for a two-source reconciliation?
cards.back: FULL OUTER JOIN on the business key, then classify: NULL on one side = missing, both present but unequal = mismatch. Bucket by break type and apply a materiality threshold before reporting.

quiz.q: A correction to an already-booked trade should be recorded as:
choices: A new cancel/rebook row; the original stays immutable
An edit to the original trade row
A delete of the original row
An email to the back office
quiz.explain: Trades are immutable events; corrections are new rows (cancel + rebook). Editing history destroys the audit trail and breaks position reconstruction. (Module 38)

quiz.q: Net position per account/instrument is computed as:
choices: SUM of signed quantity over non-cancelled trades
quiz.explain: Positions are state derived from events: buys positive and sells negative sum to the net holding. Counts, averages, and maxes do not give holdings. (Module 38)

quiz.q: A desk reports +$2M P&L; attribution shows $1.9M market_move_pnl and $0.1M new_activity_pnl. The story is:
choices: The market moved in favor of prior positions; new trading added little
quiz.explain: Attribution separates luck from activity: when market-move P&L dominates, the gain came from the market drifting favorably on existing positions, not from new trading skill. (Module 38)

quiz.q: '1-day 99% VaR of $5M' does NOT mean:
choices: It is estimated under current conditions
It describes the loss distribution's quantile
quiz.explain: VaR is a quantile, not a cap: the 1% tail beyond VaR can be far worse. Treating VaR as a maximum is the single most dangerous misreading of the concept. (Module 38)

quiz.q: Which is a genuine limit of VaR an analyst should raise in an interview?
choices: Tail blindness: VaR says nothing about how severe losses are beyond the quantile
quiz.explain: Tail blindness is the core limit: VaR tells you the threshold exceeded 1% of the time but nothing about the shape or severity of that tail. The other options are false. (Module 38)

quiz.q: Internal shows a position; the custodian shows nothing for the same key. Break type?
quiz.explain: Present on one side and absent on the other is a missing break - here missing on the custodian side. Mismatch needs both sides present with different values; timing needs a date-cutoff explanation. (Module 38)

quiz.q: Same trade appears in system A on Monday and system B on Tuesday. Most likely cause?
choices: A timing break from trade-date vs settlement-date cutoffs
quiz.explain: One-day offsets between systems almost always trace to different date keys (trade date vs settlement date). Confirm the cutoff each system uses before escalating. (Module 38)

quiz.q: A reconciliation flags a $0.004 difference on a $10M position. Best handling?
choices: Manually edit one side to match
Suppress it under the materiality threshold as rounding noise, with raw detail attached
quiz.explain: Sub-penny differences are rounding noise; thresholds exist so analysts chase real breaks. Report only above materiality, keep the raw detail for audit, and never edit source-side data to force a match. (Module 38)

modules.title: BNY Mellon Track II: Financial Reporting & Controls
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by BNY Mellon. Master the control mindset: BCBS 239 data principles, CCAR-style regulatory reporting concepts, four-eyes checks and sign-offs, and audit-trail thinking in Tableau and Power BI.
objectives: Explain the BCBS 239 risk-data principles (accuracy, integrity, completeness, timeliness) in analyst terms.
Describe CCAR-style regulatory reporting concepts at a conceptual level, without compliance advice.
Apply data-quality controls in finance: four-eyes checks, reconciliations, sign-offs, and change control.
Build audit-trail thinking into Tableau/Power BI financial reporting: certified datasets, versioning, and lineage.

notes.title: BCBS 239: principles for risk data aggregation
notes.body:
- **Conceptual only** - BCBS 239 is a real supervisory standard; this module covers its data principles as interview concepts, not compliance advice. Always defer to your firm's compliance function on obligations.
- **Accuracy** - numbers must be right: validated inputs, controlled transforms, no silent rounding or unit errors. An analyst proves accuracy with checks, not confidence.
- **Integrity** - data must be protected from unauthorized change: access controls, change logs, no manual spreadsheet edits in the reporting chain.
- **Completeness** - all in-scope data included: every book, every entity, every required field. A report missing one desk is a wrong report.
- **Timeliness** - data available when decisions and filings need it: freshness SLAs on feeds, on-time report generation, no stale snapshots presented as current.
- **Adaptability and governance** - the same principles must hold under stress, new products, and reorganizations; someone owns each dataset and each control.
- **Analyst translation** - for every report you touch, ask: is it accurate (checked?), has integrity (controlled?), complete (all books?), timely (fresh?).

notes.title: CCAR-style regulatory reporting, conceptually
notes.body:
- **Conceptual only** - CCAR (Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review) is a real Federal Reserve process; what follows is interview-level concept, not compliance or legal advice.
- **The idea** - large banks must show they would remain adequately capitalized under hypothetical severe economic scenarios (stress tests), and their capital plans (dividends, buybacks) must be defensible under those scenarios.
- **What analysts supply** - traceable, reconcilable data: exposures, losses, revenues, and capital components, each with lineage back to source systems and a clear definition.
- **Why lineage matters here** - a regulator asking 'where did this number come from' expects the full chain: source system, extract logic, transforms, controls, sign-off. 'The warehouse' fails the question.
- **Scenario thinking** - stress scenarios are hypothetical 'what-if' paths for macro variables; the analyst's job is making sure the data feeding the scenario engine is complete, timely, and controlled - not designing the scenarios.
- **Interview line** - 'CCAR-style reporting means every submitted number is traceable, reconciled, and signed off; my role as an analyst is the data integrity underneath the submission.'

notes.title: Data-quality controls in finance
notes.body:
- **Four-eyes check** - a second qualified person independently reviews logic and results before release. The reviewer re-derives, not just eyeballs.
- **Reconciliations** - every material figure ties to an independent source: subledger to general ledger, internal to custodian, report to source extract.
- **Sign-offs** - named owners attest at each stage (prepared / reviewed / approved), with timestamps. Unsigned reports do not ship.
- **Change control** - report logic changes go through request, impact analysis, testing, and approval; emergency changes get documented after-the-fact review.
- **Exception reporting** - breaks, threshold breaches, and quarantined rows surface automatically; silence is not evidence of quality.
- **Worked example** - month-end reporting control checklist:

```
[ ] Feeds arrived: row counts within tolerance vs prior period
[ ] Reconciliations: subledger = GL; internal = custodian (breaks itemized)
[ ] Logic version: report ran on approved logic v3.2 (change log checked)
[ ] Four-eyes: reviewer independently re-ran key figures (initials + time)
[ ] Exceptions: quarantine list reviewed; each item dispositioned
[ ] Sign-offs: preparer / reviewer / approver recorded with timestamps
[ ] Distribution: sent only to the approved list; no ad-hoc extracts
```

notes.title: BI for financial reporting: audit-trail thinking
notes.body:
- **Certified datasets** - reports pull from governed, certified data sources, not personal extracts or desktop files. If it is not certified, it is not the report.
- **One definition per metric** - 'net revenue' means the same in every dashboard; definitions live in the semantic layer, not in each analyst's head.
- **Versioning** - dashboard logic and definitions are versioned; you can re-run last quarter's report exactly as it ran last quarter.
- **Lineage in the tool** - Tableau and Power BI both expose data-source and field lineage; an analyst should be able to click any figure and see its upstream chain.
- **Export and access controls** - row-level security, restricted exports of sensitive figures, and audit logs of who viewed or downloaded what.
- **Worked example** - pre-publish checklist for a financial dashboard:

```
[ ] Data source is certified (not a personal extract)
[ ] Every KPI uses the shared semantic-layer definition
[ ] Filters/defaults cannot silently exclude a book or entity
[ ] Row-level security tested with two different roles
[ ] Version tagged; prior version retained for restatement comparison
[ ] Lineage panel reviewed: each visual traces to a governed source
[ ] Refresh schedule matches the freshness SLA; failures alert the owner
```

cards.front: Name the four BCBS 239 data principles in one line each.
cards.back: Accuracy: numbers are right and validated. Integrity: protected from unauthorized change. Completeness: all in-scope data included. Timeliness: available when decisions and filings need it.

cards.front: Accuracy vs integrity vs completeness - how do they differ?
cards.back: Accuracy = the values are correct. Integrity = nobody tampered with them (access control, change logs). Completeness = nothing in scope is missing. A report can be accurate yet incomplete (one desk missing).

cards.front: What is CCAR-style reporting, conceptually?
cards.back: Banks must show they stay adequately capitalized under hypothetical severe scenarios, with capital plans defensible under stress. Analysts supply traceable, reconciled data with full lineage - concept only, not compliance advice.

cards.front: What is a four-eyes check, and what makes it real?
cards.back: A second qualified person independently reviews logic and results before release. Real means re-deriving key figures, not eyeballing - with initials and timestamp recorded.

cards.front: What does a sign-off chain look like for a financial report?
cards.back: Prepared / reviewed / approved, each a named owner with a timestamp. Unsigned reports do not ship; the chain is the evidence that controls ran.

cards.front: Why is change control part of data-quality controls?
cards.back: Because unreviewed logic changes are how correct reports silently become wrong ones. Changes go through request, impact analysis, testing, and approval - emergencies get documented after-the-fact review.

cards.front: What is a certified dataset in BI reporting?
cards.back: A governed, approved data source that reports must use instead of personal extracts. Certification means its definitions, lineage, and refresh are controlled and auditable.

cards.front: What audit-trail features should a financial dashboard have?
cards.back: Versioned logic and definitions, field lineage clickable from any visual, row-level security, restricted exports, refresh tied to the freshness SLA with failure alerts, and an access/view audit log.

quiz.q: A report is accurate but missing one trading desk. Which BCBS 239 principle fails?
quiz.explain: Completeness requires all in-scope data: every book, every entity. Accuracy covers correctness of what is present; a missing desk is a completeness failure. (Module 39)

quiz.q: An analyst edits a reporting spreadsheet directly with no log. Which principle is violated?
quiz.explain: Integrity means data is protected from unauthorized, untracked change. Manual unlogged edits in the reporting chain break it even if the numbers happen to be right. (Module 39)

quiz.q: CCAR-style reporting, at the concept level, requires banks to:
choices: Demonstrate adequate capitalization under hypothetical severe scenarios with traceable data
quiz.explain: The concept: stress-test capital adequacy under severe hypothetical scenarios, supported by reconcilable, lineage-complete data. It is a supervisory capital-planning exercise, not market commentary. (Module 39)

quiz.q: In a CCAR-style data request, the analyst's core contribution is:
choices: Supplying traceable, reconciled data with full lineage back to source systems
quiz.explain: Analysts own data integrity underneath the submission: lineage, reconciliations, definitions. Scenario design, capital policy, and legal filings belong to other functions. (Module 39)

quiz.q: What makes a four-eyes check genuine rather than ceremonial?
choices: The reviewer independently re-derives key figures and records initials + timestamp
The reviewer is in another time zone
quiz.explain: Independence of derivation is the control: re-running the logic catches errors that eyeballing misses. Seniority, speed, and location do not create assurance. (Module 39)

quiz.q: Emergency logic change made during month-end close. Correct control handling?
choices: Document it and run after-the-fact review against the change-control standard
quiz.explain: Change control covers emergencies too: document what changed and why, then subject it to after-the-fact review. Undocumented changes are integrity failures. (Module 39)

quiz.q: A dashboard KPI uses an analyst's personal extract instead of the certified source. Problem?
choices: None, if the numbers match today
It breaks audit-trail thinking: uncertified sources have no governed definitions, lineage, or refresh
It is faster, so it is better
Only a problem for large banks
quiz.explain: Certified datasets exist so every figure is governed and reproducible. A personal extract can drift, lacks lineage, and cannot be re-run by anyone else. (Module 39)

quiz.q: Which dashboard feature directly supports 'where did this number come from'?
choices: Clickable field lineage from each visual to its governed source
quiz.explain: Field lineage lets anyone trace a figure to its upstream chain - the BI equivalent of the lineage reasoning from Module 37. Themes, refresh rates, and logos do not answer provenance. (Module 39)

modules.title: Day in the Life: Senior Analyst in Production
modules.summary: Independent interview prep modeled on the publicly described hiring bar; not affiliated with or endorsed by any employer. Operate like a senior: partner with quants, engineers, and PMs; own production dashboards with SLAs; run incident triage when pipelines break; and communicate uncertainty to executives with ranges, not points.
objectives: Partner effectively with quants, data engineers, and PMs: know who owns what and how handoffs work.
Own production dashboards: define freshness SLAs, monitoring, alerting, and on-call responsibility for data.
Run incident response when a pipeline breaks using a triage runbook: detect, scope, mitigate, root-cause, post-mortem.
Communicate uncertainty to executives: ranges not points, pre-mortems, and stating what would change your mind.

notes.title: Working with quants, engineers, and PMs
notes.body:
- **Who owns what** - quants own models and methodology; data engineers own pipelines and infrastructure; PMs own priorities and trade-offs; you own the analysis, the metrics, and the story. Overlap is where incidents breed, so name owners explicitly.
- **Write the handoff down** - every cross-team dependency gets a one-paragraph spec: input schema, freshness expectation, owner, and what 'done' looks like. Verbal agreements evaporate.
- **Ask in their language** - to engineers: 'what is the contract and the SLA?'; to quants: 'what are the assumptions and the valid range?'; to PMs: 'what decision does this unblock, and by when?'
- **Disagree with data, not volume** - bring the numbers, the lineage, and the alternative interpretation; seniors change minds with evidence, presented once, clearly.
- **Standing meeting hygiene** - arrive with the metric, the move, and the so-what in the first 60 seconds; details live in the doc, not the meeting.

notes.title: Owning production dashboards: SLAs, monitoring, on-call
notes.body:
- **Freshness SLA** - every production dashboard states its data-as-of expectation (e.g., 'T+1 by 8 AM ET'). An SLA nobody monitors is a wish.
- **Monitoring** - automated checks on row counts, null rates, key distributions, and refresh completion; alert the owner, not the whole company.
- **On-call for data** - seniors take a rotation for their dashboards: acknowledge within the SLA, triage with the runbook, and communicate status until resolved.
- **Ownership registry** - every dashboard has a named owner and a backup; 'the team owns it' means nobody owns it at 2 AM.
- **Retirement discipline** - dashboards nobody opens get deprecated on a schedule; stale dashboards are where executives find stale numbers.
- **Worked example** - SLA block for a daily revenue dashboard:

```
Dashboard: Daily Revenue Pulse
Owner: senior analyst (backup: analytics lead)
Freshness SLA: data through prior business day by 8:00 AM ET
Monitors: row count within 5% of trailing average; null revenue rate < 0.1%;
          refresh job success; source-feed arrival by 6:30 AM ET
Alerting: page owner on SLA breach; post status in #data-ops within 15 min
On-call: weekly rotation; acknowledge in 15 min, triage per runbook M40-N3
Review: usage + accuracy review monthly; deprecate if unused 90 days
```

notes.title: Incident response: the triage runbook
notes.body:
- **Detect** - monitors fire or a stakeholder reports 'the numbers look wrong'. Timestamp it; start a log immediately.
- **Scope** - which dashboards, which date range, which entities are affected? Bound the blast radius before theorizing.
- **Mitigate** - stale-banner the dashboard, roll back to the last good refresh, or pause the broken stage. Stop the bleeding before the diagnosis.
- **Root-cause** - use the Module 37 order: source data, transforms, definitions, then business reality. Fix at the right stage, not the symptom.
- **Post-mortem** - blameless, written, within 48 hours: timeline, root cause, what detected it (or should have), action items with owners and dates.
- **Worked example** - runbook card taped to every production dashboard:

```
TRIAGE RUNBOOK - data incident
1. LOG: open incident note with timestamp; you own it until handoff
2. SCOPE: affected dashboards / date range / entities (5 min)
3. MITIGATE: stale-banner or roll back to last good refresh (15 min)
4. COMMUNICATE: status in #data-ops: what is wrong, who is affected,
   ETA for next update (15 min, then hourly)
5. DIAGNOSE: source -> transform -> definition -> business (Module 37)
6. FIX at the right stage; backfill per the pipeline's backfill plan
7. POST-MORTEM within 48h: timeline, root cause, detection gap,
   action items with owners and dates. Blameless.
```

notes.title: Communicating uncertainty to executives
notes.body:
- **Ranges, not points** - '$4.2M, likely $3.9M-$4.6M' beats '$4.2M' because it carries the uncertainty the decision needs. A point estimate without a range is a hidden bet.
- **Name the drivers of the range** - 'the range is wide because two enterprise deals may slip' tells the executive what to watch, not just what to feel.
- **Pre-mortems** - before a big call, ask 'it is six months later and this failed; what happened?' Seniors surface risks before they are post-mortems.
- **What would change your mind** - state the evidence that would flip your recommendation. It proves the analysis is honest and gives the executive a tripwire.
- **Separate fact, inference, judgment** - 'revenue fell 8% (fact); the drop concentrates in renewals (inference); I recommend pausing expansion hiring (judgment).' Never blend the three.
- **Worked example** - executive update with uncertainty done right:

```
Subject: Q4 forecast update - range narrowed, risk flagged

Fact:      Q4 revenue forecast $4.2M, range $3.9M-$4.6M (was $3.7M-$4.8M).
Inference: the range narrowed on three closed renewals; width now comes
           almost entirely from two enterprise deals closing in December.
Judgment:  hold expansion hiring until at least one deal signs.
Tripwire:  if both deals slip past Dec 15, cut forecast to $3.8M and revisit.
Pre-mortem: the failure mode is slipped procurement, not lost deals -
           suggest weekly check-ins with both champions starting now.
```

cards.front: Who owns what among quants, data engineers, PMs, and the senior analyst?
cards.back: Quants: models and methodology. Engineers: pipelines and infrastructure. PMs: priorities and trade-offs. Analyst: the analysis, the metrics, and the story. Name owners explicitly - overlap is where incidents breed.

cards.front: What makes a dashboard freshness SLA real?
cards.back: A stated data-as-of expectation (e.g., T+1 by 8 AM ET) plus monitoring that checks it and alerts the named owner on breach. An SLA nobody monitors is a wish.

cards.front: What does 'on-call for data' mean for a senior analyst?
cards.back: Taking a rotation for your production dashboards: acknowledge within the SLA, triage with the runbook, communicate status until resolved. Every dashboard needs a named owner and a backup.

cards.front: Recite the incident triage runbook in order.
cards.back: Log (open incident note), scope (blast radius in 5 min), mitigate (stale-banner or roll back in 15 min), communicate (status in 15 min, then hourly), diagnose (source-transform-definition-business), fix at the right stage, blameless post-mortem within 48h.

cards.front: Why mitigate before diagnosing in an incident?
cards.back: Because stakeholders are making decisions on wrong numbers right now. Stale-banner or roll back first to stop the bleeding; the root-cause analysis can then proceed without the pressure of live damage.

cards.front: What is a blameless post-mortem and what must it contain?
cards.back: A written, no-fault review within 48 hours: timeline, root cause, what detected the issue (or should have), and action items with owners and dates. Blame fixes nothing; systems do.

cards.front: Why give executives ranges instead of point estimates?
cards.back: A range carries the uncertainty the decision needs; a point estimate hides a bet. '$4.2M, likely $3.9M-$4.6M' plus the drivers of the range tells the executive what to watch.

cards.front: What is a pre-mortem, and when do you run one?
cards.back: Before a big decision, ask 'it is six months later and this failed; what happened?' It surfaces risks while they are still avoidable - seniors run it before the call, not after the failure.

quiz.q: A PM asks for a metric 'by Friday'. The senior analyst's first move is to:
choices: Write a one-paragraph spec: definition, source, freshness, and what decision it unblocks
Ask an engineer to build it
quiz.explain: Written handoffs prevent the most expensive failure mode: building the wrong metric fast. Definition, source, and the decision it serves come before any query. (Module 40)

quiz.q: A dashboard has no named owner, only 'the team'. At 2 AM when it breaks:
choices: Nobody is accountable - this is the ownership gap seniors close
The most junior person fixes it
quiz.explain: Diffused ownership means no accountability under pressure. The senior move is a registry: every production dashboard gets a named owner and a backup before it breaks. (Module 40)

quiz.q: Stakeholder reports 'the numbers look wrong' at 9 AM. First two runbook steps?
choices: Diagnose the root cause, then fix it
Log the incident with a timestamp, then scope the blast radius
Wait to see if it resolves
quiz.explain: Log first (timestamp, owner), then scope which dashboards, dates, and entities are affected. Diagnosis comes after you know the blast radius; blame never helps. (Module 40)

quiz.q: During an incident, the dashboard still shows wrong numbers while you diagnose. You should:
choices: Mitigate first: stale-banner or roll back to the last good refresh
Tell stakeholders to ignore it verbally
