quiz.explain: Mitigation precedes diagnosis: stop live damage from wrong numbers before root-causing. A visible stale banner beats a verbal 'ignore it' that nobody hears. (Module 40)

quiz.q: A post-mortem is due. Which content is required?
choices: Who caused it, for the record
A promise it will never happen again
Timeline, root cause, detection gap, and action items with owners and dates
Only the fix that was applied
quiz.explain: Blameless post-mortems fix systems, not people: timeline, root cause, what detected it (or should have), and owned action items. Naming culprits kills future reporting. (Module 40)

quiz.q: 48 hours have passed since an incident resolved and no post-mortem exists. This is:
choices: A process failure: the 48-hour blameless post-mortem is how the org learns
quiz.explain: The post-mortem is the learning mechanism; skipping it guarantees repeat incidents. Every production data incident gets one, with action items tracked to closure. (Module 40)

quiz.q: Best executive forecast format?
choices: Q4 forecast $4.2M, range $3.9M-$4.6M; width driven by two December enterprise deals; tripwire: slip past Dec 15 cuts it to $3.8M
quiz.explain: Ranges plus drivers plus a tripwire give the executive the uncertainty, what to watch, and when to act. Point estimates hide bets; vague optimism hides everything. (Module 40)

quiz.q: 'What would change your mind?' is powerful in executive communication because:
choices: It proves the analysis is honest and gives the executive a tripwire for new evidence
quiz.explain: Stating the evidence that would flip your recommendation demonstrates intellectual honesty and hands the decision-maker a concrete watch-item - the mark of senior judgment. (Module 40)

modules.title: Portfolio Architecture: The 7-Project Portfolio
modules.summary: Build a portfolio of seven projects that together prove every core analyst skill: SQL depth, Python EDA, dashboarding, experimentation, ETL, statistics, and a capstone that ties them all together -- each framed around a real business question.
objectives: Map each of the 7 projects to the analyst skill it proves and the business question it answers
Select appropriate dataset types and techniques for each project slot
Define concrete deliverables (code, dashboard, write-up) for each project
Sequence the 7 projects so earlier work feeds later ones

notes.title: Project 1: SQL Deep-Dive and Project 2: Python EDA
notes.body:
- **Project 1 -- SQL deep-dive** -- Business question: "Which customer cohorts drive repeat revenue?" Dataset: multi-table transactional database (orders, customers, products). Techniques: CTEs, window functions, cohort retention queries. Deliverables: documented .sql file, schema diagram, findings memo
- **Project 2 -- Python EDA** -- Business question: "What patterns explain ride-share demand spikes?" Dataset: large public event/trip dataset (e.g., city taxi or bike-share). Techniques: pandas profiling, missing-data handling, correlation analysis, matplotlib/seaborn visuals. Deliverables: clean Jupyter notebook with markdown narrative, requirements.txt
- **Why these first** -- SQL and Python are the two screening skills; leading with them passes resume filters and technical screens
- **Public data discipline** -- use well-known open datasets so reviewers can reproduce your work without access requests

notes.title: Project 3: Dashboard and Project 4: A/B Test Analysis
notes.body:
- **Project 3 -- Dashboard** -- Business question: "How is the regional sales team tracking against target?" Dataset: sales/CRM extract. Techniques: KPI design, drill-downs, date intelligence, published interactive dashboard. Deliverables: live dashboard link, 60-second walkthrough write-up
- **Project 4 -- A/B test analysis** -- Business question: "Did the new checkout flow lift conversion?" Dataset: simulated or public experiment data. Techniques: hypothesis testing, power and sample-size reasoning, guardrail metrics, peeking discipline. Deliverables: analysis notebook, executive summary with ship/no-ship recommendation
- **Dashboard proof** -- reviewers scan dashboards in 60 seconds; yours must answer its question instantly (see Module M21)
- **Experiment rigor** -- state the hypothesis BEFORE looking at results; report p-values with confidence intervals and practical significance, not just statistical

notes.title: Project 5: ETL Pipeline and Project 6: Statistical Analysis
notes.body:
- **Project 5 -- ETL pipeline** -- Business question: "Can we automate the weekly marketing report?" Dataset: raw CSV/API extracts. Techniques: Python or SQL pipeline with cleaning, validation checks, logging, and scheduled refresh. Deliverables: pipeline code, data-quality checks, before/after timing comparison
- **Project 6 -- Statistical analysis** -- Business question: "What actually drives employee attrition?" Dataset: HR or survey data. Techniques: regression, controlling for confounders, assumption checks, honest uncertainty reporting. Deliverables: methods write-up, coefficient interpretation in plain English, limitations section
- **Pipeline proof** -- idempotent, logged, with row-count and null-rate assertions; shows you think like a data engineer, not just a notebook user
- **Statistics honesty** -- correlation is not causation; name confounders, show diagnostics, and state what the model cannot prove

notes.title: Project 7: Capstone and Portfolio Sequencing
notes.body:
- **Project 7 -- Capstone** -- an end-to-end build: ingest raw data, clean it, model it, dashboard it, write it up (full spec in Module M22)
- **Sequencing** -- do projects 1-2 first (skills), then 5 (pipeline feeds 7's ingest), then 3-4-6 (analysis depth), capstone last to reuse everything
- **One theme option** -- running all 7 against one domain (e.g., e-commerce) tells a coherent story and reuses domain knowledge
- **Deliverable standard** -- every project ships: code, a README with problem/approach/results, and a 2-minute story you can tell in an interview
- **Quality over quantity** -- seven polished projects beat fifteen half-finished ones; each must be something you can defend live

cards.front: List the 7 projects of the portfolio and the skill each proves.
cards.back: (1) SQL deep-dive -- SQL; (2) Python EDA -- Python analysis; (3) dashboard -- BI/visualization; (4) A/B test -- experimentation; (5) ETL pipeline -- data engineering; (6) statistical analysis -- statistics; (7) capstone -- end-to-end ownership.

cards.front: What techniques belong in the SQL deep-dive project?
cards.back: CTEs, window functions, cohort retention queries on a multi-table transactional database answering which customer cohorts drive repeat revenue.

cards.front: What is the business question and deliverable for the A/B test project?
cards.back: "Did the new checkout flow lift conversion?" Deliverables: analysis notebook plus an executive summary with a ship/no-ship recommendation, hypothesis stated before results.

cards.front: What makes an ETL pipeline project portfolio-worthy?
cards.back: Idempotent, logged, with row-count and null-rate validation checks and a scheduled refresh -- proving data-engineering thinking, not just notebook work.

cards.front: What honesty requirements apply to the statistical analysis project?
cards.back: Name confounders, check assumptions, report uncertainty, and state what the model cannot prove -- correlation is not causation.

cards.front: What is the recommended sequencing of the 7 projects?
cards.back: 1-2 first (SQL, Python screening skills), then 5 (pipeline feeds capstone ingest), then 3-4-6 (analysis depth), capstone last to reuse everything.

cards.front: What three things must every project ship?
cards.back: Code, a README with problem/approach/results, and a 2-minute story you can tell in an interview.

cards.front: Why might you run all 7 projects against one domain?
cards.back: A single domain (e.g., e-commerce) tells a coherent story, reuses domain knowledge, and reads as deliberate rather than scattered.

quiz.q: Which project best proves experimentation skills to a hiring manager?
choices: The A/B test analysis with a ship/no-ship recommendation
quiz.explain: The A/B test project demonstrates hypothesis testing, power reasoning, and guardrail metrics -- the experimentation skill. (Module 19)

quiz.q: In the ETL pipeline project, row-count and null-rate assertions prove:
choices: The pipeline is idempotent and monitored for data quality
quiz.explain: Validation checks with logging show data-engineering discipline, not just notebook work. (Module 19)

quiz.q: Why do the SQL and Python projects come first in the sequence?
choices: They are the two screening skills that pass resume filters and technical screens
quiz.explain: SQL and Python get you past screens; lead with what opens doors. (Module 19)

quiz.q: A portfolio has fifteen half-finished projects. The fix per this module is:
choices: Cut to seven polished, defensible projects
Hide the unfinished ones with no README
quiz.explain: Seven polished projects you can defend live beat fifteen half-finished ones. (Module 19)

quiz.q: The statistical analysis project must include a limitations section because:
choices: Honest uncertainty and confounders separate analysis from cherry-picking
quiz.explain: Naming what the model cannot prove is what makes statistics trustworthy. (Module 19)

quiz.q: For the dashboard project, the key reviewer test is:
choices: Whether a reviewer grasps its answer in 60 seconds
quiz.explain: Reviewers scan dashboards in 60 seconds; instant comprehension is the bar. (Module 19)

quiz.q: The capstone is sequenced last because:
choices: It reuses the pipeline, analysis, and dashboard skills from earlier projects
quiz.explain: The end-to-end capstone integrates ingest, modeling, and dashboarding -- skills built in projects 1-6. (Module 19)

quiz.q: Each project README must contain which three sections?
quiz.explain: Problem/approach/results frames every project as a business story, not a code dump. (Module 19)

modules.title: GitHub Portfolio Engineering
modules.summary: Turn GitHub into a hiring asset: clean repo structures, READMEs that frame problem/approach/results, notebooks that render without errors, pinned repos, requirements files, and commit hygiene that signals professional engineering habits.
objectives: Structure a project repo (README, notebooks or src, data docs, requirements) so a stranger can reproduce it
Write README templates with problem, approach, results, and how-to-run sections
Apply notebook hygiene: clean execution order, stripped outputs where appropriate, and pinned dependencies
Maintain commit hygiene and pin the strongest repos to the profile

notes.title: Repo Structure That Reproduces
notes.body:
- **Standard layout** -- README.md, notebooks/ or src/, data/ (or data/README with download instructions), requirements.txt, and a short methods note
- **Never commit large data** -- link to the public source or provide a download script; keep repos lean and cloneable
- **Data dictionary** -- document every column's meaning and grain; reviewers should not have to guess what "amt_adj" means
- **How-to-run** -- exact commands to reproduce: python version, pip install -r requirements.txt, run order of notebooks
- **One repo per project** -- monorepos bury your work; each of the 7 projects gets its own focused repository
- **License and contact** -- an MIT license and your contact links remove friction for anyone evaluating the work

notes.title: README Templates: Problem / Approach / Results
notes.body:
- **Problem** -- the business question in two sentences; who cares and what decision it informs
- **Approach** -- data sources, key techniques, and the analysis plan at a high level (details live in the notebook)
- **Results** -- the headline finding with one number and one visual embedded; link the live dashboard if one exists
- **Repo map** -- a bullet list of what lives where, so a reviewer lands oriented
- **Badges** -- build status, Python version, or last-updated badges signal maintenance at a glance
- **Keep it skimmable** -- headings, bullets, and short paragraphs; a wall of text never gets read

notes.title: Notebooks That Render
notes.body:
- **Run top-to-bottom before pushing** -- Restart & Run All, then confirm; out-of-order execution is the most common portfolio embarrassment
- **nbstripout concepts** -- strip bulky outputs (and any secrets) before committing so diffs stay readable and repos stay small
- **Markdown narrative** -- every notebook tells a story: question, exploration, finding, next step; code cells are evidence, not the story
- **No hardcoded local paths** -- use relative paths or a config so the notebook runs on any machine
- **Pin dependencies** -- requirements.txt with versions (pandas==2.x) so the notebook still runs in a year
- **Limit output size** -- sample large dataframes for display; a 10,000-row printed table helps nobody

notes.title: Commit Hygiene and Profile Pinning
notes.body:
- **Atomic commits** -- one logical change per commit with a clear message ("Add cohort retention query", not "stuff")
- **Conventional style** -- prefix with feat/fix/docs/refactor; it reads as professional habit
- **No secret leaks** -- never commit API keys, tokens, or credentials; use environment variables and a .gitignore from day one
- **Pin your best 6** -- GitHub profile pins are prime real estate; pin the strongest, most complete projects, ordered by impact
- **Profile README** -- a short profile README with your focus, skills, and links turns profile visits into portfolio tours
- **Green squares are a side effect** -- consistent commits follow from real work; never commit noise just for the graph

cards.front: What is the standard layout of a portfolio project repo?
cards.back: README.md, notebooks/ or src/, data/ (or download instructions), requirements.txt, a data dictionary/methods note, .gitignore, and a license.

cards.front: What three sections must a project README contain?
cards.back: Problem (the business question), Approach (data, techniques, plan), Results (headline finding with a number and a visual) -- plus a repo map and how-to-run.

cards.front: What does "Restart & Run All" prevent?
cards.back: Out-of-order notebook execution -- the most common portfolio embarrassment, where cells depend on state that no longer exists top-to-bottom.

cards.front: What is nbstripout for?
cards.back: Stripping bulky cell outputs (and any secrets) before committing, so diffs stay readable and repositories stay small.

cards.front: Why pin dependencies in requirements.txt?
cards.back: Pinned versions (pandas==2.x) ensure the notebook still reproduces in a year instead of breaking on a new library release.

cards.front: What is an atomic commit?
cards.back: One logical change per commit with a clear message ("Add cohort retention query"), optionally prefixed feat/fix/docs/refactor.

cards.front: Why should you never commit large data files?
cards.back: They bloat the repo and slow cloning; instead link the public source or provide a download script, and document the data dictionary.

cards.front: What belongs on your GitHub profile itself?
cards.back: Pin your 6 strongest, most complete repos ordered by impact, plus a short profile README with focus, skills, and links.

quiz.q: A reviewer clones your repo but cannot run the notebook. The most likely cause is:
quiz.explain: Hardcoded absolute paths break on any other machine; use relative paths or config. (Module 20)

quiz.q: Before pushing a notebook, the mandatory final step is:
choices: Restart & Run All, confirming top-to-bottom execution
quiz.explain: Restart & Run All catches out-of-order execution before a reviewer does. (Module 20)

quiz.q: Your repo diff is unreadable because of huge JSON outputs. The fix is:
choices: Use nbstripout-style output stripping before committing
quiz.explain: Stripping bulky outputs keeps diffs readable and repos small. (Module 20)

quiz.q: Which README structure best serves a hiring reviewer?
choices: Problem / Approach / Results with a repo map and how-to-run
Just the code with no explanation
quiz.explain: Problem/approach/results frames the business story; the repo map and run instructions enable reproduction. (Module 20)

quiz.q: You accidentally committed an API key. The correct response is:
choices: Rotate the key immediately, purge it from history, and add a .gitignore
quiz.explain: Secrets in history stay in history; rotate the credential, purge it, and prevent recurrence with .gitignore. (Module 20)

quiz.q: How many repos should you pin on your GitHub profile, and which ones?
choices: Your 6 strongest, most complete projects ordered by impact
quiz.explain: Profile pins are prime real estate; showcase the strongest complete work. (Module 20)

quiz.q: A good commit message looks like:
quiz.explain: Atomic commits with clear, conventional messages signal professional habits. (Module 20)

quiz.q: Why include a data dictionary in the repo?
choices: So reviewers understand each column's meaning and grain without guessing
quiz.explain: Undocumented columns like "amt_adj" force reviewers to guess; a dictionary removes the friction. (Module 20)

modules.title: Dashboard Portfolio: What Hiring Managers Want
modules.summary: Learn exactly what reviewers scan for in the first 60 seconds of a dashboard, how to run before/after makeovers that prove design judgment, when interactivity adds value versus clutter, and how to publish and write up dashboards that show your thinking.
objectives: Optimize a dashboard for the 60-second reviewer scan: headline KPI, trend, and insight-first titles
Execute a before/after makeover that documents specific design decisions and their rationale
Judge when interactivity (filters, drill-throughs) adds value versus clutter
Publish dashboards accessibly and write companion narratives that reveal analytical thinking

notes.title: The 60-Second Reviewer Scan
notes.body:
- **What reviewers actually do** -- open the link, glance for 60 seconds, decide "can this person communicate"; they rarely click deep on first pass
- **The three things they must find** -- the business question, the headline answer with a number, and evidence it is trustworthy (data dates, definitions)
- **First-screen test** -- everything above the fold must stand alone; assume they never scroll
- **Insight-first titles** -- "Churn concentrated in first-30-day mobile users" beats "Churn dashboard"
- **Data freshness stamp** -- "Data through Oct 6, 2026" answers the first skeptical question before it is asked
- **One dashboard, one question** -- a portfolio dashboard that tries to answer five questions answers none in 60 seconds

notes.title: Before/After Makeovers
notes.body:
- **The makeover format** -- show the original flawed visual, list each specific change, show the rebuilt version, explain why each change improves comprehension
- **What to fix** -- pie charts with 12 slices become bars; dual axes become stacked aligned charts; rainbow palettes become sequential with one highlight color
- **Document the rationale** -- "Switched to horizontal bars because category labels were truncated" proves judgment, not just taste
- **Keep the receipts** -- describe the data and grain so the makeover is reproducible, not a mockup
- **Makeover sources** -- rebuild a public "bad chart" example or one of your own early drafts; both show growth
- **Write-up length** -- 300-500 words with side-by-side screenshots; long enough to show thinking, short enough to be read

notes.title: Interactivity vs. Clutter
notes.body:
- **Interactivity earns its place** -- filters that change the business answer (region, segment, date range) add value; filters nobody touches add clutter
- **Drill-through discipline** -- one level of drill (summary to detail) is usually enough; three levels deep means the summary failed
- **Slicer budget** -- 2-4 well-chosen slicers; more than that signals you could not decide what matters
- **Default view = the story** -- the dashboard must answer its question with zero clicks; interactivity is for the curious, not the confused
- **Tooltips as footnotes** -- definitions and caveats belong in tooltips, not crowding the canvas
- **Mobile check** -- hiring managers open links on phones; verify the layout survives a small screen

notes.title: Publishing Options and Thinking Write-Ups
notes.body:
- **Publishing options** -- public links on BI platforms, embedded in a portfolio site, or exported PDF for offline review; choose whatever the reviewer can open with one click
- **No login walls** -- if a reviewer needs an account, they will not see it; public or it does not exist for hiring purposes
- **Companion write-up** -- 200-400 words: the question, the key design decisions, the headline finding, and what you would do next with more data
- **Show the thinking, not just the tool** -- "I chose a cohort heatmap because retention is a two-dimensional problem" beats "I used Tool X"
- **Version and date** -- label the dashboard version and data vintage so it reads as maintained, not abandoned
- **Link everything** -- portfolio site, GitHub, and resume all point to the same live dashboard URL

cards.front: What three things must a reviewer find in the 60-second scan?
cards.back: The business question, the headline answer with a number, and evidence of trustworthiness (data dates, definitions).

cards.front: What is the first-screen test for a dashboard?
cards.back: Everything above the fold must stand alone -- assume the reviewer never scrolls.

cards.front: What is the structure of a before/after makeover write-up?
cards.back: Original flawed visual, a list of each specific change, the rebuilt version, and why each change improves comprehension -- 300-500 words with side-by-side screenshots.

cards.front: When does interactivity add value vs. clutter?
cards.back: Filters that change the business answer (region, segment, date) add value; filters nobody touches, 3-level drills, and 5+ slicers add clutter.

cards.front: What is the "slicer budget"?
cards.back: 2-4 well-chosen slicers. More signals you could not decide what matters.

cards.front: Why must a portfolio dashboard have no login wall?
cards.back: If a reviewer needs an account, they will not see it -- public or it does not exist for hiring purposes.

cards.front: What goes in a dashboard companion write-up?
cards.back: 200-400 words: the question, key design decisions, the headline finding, and what you would do next with more data.

cards.front: What does "default view = the story" mean?
cards.back: The dashboard must answer its question with zero clicks; interactivity is for the curious, not the confused.

quiz.q: A reviewer opens your dashboard link on their phone and sees only the top third. Your best defense was:
choices: Making the above-the-fold view answer the question alone
Hiding the KPI in a tooltip
quiz.explain: The first-screen test: everything above the fold must stand alone. (Module 21)

quiz.q: Which dashboard title best serves the 60-second scan?
choices: "West region drove 70% of Q3 growth; East flat"
quiz.explain: Insight-first titles state the conclusion so the scan lands the message. (Module 21)

quiz.q: In a makeover write-up, the most convincing sentence is:
choices: "Switched to horizontal bars because long category labels were truncated"
quiz.explain: Documenting the specific rationale proves design judgment, not just taste. (Module 21)

quiz.q: A dashboard has 8 slicers, 3 drill levels, and no clear headline. The core problem is:
choices: Clutter substituting for decisions about what matters
quiz.explain: Excessive interactivity signals undecided priorities; 2-4 slicers and one drill level is the discipline. (Module 21)

quiz.q: Where do definitions and caveats belong on a dashboard?
quiz.explain: Tooltips carry definitions without crowding the visual story. (Module 21)

quiz.q: Your dashboard requires a paid BI account to view. For hiring purposes this means:
choices: Reviewers will not see it -- publish a public link or export instead
quiz.explain: No login walls: public or it does not exist for hiring. (Module 21)

quiz.q: A companion write-up should emphasize:
choices: Your design decisions and reasoning ("I chose X because...")
quiz.explain: "Show the thinking, not just the tool" is what separates analysts from button-clickers. (Module 21)

quiz.q: Why stamp "Data through Oct 6, 2026" on the dashboard?
choices: It answers the reviewer's first skeptical question about freshness before it is asked
quiz.explain: A freshness stamp is part of the trust evidence in the 60-second scan. (Module 21)

modules.title: Capstone Project Blueprint
modules.summary: A complete end-to-end capstone spec: raw ingest through cleaning, modeling, dashboarding, and a professional write-up -- with a milestone checklist, dataset selection criteria, and documentation standards that make the capstone interview-defensible.
objectives: Follow the five-stage capstone spec: ingest, clean, model, dashboard, write-up
Select a dataset using the capstone criteria: messy, joinable, business-relevant, and right-sized
Hit every item on the milestone checklist from proposal to final demo
Produce documentation (data dictionary, methods, limitations, README) to professional standards

notes.title: The Five-Stage Spec: Ingest, Clean, Model
notes.body:
- **Stage 1 -- Ingest** -- pull raw data from at least two sources (API + CSV, or two public datasets that join); script the download so it is reproducible
- **Stage 2 -- Clean** -- handle missing values with documented rules, standardize formats, dedupe on a defined key, and log every decision; keep a raw/processed split
- **Stage 3 -- Model** -- build an analytical model: this can be a star-schema mart, a set of cohort metrics, or a statistical model -- the point is a defensible analytical layer, not necessarily ML
- **Validation gates** -- row counts before/after each stage, null-rate checks, and a reconciliation of totals against source
- **Idempotency** -- re-running the pipeline from scratch must produce identical outputs; no manual steps
- **Timebox each stage** -- 1-2 weeks per stage keeps the capstone shippable instead of eternal

notes.title: Stages 4-5: Dashboard and Write-Up
notes.body:
- **Stage 4 -- Dashboard** -- one question, one screen, insight-first titles, 60-second readability, published publicly (see Module M21)
- **Stage 5 -- Write-up** -- the capstone report: executive summary (BLUF), methods, findings with visuals, limitations, and next steps; 1,500-2,500 words
- **The 2-minute demo** -- rehearse a spoken walkthrough: the question, what you built, the headline finding, what you would do next
- **Artifacts checklist** -- pipeline code, cleaned dataset (or regeneration script), dashboard link, report PDF, repo README
- **Peer review** -- have one other person run the pipeline and read the report before you call it done; fresh eyes catch broken assumptions
- **Ship date** -- set a hard deadline; a shipped capstone with rough edges beats a perfect one that never lands

notes.title: Dataset Selection Criteria
notes.body:
- **Messy enough** -- real missing values, inconsistent formats, something to actually clean; pristine toy data proves nothing
- **Joinable** -- at least two tables or sources that combine on a real key; single-table data cannot show modeling skill
- **Business-relevant** -- the question must matter to a plausible stakeholder (revenue, churn, operations), not just be interesting
- **Right-sized** -- 100K-10M rows: big enough to need real technique, small enough to run on a laptop
- **Licensed for use** -- public domain or open license; document the source and license in the README
- **Fresh enough** -- data from the last 3-5 years reads as current; 2012 data invites "so what" questions

notes.title: Milestone Checklist and Documentation Standards
notes.body:
- **Milestone 0 -- Proposal** -- one page: question, data sources, planned techniques, success criteria; get feedback before building
- **Milestone 1 -- Ingest complete** -- raw data landed, row counts logged, source snapshot saved
- **Milestone 2 -- Clean complete** -- cleaning log written, validation gates passing, data dictionary drafted
- **Milestone 3 -- Model complete** -- analytical layer built, key metrics reconciled to source totals
- **Milestone 4 -- Dashboard live** -- published, 60-second test passed with a fresh viewer
- **Milestone 5 -- Write-up and demo** -- report finalized, 2-minute demo rehearsed, repo polished
- **Documentation standard** -- every number in the report traces to a query; every query lives in the repo; the README explains how to reproduce all of it

cards.front: What are the five stages of the capstone spec?
cards.back: Ingest (scripted, 2+ sources), Clean (documented rules, raw/processed split), Model (analytical layer), Dashboard (one question, public), Write-up (BLUF report).

cards.front: What are the six dataset selection criteria?
cards.back: Messy enough, joinable (2+ sources), business-relevant, right-sized (100K-10M rows), licensed for use, fresh enough (last 3-5 years).

cards.front: What is a validation gate in the pipeline?
cards.back: Row counts before/after each stage, null-rate checks, and reconciliation of totals against the source -- proving each stage did what it claims.

cards.front: What does idempotency mean for the capstone pipeline?
cards.back: Re-running from scratch produces identical outputs with no manual steps.

cards.front: What are the capstone milestones 0 through 5?
cards.back: 0 Proposal, 1 Ingest complete, 2 Clean complete, 3 Model complete, 4 Dashboard live, 5 Write-up and demo.

cards.front: How long should the capstone report be and what does it contain?
cards.back: 1,500-2,500 words: BLUF executive summary, methods, findings with visuals, limitations, next steps.

cards.front: What is the 2-minute demo?
cards.back: A rehearsed spoken walkthrough: the question, what you built, the headline finding, and what you would do next.

cards.front: Why require a peer review before calling the capstone done?
cards.back: Fresh eyes catch broken assumptions -- have someone else run the pipeline and read the report first.

quiz.q: A capstone uses one pristine 500-row CSV from 2012. Which selection criteria does it violate?
quiz.explain: It fails messy (nothing to clean), joinable (single table), and fresh (2012 invites "so what"). (Module 22)

quiz.q: After the Clean stage, row counts dropped 40% with no log entry. The missing practice is:
choices: A validation gate with a documented cleaning log
quiz.explain: Validation gates and a cleaning log make every row-count change explainable. (Module 22)

quiz.q: Your pipeline requires three manual Excel edits before it runs. This violates:
choices: Idempotency -- re-runs must need no manual steps
quiz.explain: Idempotent pipelines reproduce identical outputs from scratch with zero manual intervention. (Module 22)

quiz.q: The capstone report's most important structural choice is:
choices: Leading with a BLUF executive summary
quiz.explain: BLUF puts the answer and recommendation first; methodology follows. (Module 22)

quiz.q: Which milestone comes first?
choices: Proposal: question, sources, techniques, success criteria
quiz.explain: Milestone 0 is the one-page proposal -- get feedback before building. (Module 22)

quiz.q: The documentation standard for the capstone is best summarized as:
choices: Every number traces to a query, every query lives in the repo, the README explains reproduction
quiz.explain: Full traceability from report number to query to reproduction instructions. (Module 22)

quiz.q: Why timebox each stage to 1-2 weeks?
choices: To keep the capstone shippable instead of eternal
quiz.explain: Timeboxes plus a hard ship date beat a perfect project that never lands. (Module 22)

quiz.q: The Model stage of the capstone must be machine learning:
choices: True -- otherwise it is not a model
False -- a star-schema mart, cohort metrics, or statistical model all qualify as an analytical layer
quiz.explain: The point is a defensible analytical layer, not necessarily ML. (Module 22)

modules.title: Senior Analyst Interview Loops
modules.summary: Prepare for every stage of the analyst interview loop: a SQL live-coding strategy that narrates your thinking, a take-home case approach that shows judgment under time pressure, business case interviews, STAR behavioral stories tailored to analysts, and smart questions to ask employers.
objectives: Apply a live-coding strategy: clarify, narrate, build incrementally, and verify SQL under pressure
Structure take-home cases with an executive summary, methods, findings, and limitations in limited time
Answer business case interviews with a hypothesis-driven, metric-first framework
Tell STAR behavioral stories anchored in analyst situations and ask revealing employer questions

notes.title: SQL Live-Coding Strategy
notes.body:
- **Clarify first** -- restate the question, confirm the grain, ask about edge cases (nulls, duplicates, ties) before writing a line
- **Narrate your thinking** -- interviewers score your reasoning, not just the answer; say what you are about to do and why
- **Build incrementally** -- start with a simple SELECT, add the join, then the window function; verify each layer
- **CTEs over nested subqueries** -- named CTEs read clearly and are easier to debug aloud
- **Handle ties deliberately** -- ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK: state which you chose and why the business question demands it
- **Verify out loud** -- "Let me sanity-check: this should return one row per customer" -- then describe what you would test with real data

notes.title: Take-Home Case Approach
notes.body:
- **Timebox ruthlessly** -- if they say 3 hours, spend 3; a polished partial answer beats an unfinished epic
- **Lead with the executive summary** -- BLUF: recommendation first, then supporting analysis; assume they read one page
- **Show your work cleanly** -- one notebook or script, markdown narrative, no dead cells, requirements listed
- **State assumptions explicitly** -- "Assumed revenue is net of refunds; flagged where the data was ambiguous"
- **Limitations section** -- what you could not verify and what you would do with more time; honesty beats bluffing
- **Do not over-model** -- a clear descriptive answer with good judgment beats a shaky predictive model in a take-home

notes.title: Business Case Interviews
notes.body:
- **Hypothesis-driven** -- state 2-3 candidate explanations for the metric movement before diving into data
- **Metric-first framing** -- define the success metric and guardrails first: "We want conversion up without refund rate rising"
- **Segment before you conclude** -- overall trends hide segment stories; always ask "for whom did this change?"
- **Structure: what, so-what, now-what** -- describe the finding, quantify the business impact, recommend the next action
- **Think in experiments** -- when asked "how would you test this," propose the design: hypothesis, randomization unit, sample size logic, guardrails
- **Watch the clock** -- business cases reward a complete structured answer over exhaustive depth; land the recommendation

notes.title: STAR Stories for Analysts and Questions to Ask
notes.body:
- **STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result** -- keep each story to 2 minutes; the Result must include a number or a decision made
- **Analyst story bank** -- prepare: a messy-data rescue, a stakeholder disagreement you resolved, an insight that changed a decision, a mistake you caught, a deadline you hit
- **Quantify results** -- "...which led marketing to reallocate $200K in spend" beats "...and it went well"
- **Own your mistakes** -- a story about catching your own error and fixing the process shows seniority more than perfection does
- **Questions to ask them** -- "What does the data stack look like?" "How are analyst recommendations received?" "What would success look like in 90 days?" "What is the messiest data problem right now?"
- **Red-flag listening** -- vague answers about data quality, no clear decision-maker for your work, or "we just need dashboards" signal a reporting role, not an analyst role

cards.front: What is the first step in SQL live-coding, before writing any code?
cards.back: Clarify: restate the question, confirm the grain, and ask about edge cases (nulls, duplicates, ties).

cards.front: Why narrate your thinking during live SQL?
cards.back: Interviewers score your reasoning, not just the answer -- saying what you are doing and why earns partial credit even if syntax slips.

cards.front: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK -- when does the choice matter?
cards.back: With ties: ROW_NUMBER arbitrarily breaks them, RANK skips numbers, DENSE_RANK does not. State which the business question demands and why.

cards.front: What is the take-home case timebox rule?
cards.back: Spend exactly the stated time (e.g., 3 hours); a polished partial answer beats an unfinished epic.

cards.front: What structure should a business case answer follow?
cards.back: What (the finding), so-what (quantified business impact), now-what (recommended action) -- hypothesis-driven and metric-first.

cards.front: What is STAR and what must the Result include?
cards.back: Situation, Task, Action, Result -- 2 minutes, with the Result including a number or a decision that was made.

cards.front: Name four stories for an analyst STAR story bank.
cards.back: A messy-data rescue, a stakeholder disagreement resolved, an insight that changed a decision, a mistake caught (plus a deadline hit).

cards.front: Name three revealing questions to ask the employer.
cards.back: "What does the data stack look like?" "How are analyst recommendations received?" "What would success look like in 90 days?" "What is the messiest data problem right now?"

quiz.q: During live SQL coding you are unsure whether ties should share a rank. You should:
choices: State the choice explicitly and tie it to the business question
quiz.explain: Deliberate tie-handling, stated aloud, shows senior judgment. (Module 23)

quiz.q: A take-home says "spend no more than 3 hours." You have a great idea needing 6 more hours. You should:
choices: Ship the polished 3-hour version and note the idea under limitations/next steps
quiz.explain: Respecting the timebox and documenting next steps beats an unfinished epic. (Module 23)

quiz.q: In a business case, "conversion is down 10%" -- your first analytical move is:
choices: State 2-3 hypotheses and segment the metric before concluding
Ask for more data with no structure
quiz.explain: Hypothesis-driven, segment-first analysis beats jumping to conclusions. (Module 23)

quiz.q: Which STAR result is strongest?
choices: "Marketing reallocated $200K in spend based on the finding"
quiz.explain: Results need a number or a decision made to prove impact. (Module 23)

quiz.q: An interviewer asks how you would test a new pricing page. The expected structure is:
choices: Hypothesis, randomization unit, sample-size logic, guardrail metrics
quiz.explain: Experiment design answers need hypothesis, randomization, sizing, and guardrails. (Module 23)

quiz.q: Why prefer CTEs over nested subqueries in live coding?
choices: Named CTEs read clearly and are easier to debug aloud
quiz.explain: Readability and debuggability under narration pressure is the win. (Module 23)

quiz.q: An employer cannot describe their data stack or who decides on analyst recommendations. This signals:
choices: A possible reporting-only role with weak data foundations -- a red flag
quiz.explain: Vague answers on stack and decision ownership warn of a dashboard-factory, not an analyst seat. (Module 23)

quiz.q: Your take-home analysis hit an ambiguous column definition. Best handling:
choices: State the assumption explicitly and flag where the data was ambiguous
quiz.explain: Explicit assumptions plus a limitations section show honest judgment. (Module 23)

modules.title: 90-Day Certification & Job-Readiness Roadmap
modules.summary: A week-by-week 90-day plan that sequences certification study, portfolio milestones, application cadence, networking, and mock interviews into one system -- ending with offer evaluation criteria so you choose the right role, not just the first one.
objectives: Sequence certification study across 90 days without cannibalizing portfolio building time
Hit dated portfolio milestones: 7 projects shipped on a realistic cadence
Run a sustainable application cadence with tracking and follow-up discipline
Evaluate offers on role quality, growth, compensation, and data maturity -- not just salary

notes.title: Weeks 1-4: Foundations and First Proof
notes.body:
- **Certification** -- pick ONE target certification and schedule the exam for week 10-12; a date on the calendar drives study
- **Study blocks** -- 60-90 minutes daily on exam topics, mapped to this course's modules; practice questions beat re-reading
- **Portfolio** -- ship Project 1 (SQL deep-dive) by end of week 2 and Project 2 (Python EDA) by end of week 4
- **GitHub setup** -- profile README, pinned repos, and repo templates in place by week 2 so every project lands cleanly
- **Resume v1** -- one page, metrics-first bullets, tailored to data analyst postings; start collecting target job descriptions
- **Weekly review** -- 30 minutes every Friday: what shipped, what slipped, next week's top three

notes.title: Weeks 5-8: Depth, Dashboard, and Pipeline
notes.body:
- **Certification** -- shift to timed practice exams; review every wrong answer and map it back to a module
- **Portfolio** -- ship Project 5 (ETL pipeline) by week 6, Project 3 (dashboard) by week 7, Project 4 (A/B test) by week 8
- **Dashboard polish** -- run the 60-second test with a friend; publish the public link
- **Networking** -- 2-3 genuine conversations per week: comment thoughtfully on analysts' posts, ask about their stack, never open with "refer me"
- **Applications** -- begin light applications (5-10/week) to roles matching completed projects; track everything in a spreadsheet
- **Study group or accountability** -- one partner or group keeps the cadence honest through the middle slump

notes.title: Weeks 9-12: Capstone, Interview Prep, Full Cadence
notes.body:
- **Certification** -- sit the exam in week 10-11; pass or fail, document lessons and schedule a retake if needed
- **Portfolio** -- ship Project 6 (statistical analysis) by week 9, capstone proposal by week 10, full capstone by week 12
- **Interview prep** -- daily SQL practice (one live-coding style problem), weekly mock behavioral using your STAR bank
- **Applications at full cadence** -- 10-15 quality applications per week, each with a tailored resume bullet set
- **Take-home readiness** -- keep a template notebook and a 3-hour timebox routine ready so cases do not derail the schedule
- **Follow-up discipline** -- follow up once per application after 7-10 days; track responses, screens, and conversion rates

notes.title: Offer Evaluation and Sustaining the System
notes.body:
- **Role quality** -- is it analysis or reporting? Who consumes your work, and do recommendations get implemented?
- **Growth** -- mentorship, learning budget, promotion path, and exposure to harder problems in year one
- **Compensation** -- base, bonus, equity, benefits as a total package; benchmark against market data, not just the last offer
- **Data maturity** -- modern stack, governed definitions, and engineering support beat a higher title on spreadsheets-from-hell
- **Decision framework** -- score each offer 1-5 on role, growth, comp, and data maturity; discuss trade-offs explicitly before signing
- **Keep the system warm** -- even after accepting, keep the portfolio updated quarterly; careers are long and proof compounds

cards.front: What is the single most important scheduling action in weeks 1-4?
cards.back: Pick ONE certification and schedule the exam for week 10-12 -- a date on the calendar drives study.

cards.front: Which portfolio projects ship by end of week 4?
cards.back: Project 1 (SQL deep-dive) by week 2 and Project 2 (Python EDA) by week 4.

cards.front: What is the recommended application cadence?
cards.back: 5-10/week in weeks 5-8, then 10-15 quality applications per week in weeks 9-12, each tracked with follow-up after 7-10 days.

cards.front: How should certification study shift in weeks 5-8?
cards.back: From topic study to timed practice exams, reviewing every wrong answer and mapping it back to a module.

cards.front: What interview prep runs daily in weeks 9-12?
cards.back: One SQL live-coding style problem daily, plus weekly mock behavioral interviews using the STAR story bank.

cards.front: What are the four offer-evaluation dimensions?
cards.back: Role quality (analysis vs. reporting), growth, total compensation, and data maturity. Score each 1-5.

cards.front: What is the Friday weekly review?
cards.back: 30 minutes: what shipped, what slipped, and next week's top three priorities.

cards.front: Why keep the portfolio updated after accepting an offer?
cards.back: Careers are long and proof compounds -- quarterly updates keep the system warm for the next move.

quiz.q: In week 1, the highest-leverage planning action is:
choices: Scheduling the certification exam for week 10-12
quiz.explain: A scheduled exam date drives all subsequent study discipline. (Module 24)

quiz.q: By end of week 8, which projects should be shipped?
quiz.explain: Weeks 1-8 ship SQL, Python EDA, ETL pipeline, dashboard, and A/B test; statistics and capstone close in weeks 9-12. (Module 24)

quiz.q: The most effective certification study method per this module is:
choices: Timed practice exams with wrong-answer review mapped to modules
quiz.explain: Practice questions and wrong-answer review beat passive re-reading. (Module 24)

quiz.q: A networking message that opens with "Can you refer me?" is:
choices: Backwards -- lead with genuine conversation about their work first
quiz.explain: 2-3 genuine conversations per week about their stack; never open with a referral ask. (Module 24)

quiz.q: After 10 days with no response to an application, you should:
choices: Apply again to the same role
Follow up once, then move on
quiz.explain: One follow-up after 7-10 days; track conversion rates and keep cadence. (Module 24)

quiz.q: An offer has the highest salary but the role is pure dashboard reporting on messy spreadsheets. Per the framework:
choices: Score it low on role quality and data maturity and weigh the trade-off explicitly
quiz.explain: Score 1-5 on role, growth, comp, and data maturity; decide on explicit trade-offs. (Module 24)

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the Friday 30-minute review?
choices: What shipped, what slipped, next week's top three
quiz.explain: A short weekly review keeps the 90-day system honest and adaptive. (Module 24)

quiz.q: Why keep a take-home template notebook ready during weeks 9-12?
choices: So interview cases do not derail the schedule -- a 3-hour timebox routine stays ready
quiz.explain: Prepared templates let you execute take-homes inside the cadence instead of blowing up the week. (Module 24)
