scriptLabs.title: Window Functions on Orders
scriptLabs.brief: Rank customers by total spend, compute per-customer running totals, and calculate month-over-month revenue growth with LAG on the orders table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount).
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Schema: orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount)
-- Task A: total spend per customer, ranked 1..N
-- YOUR CODE HERE: write the CTE + RANK() query

-- Task B: running total per customer in date order
-- YOUR CODE HERE: SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) query

-- Task C: month-over-month revenue growth using LAG()
-- YOUR CODE HERE: monthly CTE + LAG() + percent-change query
scriptLabs.required: Three working queries: (A) one row per customer with total_spend and a rank column where rank 1 is the top spender; (B) one row per order with a running_total column that is non-decreasing within each customer; (C) one row per month with prev_revenue and mom_pct percent growth.
scriptLabs.hint: RANK() goes in the SELECT, not the WHERE. For running totals the window needs both PARTITION BY customer_id and ORDER BY order_date. Wrap LAG() output in a CTE so you can compute the percentage in the outer query, and guard the division with NULLIF to avoid divide-by-zero.
scriptLabs.solution:
-- Task A: rank customers by total spend
WITH customer_totals AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id,
       total_spend,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_dense_rank,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_quartile
FROM customer_totals
ORDER BY spend_rank;

-- Task B: running total per customer in date order
SELECT order_id,
       customer_id,
       order_date,
       amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY order_date, order_id
       ) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date, order_id;

-- Task C: month-over-month revenue growth with LAG()
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(
           100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
           / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0),
           1
       ) AS mom_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

scriptLabs.title: CTEs & Recursive Org Chart
scriptLabs.brief: Write a recursive CTE over employees(id, name, manager_id) that walks the reporting chain from the CEO down, reporting each employee's depth and their full management path.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Schema: employees(id, name, manager_id)
-- manager_id is NULL for the CEO (top of the org chart).

-- Task: for every employee return id, name, depth (CEO = 0),
-- and path (e.g. 'CEO > VP Sales > Rep').
-- YOUR CODE HERE: write the recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    -- anchor member: YOUR CODE HERE
    -- recursive member: YOUR CODE HERE
)
SELECT id, name, depth, path FROM org ORDER BY path;
scriptLabs.required: A single recursive CTE that returns every employee exactly once, with depth = 0 for the CEO and incrementing by 1 per level, plus a readable path string from CEO to the employee. Ordering by path shows the tree.
scriptLabs.hint: The anchor selects the CEO with depth 0 and path = name. The recursive member joins employees to org on employees.manager_id = org.id, increments depth, and concatenates the path with || ' > ' || name.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    -- Anchor: the CEO (no manager)
    SELECT id,
           name,
           0 AS depth,
           name AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive step: direct reports of everyone already in the tree
    SELECT e.id,
           e.name,
           o.depth + 1 AS depth,
           o.path || ' > ' || e.name AS path
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth, path
FROM org
ORDER BY path;

-- Bonus: find the chain of command ABOVE a single employee (bottom-up walk)
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
    FROM employees
    WHERE id = 42          -- employee of interest
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.level + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN chain c ON e.id = c.manager_id
)
SELECT level, name FROM chain ORDER BY level DESC;

scriptLabs.title: Tune the Slow Query
scriptLabs.brief: Rewrite a SELECT * query that wraps an indexed column in a function into SARGable form, then reason about what EXPLAIN tells you before and after.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Slow query: the function on order_date defeats the index.
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2026;

-- Task A (YOUR CODE HERE): rewrite as a SARGable range predicate.

-- Task B (YOUR CODE HERE): pick only needed columns; rewrite an OR into UNION ALL
-- for the query below:
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 7 OR amount > 500;

-- Task C: write the EXPLAIN statements you would run to compare both versions,
-- and list which EXPLAIN lines change and why (as SQL comments).
scriptLabs.required: Task A: a range predicate on order_date with no function on the column. Task B: explicit column list and UNION ALL rewrite with one SARGable predicate per branch. Task C: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on both versions plus comments naming the plan changes (Seq Scan to Index Range Scan, row estimates, buffer hits).
scriptLabs.hint: A function on the left side of a comparison kills index use: convert 'year = 2026' into a half-open range ['2026-01-01', '2027-01-01'). OR across different columns rarely uses two indexes at once; UNION ALL lets each branch seek its own index.
scriptLabs.solution:
-- Task A: SARGable range predicate (index on order_date can seek)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date <  DATE '2027-01-01';

-- Task B: explicit columns + UNION ALL so each branch seeks its own index
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 7
UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <> 7
  AND amount > 500;

-- Task C: compare plans
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2026;
-- Expect: Seq Scan on orders with Filter: (EXTRACT...) ; high buffer reads,
-- actual rows scanned = whole table regardless of selectivity.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date <  DATE '2027-01-01';
-- Expect: Index Range Scan on the order_date index; Rows Removed by Filter
-- drops; Buffers: shared hit falls from thousands to dozens. If the planner
-- still seq-scans, the table may be small (fine) or stats are stale (ANALYZE).

scriptLabs.title: Clean 100k Rows with pandas
scriptLabs.brief: Build a reproducible cleaning pipeline: enforce a dtype spec, handle missing values, drop duplicates, clip outliers, and emit a cleaning log that counts every row touched.
scriptLabs.starter:
import pandas as pd

DTYPE_SPEC = {
    "order_id": "int64",
    "customer_id": "int64",
    "order_date": "datetime64[ns]",
    "amount": "float64",
    "status": "category",
}

df = pd.read_csv("orders_raw.csv")
cleaning_log = []

# 1. Enforce dtypes (parse dates) - YOUR CODE HERE

# 2. Missing values: drop rows missing order_id; fill status with "unknown" - YOUR CODE HERE

# 3. Duplicates: keep first full-row duplicate - YOUR CODE HERE

# 4. Outliers: clip amount to the 1st/99th percentiles - YOUR CODE HERE

# 5. Append one dict per step to cleaning_log with step, rows_before, rows_after, note
#    then write the cleaned frame and the log - YOUR CODE HERE
scriptLabs.required: A script that runs end to end and writes orders_clean.csv plus a cleaning_log (list of dicts or CSV) where each step records rows_before, rows_after, and a note. Dtypes match DTYPE_SPEC exactly at the end, no null order_id values remain, and amount sits within the 1st-99th percentile bounds.
scriptLabs.hint: Use pd.to_datetime with errors='coerce' so bad dates become NaT instead of crashing. astype(DTYPE_SPEC) after coercion enforces the spec in one shot. Compute clip bounds from the data BEFORE clipping, and log counts before and after each mutation.
scriptLabs.solution:
import pandas as pd

DTYPE_SPEC = {
    "order_id": "int64",
    "customer_id": "int64",
    "order_date": "datetime64[ns]",
    "amount": "float64",
    "status": "category",
}

df = pd.read_csv("orders_raw.csv")
cleaning_log = []


def log_step(step, before, after, note=""):
    cleaning_log.append({
        "step": step,
        "rows_before": int(before),
        "rows_after": int(after),
        "rows_changed": int(before - after),
        "note": note,
    })


# 1. Enforce dtypes (parse dates, coerce junk to NaT/NaN)
before = len(df)
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], errors="coerce")
df = df.astype(DTYPE_SPEC)
log_step("dtype_spec", before, len(df), "parsed dates, enforced " + str(DTYPE_SPEC))

# 2. Missing values: drop rows missing the key; fill status with "unknown"
before = len(df)
n_missing_key = int(df["order_id"].isna().sum())
df = df.dropna(subset=["order_id"]).copy()
df["status"] = df["status"].cat.add_categories("unknown").fillna("unknown")
log_step("missing_values", before, len(df),
         f"dropped {n_missing_key} rows with null order_id; filled null status")

# 3. Duplicates: keep the first occurrence of each full row
before = len(df)
n_dupes = int(df.duplicated().sum())
df = df.drop_duplicates(keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)
log_step("duplicates", before, len(df), f"removed {n_dupes} duplicate rows")

# 4. Outliers: clip amount to the 1st/99th percentiles (winsorize, don't drop)
before = len(df)
lo, hi = df["amount"].quantile(0.01), df["amount"].quantile(0.99)
n_clipped = int(((df["amount"] < lo) | (df["amount"] > hi)).sum())
df["amount"] = df["amount"].clip(lo, hi)
log_step("outlier_clip", before, len(df),
         f"clipped {n_clipped} amounts to [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")

# 5. Write outputs
df.to_csv("orders_clean.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame(cleaning_log).to_csv("cleaning_log.csv", index=False)
print(pd.DataFrame(cleaning_log).to_string(index=False))
print("final dtypes: " + str(dict(df.dtypes.astype(str))))

scriptLabs.title: A/B Test Sample Size Calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Write pure-Python functions (no scipy) that compute per-group sample size for a two-proportion z-test and run a chi-square Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) check on observed traffic splits.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math


def z_inverse(p):
    """Return z with P(Z <= z) = p for standard normal Z. YOUR CODE HERE."""
    raise NotImplementedError("YOUR CODE HERE")


def sample_size_two_proportion(p1, p2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8):
    """Per-group sample size for a two-sided two-proportion z-test.
    YOUR CODE HERE."""
    raise NotImplementedError("YOUR CODE HERE")


def srm_check(control_n, variant_n, expected_ratio=0.5):
    """Chi-square SRM check. Return (chi2, p_value, flagged).
    YOUR CODE HERE."""
    raise NotImplementedError("YOUR CODE HERE")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Baseline 10% conversion, detect lift to 12%, alpha 0.05, power 0.8
    print("n per group:", sample_size_two_proportion(0.10, 0.12))
    print("SRM:", srm_check(5120, 4880))
scriptLabs.required: sample_size_two_proportion(0.10, 0.12) returns 3841 per group. srm_check returns a (chi2, p_value, flagged) tuple; a 5120/4880 split is not flagged, while a 5600/4400 split is flagged. No third-party imports beyond math.
scriptLabs.hint: The standard formula: n = ((z_a * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2))) / |p2-p1|)^2, with z_a the two-sided critical value and z_b the power quantile. For chi-square(1), the survival function is 1 - erf(sqrt(chi2/2)). Use an inverse-normal approximation (e.g. Acklam) since scipy is off-limits.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math


def z_inverse(p):
    """Inverse standard-normal CDF via the Acklam rational approximation."""
    if not 0.0 < p < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("p must be in (0, 1)")
    a = [-3.969683028665376e+01, 2.209460984245205e+02, -2.759285104469687e+02,
         1.383577518672690e+02, -3.066479806614716e+01, 2.506628277459239e+00]
    b = [-5.447609879822406e+01, 1.615858368580409e+02, -1.556989798598866e+02,
         6.680131188771972e+01, -1.328068155288572e+01]
    c = [-7.784894002430293e-03, -3.223964580411365e-01, -2.400758277161838e+00,
         -2.549732539343734e+00, 4.374664141464968e+00, 2.938163982698783e+00]
    d = [7.784695709041462e-03, 3.224671290700398e-01, 2.445134137142996e+00,
         3.754408661907416e+00]
    plow, phigh = 0.02425, 1.0 - 0.02425
    if p < plow:
        q = math.sqrt(-2.0 * math.log(p))
        num = (((((c[0] * q + c[1]) * q + c[2]) * q + c[3]) * q + c[4]) * q + c[5])
        den = ((((d[0] * q + d[1]) * q + d[2]) * q + d[3]) * q + 1.0)
        return num / den
    if p > phigh:
        q = math.sqrt(-2.0 * math.log(1.0 - p))
        num = (((((c[0] * q + c[1]) * q + c[2]) * q + c[3]) * q + c[4]) * q + c[5])
        den = ((((d[0] * q + d[1]) * q + d[2]) * q + d[3]) * q + 1.0)
        return -num / den
    q = p - 0.5
    r = q * q
    num = (((((a[0] * r + a[1]) * r + a[2]) * r + a[3]) * r + a[4]) * r + a[5]) * q
    den = (((((b[0] * r + b[1]) * r + b[2]) * r + b[3]) * r + b[4]) * r + 1.0)
    return num / den


def sample_size_two_proportion(p1, p2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8):
    """Per-group n for a two-sided two-proportion z-test."""
    if p1 == p2:
        raise ValueError("p1 and p2 must differ")
    p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2.0
    z_a = z_inverse(1.0 - alpha / 2.0)
    z_b = z_inverse(power)
    se_a = math.sqrt(2.0 * p_bar * (1.0 - p_bar))
    se_b = math.sqrt(p1 * (1.0 - p1) + p2 * (1.0 - p2))
    n = ((z_a * se_a + z_b * se_b) / abs(p2 - p1)) ** 2
    return math.ceil(n)


def srm_check(control_n, variant_n, expected_ratio=0.5):
    """Chi-square SRM check on the traffic split; flags p < 0.05."""
    total = control_n + variant_n
    exp_c = total * expected_ratio
    exp_v = total * (1.0 - expected_ratio)
    chi2 = (control_n - exp_c) ** 2 / exp_c + (variant_n - exp_v) ** 2 / exp_v
    p_value = 1.0 - math.erf(math.sqrt(chi2 / 2.0))  # chi-square(1) survival
    return chi2, p_value, p_value < 0.05


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("n per group:", sample_size_two_proportion(0.10, 0.12))  # 3841
    print("SRM 5120/4880:", srm_check(5120, 4880))  # not flagged
    print("SRM 5600/4400:", srm_check(5600, 4400))  # flagged

scriptLabs.title: DAX Measures That Matter
scriptLabs.brief: Write the DAX measures every analyst reaches for: YTD sales with a date table, CALCULATE-driven dynamic filtering, and examples that expose the classic filter-context pitfalls.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Model: Sales[Amount], Sales[OrderDate], 'Date'[Date] (marked date table)

-- 1. Base measure - YOUR CODE HERE
-- Total Sales =

-- 2. Year-to-date sales - YOUR CODE HERE
-- Sales YTD =

-- 3. Same-period-last-year sales - YOUR CODE HERE
-- Sales SPLY =

-- 4. Dynamic filter: sales on orders over $1,000, slicers still apply - YOUR CODE HERE
-- High-Value Sales =

-- 5. Pitfall demo: explain in a comment why each of these is wrong:
--    Bad A = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Amount] * 1.1) used as a "10% uplift" measure
--    Bad B = CALCULATE([Total Sales], 'Date'[Year] = 2026) on a visual sliced by month
scriptLabs.required: Five working measures: Total Sales, Sales YTD (uses TOTALYTD against the marked date table), Sales SPLY (SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR), High-Value Sales (CALCULATE with a > 1000 filter that preserves slicer context), and comments correctly diagnosing both pitfall examples.
scriptLabs.hint: TOTALYTD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR need the date table's date column, not the fact's date column. A filter argument in CALCULATE overrides filters on that same column but leaves slicers on other columns intact. Bad B fails because the visual's month context conflicts with a hard year filter.
scriptLabs.solution:
-- 1. Base measure
Total Sales = SUM ( Sales[Amount] )

-- 2. Year-to-date sales (marked date table 'Date' required)
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD ( [Total Sales], 'Date'[Date] )

-- 3. Same period last year
Sales SPLY = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )

-- YoY growth %, safe against divide-by-zero
Sales YoY % =
DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - [Sales SPLY], [Sales SPLY] )

-- 4. Dynamic filtering: orders over $1,000; slicers on other columns still apply
High-Value Sales =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    Sales[Amount] > 1000
)

-- Filter-context override done right: ignore the product slicer, keep the rest
Sales All Products =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( Sales[Product] ) )

-- 5. Pitfall diagnoses
-- Bad A: SUMX(Sales, Sales[Amount] * 1.1) hard-codes the 1.1 multiplier inside row
-- context. It "works" numerically but it is not a real uplift measure: it cannot
-- respond to slicers, it double-counts any future logic change, and it hides the
-- business rule. Correct: define Uplift Factor as its own measure or parameter
-- and write SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Amount] * [Uplift Factor] ).
-- Bad B: CALCULATE([Total Sales], 'Date'[Year] = 2026) on a visual sliced by month
-- creates a filter on 'Date'[Year] that REPLACES the visual's month context only
-- at the year level; the months then show the full-year total repeated per month
-- (or blank, depending on relationships), which looks like flat monthly sales.
-- Correct: keep the visual's natural filter context and use Sales YTD, or scope
-- the override explicitly with DATESYTD / a proper time-intelligence pattern.

scriptLabs.title: dbt-Style Staging to Mart
scriptLabs.brief: Build a dbt-style staging model that cleans and renames raw columns, then a mart model that joins the star schema. Config blocks, tests, and documentation comments included.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql
-- YOUR CODE HERE: config block (materialized view, schema staging)
-- YOUR CODE HERE: select from source raw_orders, rename orderID -> order_id,
--    cast amount to numeric, filter out test orders (is_test = true)

-- models/marts/fct_orders.sql
-- YOUR CODE HERE: config block (materialized table, schema marts)
-- YOUR CODE HERE: join stg_orders to stg_customers (dim) and stg_products (dim),
--    keep surrogate keys, add order_month grain column

-- models/schema.yml
-- YOUR CODE HERE: not_null + unique tests on order_id; accepted_values on status
scriptLabs.required: Three files worth of SQL/YAML: stg_orders cleans, renames, and filters test rows; fct_orders joins two dims with surrogate keys and a month-grain column; schema.yml declares not_null/unique on order_id and accepted_values on status.
scriptLabs.hint: In dbt, {{ source('raw', 'raw_orders') }} and {{ ref('stg_customers') }} are the correct references. Staging does light cleaning only (rename, cast, filter); business logic and joins live in the mart.
scriptLabs.solution:
-- ============ models/staging/stg_orders.sql ============
{{ config(materialized='view', schema='staging') }}

WITH source AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ source('raw', 'raw_orders') }}
),
renamed AS (
    SELECT
        orderID                    AS order_id,
        custID                     AS customer_id,
        productSKU                 AS product_sku,
        CAST(order_total AS NUMERIC(12, 2)) AS amount,
        CAST(order_ts AS TIMESTAMP)         AS ordered_at,
        LOWER(TRIM(order_status))  AS status
    FROM source
    WHERE is_test IS DISTINCT FROM TRUE   -- drop test orders
      AND orderID IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT * FROM renamed;

-- ============ models/marts/fct_orders.sql ============
{{ config(materialized='table', schema='marts') }}

WITH orders AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
),
customers AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_customers') }}
),
products AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_products') }}
)
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    c.customer_sk,                       -- surrogate keys from dims
    p.product_sk,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', o.ordered_at) AS order_month,  -- mart grain helper
    o.amount,
    o.status,
    o.ordered_at
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN products p  ON o.product_sku  = p.product_sku;

-- ============ models/schema.yml ============
version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: "One row per order; joins the customer and product dimensions."
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: "Natural key from the raw orders feed."
        tests:
          - not_null
          - unique
      - name: amount
        tests:
          - not_null
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled', 'unknown']
      - name: customer_sk
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_customers')
              field: customer_sk

scriptLabs.title: Data Quality Test Suite
scriptLabs.brief: Write a single SQL script that runs null, uniqueness, freshness, and referential-integrity checks over orders and customers and emits a pass/fail report table.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Tables: orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount, status)
--          customers(customer_id, email, created_at)
-- SLA: orders must be fresh within 24 hours.

-- YOUR CODE HERE: one CTE per check, each returning
--   (check_name, records_tested, failures)
-- Checks needed:
--   1. null order_id in orders
--   2. duplicate order_id in orders
--   3. null/negative amount in orders
--   4. orders.customer_id with no match in customers (orphans)
--   5. freshness: max(order_date) older than 24 hours
--   6. invalid status values outside the allowed list
-- Then a final SELECT producing check_name, status ('PASS'/'FAIL'),
-- records_tested, failures, and a details message.
scriptLabs.required: A single runnable script producing one row per check with PASS/FAIL, records_tested, failure counts, and a details message. Each of the six checks must detect at least one seeded violation when run against a dirty fixture, and report PASS on clean data.
scriptLabs.hint: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) or SUM(CASE WHEN ...) counts violations in one pass. Duplicates: GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Freshness: compare MAX(order_date) to NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'. Union the per-check CTEs and derive PASS/FAIL from failures = 0.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH
null_keys AS (
    SELECT 'null_order_id' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE order_id IS NULL) AS failures,
           'order_id must never be null' AS details
    FROM orders
),
dup_keys AS (
    SELECT 'duplicate_order_id' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
               SELECT order_id FROM orders
               GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) d) AS failures,
           'order_id must be unique' AS details
),
bad_amount AS (
    SELECT 'null_or_negative_amount' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0) AS failures,
           'amount must be present and non-negative' AS details
    FROM orders
),
orphans AS (
    SELECT 'orphan_customer_id' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL) AS failures,
           'every orders.customer_id must exist in customers' AS details
    FROM orders o
    LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
),
freshness AS (
    SELECT 'stale_orders_feed' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           CASE WHEN MAX(order_date) < NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS failures,
           'max(order_date) = ' || MAX(order_date)::TEXT ||
           '; SLA is 24 hours' AS details
    FROM orders
),
bad_status AS (
    SELECT 'invalid_status' AS check_name,
           COUNT(*) AS records_tested,
           COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status NOT IN
               ('pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled', 'unknown')) AS failures,
           'status must be in the allowed list' AS details
    FROM orders
),
all_checks AS (
    SELECT * FROM null_keys
    UNION ALL SELECT * FROM dup_keys
    UNION ALL SELECT * FROM bad_amount
    UNION ALL SELECT * FROM orphans
    UNION ALL SELECT * FROM freshness
    UNION ALL SELECT * FROM bad_status
)
SELECT check_name,
       CASE WHEN failures = 0 THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END AS status,
       records_tested,
       failures,
       details
FROM all_checks
ORDER BY status DESC, check_name;

drills.title: Pick the Window Function
drills.prompt: You need the top 3 orders by amount within each customer, keeping ties. Which window function belongs in the outer WHERE clause?
choices: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)
LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
drills.explain: DENSE_RANK keeps ties without gaps, so tied 3rd-place orders are all kept. ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily drop one tied row, SUM is an aggregate, and LAG looks at previous rows instead of ranking.

drills.title: p-Value Interpretation
drills.prompt: An A/B test returns p = 0.04 at alpha = 0.05. What does the p-value mean?
choices: There is a 4% chance the variant is better than control.
If there were truly no difference, you would see a result this extreme about 4% of the time.
There is a 96% chance the result replicates in a rerun.
The variant lifts conversion by 4 percentage points.
drills.explain: The p-value is P(data this extreme | null true), not P(null true | data). It says nothing about replication probability or effect size; it only measures incompatibility with the null.

drills.title: Star vs Snowflake
drills.prompt: Which statement best describes a star schema?
choices: Fact table joined directly to denormalized dimension tables; fewer joins, faster analytic queries.
Every dimension fully normalized into sub-dimensions; best for write-heavy OLTP.
A schema with no fact table, only dimension tables linked in a ring.
A schema where slowly changing dimensions are forbidden.
drills.explain: Star schemas denormalize dimensions around one fact table, minimizing joins for BI queries. Snowflake normalizes dimensions further; SCDs are handled in either via dimension versioning.

drills.title: DAX Filter Context
drills.prompt: A measure is CALCULATE([Total Sales], Region[Name] = "West"). A slicer selects Region = East. What does the measure return?
choices: East sales, because slicers always win.
Total sales, because CALCULATE removes all filters.
West sales, because the CALCULATE filter overrides the slicer on the same column.
drills.explain: A filter argument in CALCULATE overrides existing filters on the same column (it does not intersect them). Slicers on other columns still apply; ALL() would be needed to remove everything.

drills.title: CTE vs Subquery
drills.prompt: Why prefer a CTE over a nested subquery for a multi-step transformation?
choices: CTEs always run faster because they are materialized.
CTEs can be referenced multiple times by name and make the query readable; subqueries cannot be reused.
drills.explain: CTEs are named, reusable, and read top-to-bottom, which beats deep nesting for maintainability. They are not automatically faster or materialized, and subqueries support window functions fine.

drills.title: Confidence Interval Meaning
drills.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for mean order value is [$42, $48]. The correct interpretation is:
choices: There is a 95% probability the true mean is in [$42, $48].
If you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built that way would contain the true mean.
The sample mean is $45 with 95% certainty.
drills.explain: Frequentist CIs are about the procedure's long-run capture rate, not the probability that this specific interval contains the parameter, and not a statement about individual orders.

drills.title: ETL vs ELT
drills.prompt: Your warehouse is cloud-based with cheap scalable compute. Raw clickstream data lands first, then you model it. This is:
choices: ETL, because modeling always happens before loading.
Reverse ETL, because the data moves backward.
ELT, because you load raw data first and transform inside the warehouse.
drills.explain: ELT loads raw data into the warehouse and transforms it there, exploiting cheap elastic compute. ETL transforms before loading, typical of legacy on-prem pipelines with limited target compute.

drills.title: Join Types
drills.prompt: You need all customers plus their orders, including customers who never ordered. Which join?
choices: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders.
INNER JOIN from customers to orders.
RIGHT JOIN from customers to orders.
CROSS JOIN from customers to orders.
drills.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (customers) with NULLs where no order matches. INNER would drop order-less customers, CROSS would produce a cartesian product.

drills.title: The Peeking Problem
drills.prompt: A stakeholder checks the A/B test dashboard daily and wants to stop early when p < 0.05. Why is this dangerous?
choices: It is not dangerous; more looks means more accuracy.
It only matters if the sample is under 1,000.
Repeated testing inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal alpha.
Early stopping is fine as long as you use a t-test.
drills.explain: Every peek is another chance to get lucky under the null, so the real Type I error rate compounds well above 5%. Fix it with a fixed horizon, alpha spending, or sequential methods designed for peeking.

drills.title: SCD Type 2
drills.prompt: A customer moves from Boston to Austin and you must preserve both addresses for historical reporting. Which slowly changing dimension technique?
choices: Type 0: keep the original value forever.
Type 2: add a new dimension row with effective dates; keep the old row.
Type 1: overwrite the old value in place.
Type 3: store only the current value plus one previous column.
drills.explain: Type 2 versions the dimension row (new surrogate key, effective/expiry dates), so facts before the move join to Boston and facts after join to Austin. Type 1 would destroy history.

drills.title: Percent Change on Weekly Sales
drills.prompt: A store's weekly sales were $8,400 and rose to $10,500. What is the percent change?
drills.explain: Step 1: change = new - old = 10,500 - 8,400 = 2,100. Step 2: divide by the OLD value: 2,100 / 8,400 = 0.25. Step 3: as a percent = 25% increase. (Module 26)

drills.title: Slope as Resolution Rate
drills.prompt: A support team resolved 240 tickets by day 2 and 840 tickets by day 6 (cumulative). What is the average resolution rate in tickets per day?
drills.explain: Slope = rise/run = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) = (840 - 240)/(6 - 2) = 600/4 = 150 tickets per day. The slope of the cumulative curve is the daily rate. (Module 27)

drills.title: Annual Growth Factor from a Log Chart
drills.prompt: A chart's y-axis is log10. Revenue is $10,000 at year 1 and $1,000,000 at year 3. Assuming constant annual growth, by what factor did revenue grow each year?
drills.explain: Step 1: total growth factor = 1,000,000 / 10,000 = 100 over 2 years. Step 2: annual factor = sqrt(100) = 10. Check on the log axis: log10(10,000) = 4, log10(1,000,000) = 6, a gap of 2 log-units over 2 years = 1 log-unit/year = 10x per year. (Module 28)

drills.title: Expand and Evaluate a Sigma Sum
drills.prompt: Evaluate: sum_{i=1}^{4} (3i - 1).

drills.title: Venn Inclusion-Exclusion
drills.prompt: Of 100 customers, 60 bought Product A, 50 bought Product B, and 30 bought both. How many bought at least one?
drills.explain: Inclusion-exclusion: |A UNION B| = |A| + |B| - |A INTERSECT B| = 60 + 50 - 30 = 80. The 30 who bought both were counted twice, so subtract the overlap once. (Module 30)

drills.title: Sample Variance by Hand
drills.prompt: Compute the SAMPLE variance of 4, 8, 6 (divide by n-1).
drills.explain: Step 1: mean = (4 + 8 + 6)/3 = 18/3 = 6. Step 2: deviations = -2, 2, 0. Step 3: squared = 4, 4, 0. Step 4: sum = 8. Step 5: sample variance = 8/(3-1) = 8/2 = 4. (Module 31)

drills.title: Bayes on a Spam Filter
drills.prompt: 2% of emails are spam. The filter catches 95% of spam but wrongly flags 3% of legit mail. If an email is flagged, what is the probability it is actually spam?
drills.explain: Step 1: P(flagged) = P(flagged|spam)*P(spam) + P(flagged|legit)*P(legit) = 0.95*0.02 + 0.03*0.98 = 0.019 + 0.0294 = 0.0484. Step 2: Bayes: P(spam|flagged) = 0.019/0.0484 ~ 0.393 = about 39%. The rare base rate keeps it far below the 95% catch rate. (Module 32)

drills.title: Dot Product as Similarity
drills.prompt: Compute [2, 3] . [4, -1] and state what the sign of the result means.
drills.explain: Dot product = 2*4 + 3*(-1) = 8 - 3 = 5. A positive dot product means the angle between the vectors is under 90 degrees: they point roughly the same direction, i.e. similar. (Module 33)

drills.title: Minimize a Cost Curve
drills.prompt: The cost curve is C(x) = 2x^2 - 40x + 300, where x is batch size in hundreds of units. Find the batch size that minimizes cost.
drills.explain: Step 1: derivative C'(x) = 4x - 40. Step 2: set to zero: 4x - 40 = 0, so x = 10. Step 3: the x^2 coefficient (2) is positive, so the parabola opens upward and x = 10 is a minimum: 1,000 units. (Module 34)

drills.title: Combinatorics: Counting Outcomes
drills.prompt: A dashboard filter lets users pick any 3 of 10 metrics to display. How many distinct 3-metric combinations are possible?
drills.explain: Combinations: C(10,3) = 10!/(3!7!) = 120. Order does not matter for a displayed set, so permutations (720) overcount. (Module 32)

drills.title: Conditional Probability: Base Rates
drills.prompt: A fraud model flags 1% of transactions. It catches 90% of real fraud, but 5% of legitimate transactions are flagged. If fraud is truly 0.1% of volume, what is P(fraud | flagged)?
drills.explain: Bayes: P(F|+) = 0.9*0.001 / (0.9*0.001 + 0.05*0.999) = 0.0009/0.05085 ≈ 1.8%. Base rates dominate — the classic analyst trap. (Module 32)

drills.title: Simpson's Paradox
drills.prompt: Campaign A beats Campaign B in every region, yet B wins overall. What happened?
choices: A lurking variable (e.g., region size/mix) reverses the aggregate trend — Simpson's paradox
drills.explain: Simpson's paradox: subgroup trends reverse in aggregate when group sizes differ. Always segment before trusting a top-line number. (Module 10)

drills.title: Fermi Estimation
drills.prompt: Estimate daily SQL queries run by analysts at a 5,000-person bank. Which approach is sound?
choices: Decompose: analysts × queries/day each, sanity-check each factor, multiply ranges
drills.explain: Fermi method: break into estimable factors (e.g., 800 analysts × 20 queries = 16,000/day), sanity-check each, report a range. Interviewers grade the decomposition, not the number. (Module 36)

scenarios.title: Just Give Me a Dashboard
scenarios.context: A VP stops you in the hallway: 'Just give me a dashboard on sales.' No metrics named, no decisions named, no deadline. You have one 30-minute discovery meeting tomorrow. This scenario tests requirements discovery.

steps.prompt: First question to ask in the discovery meeting?

options.text: What decision will this dashboard change, and who makes it?
options.why: Anchors the work to a decision and a decision-maker; everything else (metrics, grain, refresh) follows from that.

options.text: Which chart types do you prefer - bar, line, or pie?
options.why: Visual preferences come after the decision and metrics are defined; leading with charts builds a pretty, useless dashboard.

options.text: Should I use Tableau or Power BI for this?
options.why: Tool choice is an implementation detail. Requirements first, tooling second.

steps.prompt: She says 'I want to see how sales are doing.' Your next move?

options.text: Start building with total revenue; you can iterate later.
options.why: 'Sales' could mean revenue, units, orders, or margin. Building on a guess guarantees rework.

options.text: Ask her to define 'doing well' with 2-3 concrete metrics and a comparison baseline.
options.why: Metrics need definitions and baselines (vs target, vs last year) to be interpretable. Pin these down in writing.

options.text: Pull every sales-related column into one wide dashboard.
options.why: A data dump is not a dashboard. More columns increase the chance she misreads it and decrease the chance she uses it.

options.text: Schedule three more meetings to keep discussing.
options.why: Discovery should converge, not sprawl. One focused session with written follow-up beats meeting churn.

steps.prompt: Before you build, what do you confirm in writing?

options.text: Audience, decisions, metric definitions, grain, refresh cadence, and what is explicitly out of scope.
options.why: A one-page brief signed off by the stakeholder is the contract. It prevents scope creep and gives you something to point to when 'just one more chart' arrives.

options.text: Just the deadline; the rest can stay verbal for speed.
options.why: Verbal scope evaporates. The first disagreement about what was promised will cost more than the brief ever did.

options.text: The color palette and logo placement.
options.why: Cosmetics last. Confirm semantics first.

scenarios.title: Peeking and SRM Mid-Experiment
scenarios.context: Day 4 of a 14-day checkout A/B test. The PM Slacks you: 'Variant is up 8%, p = 0.03 - can we ship it?' Your SRM check just flagged a traffic-split anomaly. Decide what happens next.

steps.prompt: The PM wants to ship on p = 0.03 at day 4 of a 14-day test. You respond:

options.text: Ship it - p < 0.05 is significant.
options.why: Peeking at day 4 of a 14-day test inflates the false-positive rate. A single early p-value is not a decision rule.

options.text: Hold. The test was designed for a 14-day fixed horizon; we decide at day 14, not on an early peek.
options.why: The fixed-horizon design controls the error rate only if you honor the horizon. Early stopping needs a sequential method specified up front.

options.text: Extend the test another 14 days to be safe.
options.why: Extending after peeking is just another form of optional stopping and compounds the same error-rate inflation.

steps.prompt: Your SRM check flagged the traffic split (58/42 instead of 50/50). What does this mean and what do you do?

options.text: It means randomization is broken or assignment is leaking; pause the test and debug the bucketing logic before trusting any result.
options.why: SRM means the groups are not comparable - bots, caching, or sticky bucketing bugs. No p-value from a broken randomization is valid.

options.text: Ignore it; 58/42 is close enough to 50/50.
options.why: The chi-square test already accounts for sampling noise. A flagged SRM is a real anomaly, not bad luck.

options.text: Re-weight the results to 50/50 and keep going.
options.why: Re-weighting cannot fix unknown assignment bias - you do not know WHY the split skewed, so you cannot correct for it.

options.text: Restart the test immediately without investigating.
options.why: Restarting without a root cause just re-runs the same bug. Debug first, then restart clean.

steps.prompt: Root cause found: a CDN cached the variant page for logged-out users. Test restarted clean. What process change do you propose?

options.text: Add an automated SRM check to the experiment monitoring that pages the team on day 1 of every test.
options.why: SRM on day 1 catches bucketing bugs before they burn two weeks of traffic. Make it a gate, not a day-4 surprise.

options.text: Ban the PM from looking at the dashboard.
options.why: Punishing curiosity does not fix the process. Give stakeholders a dashboard that hides p-values until the horizon, and educate on peeking.

options.text: Run all future tests for 30 days regardless of power analysis.
options.why: Longer is not automatically better; it delays decisions and still does not fix peeking or SRM. Size tests by power, guard them with monitoring.

scenarios.title: 6 AM Pipeline Failure Triage
scenarios.context: Your phone buzzes at 6 AM: the daily orders pipeline failed. The 8 AM executive sales report depends on it. Triage like a senior analyst.

steps.prompt: First 10 minutes: what do you check, in order?

options.text: Rerun the whole pipeline immediately to save time.
options.why: Blind reruns can duplicate data or mask the root cause. Diagnose before you act.

options.text: Check the run logs for the failing step, then check source freshness and row counts at each stage to isolate where it broke.
options.why: Logs name the failing step; stage-level row counts tell you whether it is a source delay, a transform error, or a load failure. Ten minutes of reading beats an hour of guessing.

options.text: Email the executives that the report will be late.
options.why: Communicate after you know the blast radius and ETA. A 'it failed, unknown ETA' email at 6 AM creates panic, not clarity.

options.text: Roll back yesterday's dbt model changes.
options.why: Maybe the cause, maybe not. Evidence first; rollbacks are a treatment, not a diagnosis.

steps.prompt: Logs show: the staging model failed on a new 'amount' value 'N/A' from the source feed. The mart is untouched. Your fix?

options.text: Patch the staging model to coerce 'N/A' to NULL with a logged warning, backfill the failed run, and add a schema/contract test on the source feed.
options.why: Fix the immediate failure defensively, backfill so the 8 AM report is whole, and add a contract test so the next bad value pages you before it breaks the run.

options.text: Ask the source team to fix their feed and wait.
options.why: Correct long-term, but the 8 AM report cannot wait. Defensive handling plus a follow-up ticket covers both horizons.

options.text: Delete the 'N/A' rows from the raw table and rerun.
options.why: Mutating raw data destroys the audit trail and hides the upstream bug. Handle it in staging; never edit raw.

steps.prompt: The 8 AM report is at risk. How do you communicate?

options.text: Say nothing unless someone asks.
options.why: Silence until the meeting is how trust dies. Stakeholders would rather hear '20 minutes late, data will be complete' than discover a gap themselves.

options.text: Send a brief status: what broke, ETA, and that the data will be complete (not partial) when it lands.
options.why: Three facts stakeholders need: cause in plain language, when to expect it, and whether the numbers will be trustworthy. Promise completeness or clearly label it partial.

options.text: Publish the report on time with yesterday's data and fix it quietly later.
options.why: Shipping stale data as if it were fresh is a lie that compounds. Label it or delay it - never silently substitute.

options.text: Blame the source team in the status update.
options.why: Blame assigns no ETA and burns a relationship you need for the contract test. Own the pipeline, fix the feed together.

steps.prompt: Postmortem: which lasting change matters most?

options.text: A data contract + freshness/quality tests on the source feed, with alerts before the mart run.
options.why: Shift-left validation: catch bad values at ingestion with an alert, not at 6 AM in a failed staging model. This is the structural fix.

options.text: A stricter on-call rotation.
options.why: Faster human response to the same failure is not a fix; it is a treadmill. Prevent the class of failure instead.

options.text: More detailed logging.
options.why: Logging helped diagnose this once, but it does not prevent the next bad value. Tests and contracts do.

scenarios.title: The Exec Misreads the Chart
scenarios.context: In a quarterly review, the COO points at your dashboard and says: 'Churn doubled last quarter - we need to act now.' You know the spike is a denominator artifact from a one-time plan migration, not real churn. Recover the meeting.

steps.prompt: The COO declares 'churn doubled' in front of the room. Your first sentence?

options.text: 'You are reading it wrong.'
options.why: Correcting an executive's competence in public ends the conversation and your credibility with it.

options.text: 'That spike caught my eye too - can I show you what is driving it? The denominator changed during the plan migration.'
options.why: Validate the observation, then redirect to the cause. You agree the spike is real and worth explaining, which keeps the room with you.

options.text: Stay silent; the chart speaks for itself.
options.why: Silence lets a false narrative become the meeting's conclusion and possibly a misguided initiative.

steps.prompt: How do you prove it is a denominator artifact, live?

options.text: Show churned customers (numerator) and total customers (denominator) as separate series, then the rate with the migration cohort excluded.
options.why: Decomposing the rate into its parts makes the artifact visible: numerator flat, denominator dipped during migration. The adjusted series shows true churn unchanged.

options.text: Switch to a 3D chart for dramatic effect.
options.why: Chartjunk does not persuade; decomposed evidence does.

options.text: Quote the SQL query from memory.
options.why: Implementation details do not persuade executives. Show the business logic, not the code.

options.text: Promise a deeper analysis next week.
options.why: Delay cedes the narrative. You have the decomposition - show it now, follow up with the write-up later.

steps.prompt: The room accepts the explanation. What do you change so this never happens again?

options.text: Annotate the dashboard at the migration date and add a footnote defining the churn formula and its denominator.
options.why: Annotations put the context where the misreading happens. A visible formula definition stops the next executive from repeating the mistake.

options.text: Remove the churn chart entirely.
options.why: Hiding a metric people care about just moves the misreading to a spreadsheet someone builds themselves.

options.text: Restrict dashboard access to the analytics team.
options.why: Gatekeeping destroys trust and adoption. Fix the communication, not the audience.

trainers.title: Window vs Aggregate Function Recall
trainers.brief: Rapid-fire recall: given a function name, classify it as window-only, aggregate, or both, and recite its signature. Builds the instant recognition the exam's SQL section rewards.

trainers.title: Statistics Formula Sprint
trainers.brief: Timed numeric recall: z-score, standard error of the mean, confidence interval bounds, and two-proportion sample-size inputs. Type the value; speed and accuracy both count.

terminalSims.title: Python: pandas Exploration
terminalSims.brief: A simulated Python REPL: load a CSV, inspect it, aggregate with groupby, and summarize distributions with describe.

mockTasks.q: Module 1 - Role & workflow: A stakeholder asks for 'a quick number' for the board deck. What is the senior analyst's first move?
choices: Query the warehouse immediately; speed matters most for board requests.
Decline; board requests must go through the data engineering team.
Ask which decision the number supports, confirm the metric definition and time window, then deliver with caveats in writing.
Send last quarter's number since definitions rarely change.
mockTasks.explain: Senior analysts anchor every request to a decision and a written metric definition. 'Quick numbers' without definitions become wrong numbers quoted in board meetings.

mockTasks.q: Module 2 - SQL fundamentals: Which query correctly returns customers who placed more than 5 orders in 2026?
choices: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 AND order_date >= '2026-01-01';
SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY customer_id;
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2027-01-01' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
mockTasks.explain: Row filters go in WHERE, group filters in HAVING. The half-open date range is SARGable and the HAVING clause applies after grouping.

mockTasks.q: Module 3 - Joins: orders has 10,000 rows; customers has 2,000 rows. Every order has a valid customer_id. How many rows does SELECT * FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id return?
choices: It depends on duplicate customer_id values in customers.
mockTasks.explain: INNER JOIN keeps one output row per match. With every order matching exactly one customer row, the result has exactly 10,000 rows.

mockTasks.q: Module 4 - Window functions: What is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK() when two rows tie for first?
choices: RANK gives both rows 1 and the next row 2; DENSE_RANK gives both rows 1 and the next row 3.
They are identical in all cases.
RANK gives both rows 1 and the next row 3; DENSE_RANK gives both rows 1 and the next row 2.
DENSE_RANK cannot handle ties and returns NULL.
mockTasks.explain: RANK leaves gaps after ties (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2). Choose based on whether the ranking positions must be gap-free.

mockTasks.q: Module 5 - CTEs: A recursive CTE on employees runs forever. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The anchor member selects too many rows.
A cycle in the data (an employee who is their own manager, directly or indirectly) with no cycle guard.
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL.
Naming the CTE with more than 10 characters.
mockTasks.explain: Cycles make the recursive member generate rows forever. UNION (distinct) can mask small cycles but not fix them; add a depth cap or a visited-path check.

mockTasks.q: Module 6 - Query tuning: A query filters on LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' and seq-scans a 50M-row table with an index on email. Best fix?
choices: Rewrite as email = 'a@b.com' OR email = 'A@B.COM' so the index can be used, or add a functional index on LOWER(email).
Add more RAM to the warehouse.
Change the filter to email LIKE '%a@b.com%'.
Partition the table by email domain.
mockTasks.explain: The function on the column defeats the index. Either remove the function (if data is already lowercase) or create an index on the expression LOWER(email).

mockTasks.q: Module 7 - Data cleaning: A revenue column has values [12, 15, 14, 13, 999999]. The 999999 is a data-entry error but you cannot verify the true value. Best treatment for a monthly report?
choices: Drop the row; one row never matters.
Keep it; the data is the data.
Replace it with the column mean of the remaining values.
Winsorize or cap it at a defensible bound (e.g., 99th percentile) and document the treatment in the cleaning log.
mockTasks.explain: Capping preserves the row while neutralizing the distortion, and the cleaning log keeps it auditable. Dropping or mean-imputation hides the problem silently.

mockTasks.q: Module 8 - Python for analysis: Which snippet correctly computes conversion rate by channel from a DataFrame with columns channel and converted (0/1)?
mockTasks.explain: Grouping by channel and taking the mean of a 0/1 column gives the conversion rate per channel directly.

mockTasks.q: Module 9 - pandas: df.merge(other, on='id', how='left') returns MORE rows than df has. What happened?
choices: The 'id' column has duplicates in other, so matching rows fan out.
The merge sorted the data and counted wrong.
mockTasks.explain: A left merge preserves every left row but fans out when the right side has duplicate keys. Validate with other['id'].duplicated().any() and dedupe or aggregate first.

mockTasks.q: Module 10 - Statistics fundamentals: Mean = $100, median = $60 for order values. What does this tell you?
choices: The distribution is right-skewed; a few large orders pull the mean up. Report the median for 'typical' order value.
The mean is wrong and should be recomputed.
The distribution is left-skewed; report the mean.
mockTasks.explain: Mean > median signals right skew. The median better represents the typical order; the mean better represents total revenue per order.

mockTasks.q: Module 11 - Probability: Daily conversions are independent with p = 0.05 per visitor. With 100 visitors, what is the expected number of conversions?
mockTasks.explain: Expected value of a binomial is n*p = 100 * 0.05 = 5.

mockTasks.q: Module 12 - Hypothesis testing: You run 20 independent A/B tests at alpha = 0.05 with no real effects. Approximately how many false positives do you expect?
choices: 0 - alpha controls this to zero across the family.
mockTasks.explain: Expected false positives = 20 * 0.05 = 1. This is the multiple-comparisons problem; without correction (Bonferroni, FDR), one 'significant' result is expected by chance.

mockTasks.q: Module 13 - A/B testing: Which design choice MOST reduces the risk of novelty effects contaminating results?
choices: Running the test only on weekends.
Running the test for at least one full business cycle and checking for time-decaying effects.
Peeking daily to catch novelty early.
mockTasks.explain: Novelty effects decay over time, so a full-cycle run plus a time-based segment analysis reveals them. Split ratio and peeking do not address novelty.

mockTasks.q: Module 14 - Regression: In a simple linear regression of sales on ad spend, R-squared = 0.82. Correct interpretation?
choices: 82% of the variation in sales is explained by ad spend in this model; it does not prove ad spend causes sales.
The correlation between ad spend and sales is 0.82.
82% of predictions will be exactly correct.
mockTasks.explain: R-squared is explained variance, not causation and not prediction accuracy. Correlation would be sqrt(0.82) ~ 0.91 for simple regression.

mockTasks.q: Module 15 - Visualization: A line chart of monthly revenue uses a y-axis starting at $900k instead of $0, making a 2% change look dramatic. This is:
choices: Best practice; it highlights the change.
Acceptable for line charts but never bar charts.
A truncated-axis distortion; start at zero or clearly annotate the axis break.
Required by most BI tools for revenue charts.
mockTasks.explain: Truncated axes exaggerate small changes. Either start at zero or make the break unmissable with annotation.

mockTasks.q: Module 16 - Tableau: A calculated field IF [Profit] > 0 THEN 'Profitable' ELSE 'Loss' END returns an error on some rows. Most likely cause?
choices: Tableau cannot compare measures to zero.
The field name needs double quotes.
Some rows have NULL profit; comparisons with NULL yield NULL, so add IFNULL([Profit], 0).
mockTasks.explain: NULL comparisons propagate NULL instead of TRUE/FALSE, breaking the IF. Wrapping with IFNULL (or ZN) makes the logic total.

mockTasks.q: Module 17 - Power BI & DAX: Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], 'Date'[Date]) shows the same value for every month. The model has no marked date table and 'Date' is a regular table. Fix?
choices: Mark 'Date' as the date table (or use a proper continuous date column); TOTALYTD needs valid date-table metadata to compute period filters.
Convert the measure to a calculated column.
mockTasks.explain: Time-intelligence functions require a marked date table with a contiguous date column. Without it, the period logic cannot resolve and every month shows the same total.

mockTasks.q: Module 18 - Data modeling: A product dimension stores category attributes inline (product_name, category_name, category_manager). Normalizing category into its own table converts the design from:
mockTasks.explain: Star schemas keep dimensions denormalized; splitting a dimension into sub-dimensions is the defining move toward a snowflake.

mockTasks.q: Module 19 - dbt & ELT: Where should a filter removing test orders (is_test = true) live?
choices: In the BI tool, so analysts can toggle it.
Nowhere; test orders are useful for volume metrics.
In the staging model, so every downstream mart and dashboard inherits clean data.
In the raw ingestion script, by deleting the rows.
mockTasks.explain: Staging is the single choke point: filter once there and all marts agree. BI-level filters diverge across dashboards; deleting raw rows destroys the audit trail.

mockTasks.q: Module 20 - Data quality: The orders mart usually loads 8,000-10,000 rows daily; today it loaded 14. Best classification and response?
choices: A uniqueness failure; add a unique test on order_id.
A completeness/freshness anomaly; quarantine the partial load, alert stakeholders, and investigate the source before the 8 AM report.
A referential integrity failure; rebuild the customer dimension.
mockTasks.explain: A 99%+ volume drop is a completeness failure, not normal variance. Quarantine prevents a wrong report; alerting with an ETA preserves trust.

mockTasks.q: Module 21 - Metrics & KPIs: Marketing celebrates a 40% lift in signups while revenue is flat. As senior analyst you diagnose:
choices: A vanity-metric trap: signups rose but activation or conversion did not, so define the KPI at the decision point (activated, paying users), not the top of the funnel.
Revenue attribution is always wrong; ignore it.
Marketing should be excluded from metrics reviews.
mockTasks.explain: Top-of-funnel metrics that do not connect to the business outcome are vanity metrics. Good KPIs sit at the decision point and move with the outcome you care about.

mockTasks.q: Module 22 - Storytelling: Your analysis shows the new pricing test LOST money, but the PM championed it. How do you present?
choices: Lead with the bottom line ('the test lost $180k net'), show the evidence trail, then recommend next steps. Deliver bad news early and plainly.
Bury the loss in the appendix and lead with engagement wins.
Present only the methodology; let them draw conclusions.
Delay the readout until you can re-run the test.
mockTasks.explain: BLUF (bottom line up front) with evidence respects the audience's time and your own credibility. Softening bad news just delays the same conversation.

mockTasks.q: Module 23 - Excel: A VLOOKUP returns #N/A for values you can see in the lookup table. Most likely cause?
choices: VLOOKUP cannot handle more than 100 rows.
Type mismatch (text vs numbers) or trailing spaces; also check the range_lookup argument is FALSE for exact match.
The lookup table must be sorted descending.
mockTasks.explain: Text '123' never equals numeric 123, and trailing spaces break matches invisibly. Use exact match (FALSE) and normalize types with VALUE() or TRIM().

mockTasks.q: Module 24 - Portfolio & exam strategy: For the certification exam's scenario questions, the highest-yield tactic is:
choices: Answer from the senior-analyst mindset: decision first, definitions in writing, validate before acting - the distractors usually reward rushing.
Always pick the longest answer choice.
Skip all scenario questions and return later.
mockTasks.explain: Scenario distractors are written to catch the 'just query it' impulse. The senior mindset (decision, definition, validation) eliminates most of them on the first read.

mockTasks.q: Module 4 (extra) - Window functions: Which query computes each order's share of its customer's total spend?
choices: SELECT order_id, amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS share FROM orders;
SELECT order_id, amount / SUM(amount) OVER () AS share FROM orders;
SELECT order_id, amount / TOTAL(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
mockTasks.explain: The window must partition by customer_id so the denominator is that customer's total. The unpartitioned version divides by the grand total instead.

mockTasks.q: Module 13 (extra) - A/B testing: Minimum detectable effect (MDE) is best described as:
choices: The smallest effect size your test is powered to detect; smaller MDEs need larger samples.
The largest lift you have ever observed.
The p-value threshold divided by sample size.
A fixed 5% relative lift for all tests.
mockTasks.explain: MDE links business relevance to statistics: pick the smallest lift worth acting on, then size the sample to detect it with the chosen power.

mockTasks.q: Module 17 (extra) - DAX: What does CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Region)) do on a visual sliced by Region?
choices: Returns an error; ALL cannot be used in CALCULATE.
Removes the Region filter, so every row shows total sales across all regions.
Keeps only the selected region's sales, doubling them.
mockTasks.explain: ALL(Region) strips filters on the Region table/column inside the CALCULATE evaluation, producing the grand total on every visual row - the classic percent-of-total denominator.

mockTasks.q: Module 18 (extra) - Data modeling: A fact table at order-line grain is joined to a monthly budget table. The correct approach is:
choices: Join directly; the warehouse will figure out the grain.
Aggregate the fact to month first, then join - joining mixed grains fans out or misallocates the budget.
Put the budget in the fact table as a column.
Use a CROSS JOIN and filter later.
mockTasks.explain: Mixed-grain joins are a classic fan-out trap: each budget row would repeat per order line. Conform the grains before joining.

mockTasks.q: Module 7 (extra) - Data cleaning: Two systems record the same customers with different IDs and slightly different names ('Acme Inc' vs 'Acme Inc.'). Resolving them is called:
choices: Entity resolution (record linkage); use normalized keys plus fuzzy matching, with a human review queue for low-confidence pairs.
mockTasks.explain: Entity resolution matches real-world entities across systems. Normalize (lowercase, strip punctuation), fuzzy-match, and keep humans in the loop below a confidence threshold.

mockTasks.q: Module 12 (extra) - Hypothesis testing: A 99% confidence interval is wider than a 95% interval from the same data because:
choices: The standard error increases with confidence level.
Higher confidence requires a larger critical value to capture the parameter more often.
mockTasks.explain: Same data, same standard error; only the critical value grows (2.58 vs 1.96). More confidence means a wider net - there is no free lunch.

blocks.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Never put an aggregate in WHERE.
blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'   -- row filter
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;                        -- group filter

blocks.body: OVER() defines the window. PARTITION BY slices it into groups; ORDER BY sets row order inside each slice; frame clauses (ROWS BETWEEN) set which rows the function sees.
blocks.code:
SELECT order_id,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                           ORDER BY order_date
                           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders;

blocks.body: ROW_NUMBER: unique, arbitrary among ties. RANK: ties share a rank, gaps follow. DENSE_RANK: ties share, no gaps. NTILE(n): bucket into n groups.
blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, total,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS drnk
FROM customer_totals;

blocks.body: LAG(col) looks at the previous row in the window - the standard tool for month-over-month and year-over-year deltas.
blocks.code:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS mo, SUM(amount) AS rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT mo, rev,
       LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mo) AS prev_rev,
       (rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mo)) / NULLIF(LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mo), 0) AS growth
FROM m;

blocks.body: Keep indexed columns bare: no functions, no arithmetic, no implicit casts on the column side. Rewrite date-part filters as half-open ranges.
blocks.code:
-- slow:  WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2026
-- fast:
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date <  DATE '2027-01-01';

blocks.body: Anchor member selects the roots; recursive member joins back to the CTE. UNION ALL keeps duplicates for tree walks; always consider a depth cap or cycle guard.
blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, name AS path
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1, o.path || ' > ' || e.name
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT * FROM org;

blocks.body: Z-score standardizes a value: how many standard deviations from the mean. Standard error of the mean shrinks with sqrt(n) - bigger samples, tighter estimates.
blocks.code:
z = (x - mean) / std
se_mean = std / sqrt(n)
# 95% CI for the mean:
ci_low, ci_high = mean - 1.96 * se_mean, mean + 1.96 * se_mean

blocks.body: p = P(data this extreme | null is true). It is NOT P(null is true | data), NOT the chance the result replicates, and NOT the effect size.
blocks.code:
# Decision rule for a fixed-horizon test:
# if p_value < alpha: reject the null (act)
# else: fail to reject (do not claim 'no effect')
# Never peek mid-test without a sequential design.

blocks.body: Size the test from the minimum detectable effect: the smallest lift worth acting on. Smaller MDE or higher power both demand bigger n.
blocks.code:
from math import sqrt, ceil
z_a, z_b = 1.96, 0.84  # alpha=0.05 two-sided, power=0.8
p_bar = (p1 + p2) / 2
n = ((z_a * sqrt(2*p_bar*(1-p_bar)) + z_b * sqrt(p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2))) / abs(p2-p1))**2
n_per_group = ceil(n)

blocks.body: Sample Ratio Mismatch: compare observed traffic split to the expected ratio with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Flag on day 1 of every test - a broken randomization invalidates everything.
blocks.code:
chi2 = (obs_c - exp_c)**2/exp_c + (obs_v - exp_v)**2/exp_v
# df=1; flag if p < 0.05 (use a chi-square table or 1 - erf(sqrt(chi2/2)))
# If flagged: pause, debug bucketing, restart clean. Never re-weight.

blocks.body: Every peek is another roll of the dice under the null, so the real false-positive rate compounds far above alpha. Use a fixed horizon, alpha spending, or sequential methods (e.g., always-valid p-values) if early stopping matters.
blocks.code:
# Anti-peeking checklist:
# 1. Pre-register horizon + primary metric + decision rule
# 2. Hide p-values on dashboards until the horizon
# 3. Day-1 SRM gate on every experiment
# 4. Document peeks; adjust with sequential methods if used

blocks.body: R-squared is explained variance, not causation. Check residuals for patterns (non-linearity), watch for multicollinearity (inflated standard errors), and never extrapolate beyond the data range.
blocks.code:
# Before trusting a regression:
# - plot residuals vs fitted (look for curves/funnels)
# - check VIF < 5 for multicollinearity
# - confirm the relationship is plausibly causal before acting

blocks.body: Every visual cell computes a measure under a filter context (slicers, rows, columns). CALCULATE modifies that context: filter arguments override filters on the same column, leave others alone.
blocks.code:
Total Sales = SUM ( Sales[Amount] )

West Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], Region[Name] = "West" )
-- overrides any Region slicer; keeps all other slicers

blocks.body: Mark a proper date table (contiguous dates) first - TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, and DATESMTD all depend on it. DIVIDE() is the safe division.
blocks.code:
Sales YTD  = TOTALYTD ( [Total Sales], 'Date'[Date] )
Sales SPLY = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
Sales YoY % = DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - [Sales SPLY], [Sales SPLY] )

blocks.body: ALL() removes filters - the standard trick for percent-of-total and for measures that must ignore slicers.
blocks.code:
Pct of Total = DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( Sales ) ) )

Sales Ignore Product Slicer = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( Product ) )

blocks.body: Star: fact table joined to denormalized dimensions - fewer joins, faster BI queries, the default for analytics. Snowflake: dimensions normalized into sub-dimensions - saves storage, costs joins; rarely worth it in modern columnar warehouses.
blocks.code:
-- star:     fct_orders -> dim_customers (wide, denormalized)
-- snowflake: fct_orders -> dim_products -> dim_categories -> dim_departments
-- rule of thumb: start star; snowflake only with a real storage/correctness reason

blocks.body: Type 1: overwrite (history lost). Type 2: new versioned row with effective dates (history preserved - the analytics default). Type 3: keep current + one previous column only.
blocks.code:
-- dim_customers_scd2:
-- customer_sk (PK), customer_id (natural key),
-- city, eff_start_date, eff_end_date, is_current
-- facts join on customer_sk -> history preserved per transaction

blocks.body: One fact table, one grain, stated in the table description. Mixed-grain joins fan out. Aggregate the finer grain up before joining to a coarser one.
blocks.code:
-- fct_order_lines: one row per order line (finest grain)
-- fct_orders:      one row per order
-- joining monthly budgets: aggregate facts to month FIRST, then join

blocks.body: Read the last sentence first (what is actually being asked), then eliminate distractors that reward rushing: blind querying, deleting raw data, silent substitution, peeking.
blocks.code:
1. Read the question stem's final ask
2. Cross out 'just query it' / 'delete raw' / 'say nothing' options
3. Pick the decision-first, written-definition, validate-before-acting answer
4. Flag and move on if stuck > 90 seconds

blocks.body: Budget roughly one minute per question. First pass: answer everything you know cold. Second pass: flagged items. Never leave blanks - there is no penalty for guessing.
blocks.code:
pass 1: easy wins, mark the rest
pass 2: flagged questions with fresh eyes
pass 3: blind guesses on anything remaining
reserve 10 min at the end for review

blocks.body: Exam SQL almost always tests: WHERE vs HAVING placement, window vs aggregate choice, join type from the business need, and SARGable rewrites. Sketch the grain of the result before writing anything.
blocks.code:
-- mental checklist per SQL question:
-- [ ] what grain should each output row be?
-- [ ] row filter (WHERE) or group filter (HAVING)?
-- [ ] window (keep rows) or aggregate (collapse rows)?
-- [ ] which join keeps the required rows?

blocks.body: The exam loves: p-value misreadings, CI misreadings (procedure vs probability), correlation-is-not-causation, peeking, and SRM. If an option says 'prove', it is wrong - statistics quantifies uncertainty, never proves.
blocks.code:
p-value  = P(data | null), not P(null | data)
95% CI    = long-run capture rate, not '95% chance'
R-squared = explained variance, not causation
peeking   = inflated false positives, always

blocks.body: Hiring managers skim for: an end-to-end SQL + dashboard project, a cleaning/EDA notebook with a real cleaning log, an A/B test write-up with power analysis, and one dbt/SQL modeling project with tests.

project 2: messy CSV -> cleaning log -> EDA notebook
project 3: experiment design -> sample size -> results + SRM check
project 4: staging -> mart dbt-style models with data tests

blocks.body: Percent change = (new - old) / old. Percentage points = simple difference of two percentages.
blocks.code:
pct_change = (new-old)/old
ratio a:b -> a/b

blocks.body: Logarithm undoes exponentiation. Log scales turn exponential curves into straight lines.
Sigma adds a sequence. Mean is the sum divided by count — the bridge to SQL AVG().
blocks.code:
mean = (1/n) * SUM(x_i)
SUM(a+b) = SUM(a) + SUM(b)

blocks.body: Variance = average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation = its square root, in original units.
blocks.code:
var = SUM((x - mean)^2) / n
std = sqrt(var)

blocks.body: Conditional probability P(A|B); Bayes flips it using base rates.
blocks.code: P(A|B) = P(B|A)*P(A) / P(B)

blocks.body: Simple regression fits the line minimizing squared errors; coefficients are slopes.
blocks.code: y = a + b*x   (b = rise/run)

answerBank.q: Walk me through how you would take a vague stakeholder request like 'sales are down, figure it out' and turn it into analysis.
answerBank.a: First I pin down the decision: what will they do differently based on the answer, and by when. Then I get the metric definition in writing - 'sales' could be revenue, units, or orders - plus the time window and comparison baseline. Only then do I decompose: is it a numerator problem (fewer orders), a denominator problem (returns, refunds), or a mix effect (segment shift)? I validate the data before presenting, lead with the bottom line, and bring one recommended next step, not just charts.

answerBank.q: How do you design an A/B test so the result is trustworthy?
answerBank.a: I start from the minimum detectable effect - the smallest lift worth acting on - and compute sample size for 80% power at alpha 0.05 before launch. I pre-register the primary metric, the fixed horizon, and the decision rule, and I put a day-1 SRM check on the traffic split so bucketing bugs get caught immediately. During the run nobody peeks at p-values to make decisions; at the horizon I report the effect size with a confidence interval, not just significance, and I segment by time to check for novelty effects.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a time a dashboard or report misled someone. What did you do?
answerBank.a: An executive once read a churn spike as a crisis, but the denominator had dipped during a plan migration - the rate moved while actual churn was flat. In the meeting I validated the observation, then decomposed the rate live into numerator and denominator series so the artifact was visible. Afterward I annotated the dashboard at the migration date and added a visible formula definition. The structural lesson: every rate on a dashboard needs its definition and known caveats displayed where the misreading happens.

answerBank.q: How do you decide between a star and snowflake schema, and how do you handle changing dimensions?
answerBank.a: I default to a star schema: one fact table at a clearly stated grain joined to denormalized dimensions, because it minimizes joins and matches how BI tools query. I only snowflake when there is a concrete storage or consistency reason, since modern columnar warehouses make the savings marginal. For changing attributes I use SCD Type 2 - a new versioned dimension row with effective dates - so historical facts keep their historical context, and I reserve Type 1 overwrites for true corrections like typos.

answerBank.q: Your pipeline failed at 6 AM and the executive report is due at 8 AM. Walk me through your response.
answerBank.a: First ten minutes: read the logs to find the failing step, then check row counts at each stage to isolate source delay versus transform error versus load failure - no blind reruns. Then I communicate early with three facts: what broke in plain language, the ETA, and whether the data will be complete or labeled partial when it lands. After recovery I do a blameless postmortem and push validation left: a data contract and freshness tests on the source feed so the next bad value pages us at ingestion instead of breaking the run.

answerBank.q: What separates a senior data analyst from a junior one, in your view?
answerBank.a: Juniors answer the question asked; seniors make sure it is the right question by tying every request to a decision and a written metric definition. Seniors validate before presenting, communicate uncertainty honestly - effect sizes with intervals, not just p-values - and build durable assets: tested models, documented definitions, annotated dashboards. And when the data says the championed initiative failed, a senior delivers that news early, plainly, and with evidence, because credibility is the whole job.
